en: The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Cultivation and Realization of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata’s Great Uṣṇīṣa and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas, Scroll One;
also known as the Scripture of the Great Maṇḍala of Nālandā in Central India, excerpted for separate circulation from the Abhiṣeka Section.

In the first year of the Shénlóng era of the Great Táng, the year of Yǐsī (4849), on the twenty-third day of the fifth month, the day of Xīnchōu, the Indian Śramaṇa Prajñāmitra translated [this text] at the Zhìzhì Dàochǎng in Guǎngzhōu. It was orally transmitted by the Bodhisattva-śrāmaṇera Fáng Róng, formerly the Grand Master of Remonstrance, concurrently Minister of the Department of State Affairs and Vice-President of the Secretariat, of the Qīnghé clan. The Śramaṇa Mīqiáshìjiā of the Wúzhāng Kingdom served as the interpreter. Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Jētavana Monastery in the city of Śrāvastī, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus, all of whom were great Arhats free from outflows.

The Buddha’s disciples abide in the maintenance of the Dharma, skillfully transcending all realms of existence; they are able to perfect majestic deportment within the lands, and having received the Buddha’s entrustment as he turns the wheel of the Dharma, they purify the *vinaya* and establish a grand model for the three worlds. With infinite responsive bodies, they deliver sentient beings, rescuing those of the future and enabling them to transcend all worldly entanglements.
Their names were:
the Greatly Wise Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākauṣṭhila, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Subhūti, Upāliśata, and others who served as the leaders.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable Pratyekabuddhas, both those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and those at the stage of initial resolve, who came together to the Buddha’s presence. At this time, the bhikṣus were observing the *pravāraṇā* ceremony at the end of the summer retreat;
Bodhisattvas from the ten directions consulted him to resolve their doubts, reverently honoring his compassionate yet majestic authority as they sought its profound meaning.

Thereupon, the Tathāgata arranged his seat and sat in peaceful repose, proclaiming the profound and abstruse teachings to those in the assembly. The pure multitude at the Dharma feast attained what they had never experienced before; the kalaviṅka-like celestial voice reached throughout the worlds of the ten directions, and Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges gathered at the site of enlightenment, with Mañjuśrī as their leader.

At that time, King Prasenajit was observing a fast on the anniversary of his father’s death; he invited the Buddha to the palace and personally went out to welcome the Tathāgata. He prepared an extensive array of rare delicacies and unsurpassed, exquisite flavors, and also personally extended invitations to the great Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, there were elders and lay devotees within the city who simultaneously provided a meal for the Sangha, awaiting the Buddha’s arrival to respond to their offerings.
The Buddha commanded Mañjuśrī to lead the bodhisattvas and arhats to attend to the various hosts of the *śrāddha* feasts;

however, Ānanda alone had previously accepted a separate invitation and, having traveled far and not yet returned, was unable to join the assembly in due order. Since he had neither a senior elder (*sthavira*) nor a preceptor (*ācārya*), he returned alone from the road, and on that day there was no offering for him.

At that moment, Ānanda took up his alms bowl and went through the city he was visiting, begging from house to house in order. From the very beginning, he sought out the final donor to serve as the host for his midday meal; regardless of whether they were pure or impure, of noble Kṣatriya lineage or of the Caṇḍāla caste, he practiced universal compassion, making no distinction between the lowly and the humble, resolving to bring to full completion the immeasurable merit of all sentient beings.
Ānanda already knew that the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, had rebuked Subhūti and Mahākāśyapa for being Arhats whose minds were not impartial;
he now reverently admired how the Tathāgata had expounded the unobstructed Dharma to deliver all those who harbored doubts and slander.
Passing through the city moat, he walked slowly toward the city gate, maintaining a solemn and dignified demeanor and observing the rules of pure discipline with reverence.

At that time, as Ānanda was on his almsround, he passed by a brothel where he encountered the great sorceress Matangi, who used the *Sāvikāra-pūrvabrahmadeva-mantra* to draw him into her bedchamber; there, she touched his body with lustful intent, nearly destroying his precept-body.
The Tathāgata, knowing that he had been subjected to the arts of seduction, returned immediately after the meal;
the king, along with his ministers, elders, and householders, all came to follow the Buddha, wishing to hear the essentials of the Dharma.

At that time, the World-Honored One emitted from the crown of his head a hundred-jeweled light of fearlessness. From within this light, thousand-petaled jeweled lotuses emerged, upon which transformation Buddhas sat cross-legged and proclaimed divine mantras. He commanded Mañjuśrī to take these mantras and go forth to protect [the world], so that evil spells might be extinguished. He then exhorted Ānanda and the daughter of Matanga to return to the presence of the Buddha.

Seeing the Buddha, Ānanda prostrated himself and wept with grief, lamenting that from time immemorial he had been devoted solely to extensive learning without fully perfecting the power of the Way. He earnestly entreated the Tathāgatas of the ten directions for the initial expedient means by which they attained the wondrous *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna* of Bodhi.

At that time, there were also Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, as well as great Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas from the ten directions, all of whom wished to hear [the teaching] with joy; they withdrew to their seats and remained silent to receive the holy instructions.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"You and I share the same vital breath, our affection equal to that of natural kin. When you first resolved to seek enlightenment, what superior signs did you perceive within my Dharma that caused you to suddenly renounce the profound and heavy bonds of worldly love?"
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
“I have seen the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks, supremely wonderful and peerless; his physical form is translucent, like lapis lazuli.
I have constantly reflected upon this:”
"This mark is not produced by the craving of desire. Why is this?
The vapor of desire is coarse and turbid;
it is a mixture of putrid odors and sexual union, a chaotic jumble of pus and blood, incapable of giving rise to the supreme, pure, wondrously bright mass of purple-gold light."
"It is for this reason that I have yearned with thirsting longing to follow the Buddha and shave my head.
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, Ānanda!"

"You all should know that all sentient beings, from time immemorial, have continued in the cycle of birth and death because they do not understand the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of pure and luminous nature. By employing various false thoughts, and because these thoughts are not true, there is this revolving wheel of existence."
If you now wish to investigate the true nature of the luminous clarity of unsurpassed Bodhi, you should respond to my questions with a straightforward mind.

Because the Tathāgatas of the ten directions share one and the same path, they all rely on a straightforward mind to transcend birth and death. Since their minds and words are straightforward, from the beginning stages through to the final positions, there is never any trace of deviousness or circuitousness along the way.
Ānanda! I now ask you:
when you first resolved your mind upon the thirty-two marks of a Tathāgata, what did you see, and who was it that you took delight in?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
It is this craving and delight that employs my mind and eyes."
"Because I beheld the sublime marks of the Tathāgata with my own eyes and my heart gave rise to love and joy, I resolved to abandon birth and death.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"What you have said is true; such love and joy stem from the eye and the mind. If you do not know where the eye and the mind reside, you will be unable to subdue the afflictions of the world."
It is like a king who, when invaded by bandits, dispatches troops to eliminate them; those troops must first know where the bandits are located.
It is your mind and eyes that cause you to wander in saṃsāra—this is the fault.
"I now ask you: where, precisely, do this mind and these eyes currently reside?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One!"
All ten classes of ordinary beings in the world alike maintain that the conscious mind resides within the body;

even when observing the Tathāgata’s blue-lotus eyes, they see them as being upon the Buddha’s face. Now, when I observe these four types of sensory objects of the physical eye-organ, I find they are merely upon my own face; thus, this conscious mind truly resides within the body.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"You are now sitting here in the Tathāgata’s lecture hall; look at where the Jeta Grove is now.
[Ānanda replied: "World-Honored One!"
"This great multi-storied pavilion and pure lecture hall is within the Anāthapiṇḍika Garden; the Jeta Grove is actually outside the hall. "Ānanda!
What did you first see within the hall just now?"
“World-Honored One!
While I was in the hall, I first saw the Tathāgata, then observed the great assembly; only after looking out in this manner did my gaze fall upon the grove.
“Ānanda! [the Buddha said.]
“By what means do you behold this grove?
“World-Honored One!
Because the doors and windows of this great lecture hall are wide open, I am able to gaze afar from within the hall.”
At that time, the World-Honored One, amidst the great assembly, extended his golden arm and stroked Ānanda’s crown, announcing to Ānanda and the entire multitude:

"There is a samādhi called the Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama King, which fully encompasses the myriad practices and is the wondrously adorned path through which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions transcend in a single gate."
"Listen attentively now!
Ānanda prostrated himself and humbly accepted the compassionate instruction.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"As you have said, while your body is in the lecture hall, with doors and windows wide open so that one can gaze afar at the groves and gardens, there are also sentient beings within this hall who do not see the Tathāgata but only see what is outside the hall."
Ānanda replied, “World-Honored One!
It is impossible that one who is inside the hall and does not see the Tathāgata could see the groves and springs; such a thing cannot be.”
“Ānanda! You are also like this!
Your mind is spiritually lucid and understands all things clearly.”
If this mind that you clearly perceive before you were actually within your body, then you ought first to be aware of your internal body.

Is there any sentient being who first sees what is inside their body and only afterwards observes external objects? Even if you cannot see the heart, liver, spleen, or stomach, you certainly ought to be clearly aware of the growth of nails, the lengthening of hair, the shifting of tendons, and the throbbing of veins; how is it that you do not know these things?
Since you certainly do not know what is within, how can you know what is without?
Therefore, you should understand that your statement—
“the mind that perceives and knows dwells within the body”— is incorrect.
"Such a thing is impossible.
Ānanda bowed his head to the ground and said to the Buddha:
"Having heard such a Dharma-sound from the Tathāgata, I have realized that my mind truly resides outside my body."

Why is this so? It is like a lamp burning within a room: that lamp must first illuminate the interior of the room, and only thereafter reach the door and the courtyard. All sentient beings do not see within their own bodies but see only outside their bodies, just as a lamp situated outside a room cannot illuminate its interior.
"If this meaning is clarified, there will surely be no further confusion; by attaining the Buddha’s definitive teaching, will we not be free from delusion?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"These bhikṣus have just now come from the city of Śrāvastī with me, begging for alms-food and returning to the Jeta Grove. I have already finished my meal. Do you observe that when one bhikṣu eats, all the others are satiated?"
Ānanda replied,
“No, World-Honored One.”
"Why is this? Although these bhikṣus are all arhats, their physical bodies and life spans differ; how could one person alone cause the multitude to be satiated?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"If your mind that perceives, knows, and sees were truly outside the body, then since the body and mind would exist externally to one another and be unrelated, the body could not perceive what the mind knows, and the mind could not know what is perceived at the boundaries of the body."
"I now show you my hand of tūla-cotton; when you see it with your eyes, does your mind not make a conceptual distinction?
Ānanda replied, "It is so, World-Honored One!"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If they are mutually perceived, how could they be external?
Therefore, you should understand that what you said—"
"That the mind which is capable of awakening and knowing dwells outside the body—
this is impossible.
Ānanda said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has said, because one does not perceive the internal, it does not abide within the body;
yet because the body and mind know one another and are not separate from each other, it does not exist outside the body.”
"I have now reflected and know that it is located in one place.
The Buddha asked,
"Where is that place now?"

Ānanda said: "This consciousness that knows is unable to know the interior yet is able to see the exterior. As I reflect upon it, it must be hidden within the faculties. It is like someone taking a crystal bowl and placing it over both eyes; although something covers them, there is no obstruction. That faculty follows what is seen and immediately discriminates it. Thus, I realize that the mind capable of knowing does not see the interior because it resides within the faculties, while its clear vision of the exterior without obstruction is due to its being hidden inside the faculties."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"According to what you say, that which is hidden within the faculties is like lapis lazuli.
Suppose that person were to cover their eyes with a lapis lazuli lens; would they see the mountains and rivers, yet also see the lapis lazuli?"
"So it is, World-Honored One!
This person would have lapis lazuli covering their eyes, yet they would truly see the lapis lazuli.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If your mind were joined with the eyes as if by lapis lazuli, you should see the mountains and rivers; why then do you not see your own eyes?
If you could see your own eyes, the eye would be identical to its objects, and thus the principle of 'following' (the objects) could not be established.
If you cannot see them, how can you say that this cognizing mind lies hidden within the faculties like lapis lazuli joined [to them]?"
Therefore, you should know that your statement—
"the mind that is capable of cognition and awareness lies latent within the sense organs like glass joined together"— is impossible.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I have now further reflected in this way:”
"This body of a sentient being has its internal organs within and its apertures on the outside; where there are organs, there is darkness, and where there are apertures, there is light.
Now, as I face the Buddha, when I open my eyes and see light, it is called "seeing the outside"; when I close my eyes and see darkness, it is called "seeing the inside. What is the meaning of this?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"When you close your eyes and perceive darkness, does this realm of darkness face the eye,
or does it not face the eye?"
If it were in opposition to the eye, how could darkness in front of the eyes constitute the "internal"?
If it did constitute the internal, then when one stays in a dark room without the sun, moon, or lamps, would this entire darkness within the room be your own stomach?
If it does not face [the object], how can it constitute seeing?

If you claim that internal seeing is established by being separated from external seeing, then when one closes the eyes and sees darkness, this is called "seeing within the body"; yet when one opens the eyes and sees light, why does one not see one's own face?
If you do not see the face, internal perception cannot be established.
If seeing the face were established, then this cognizing mind and the eye faculty would be located in empty space; how could they be said to be within?
If it were in empty space, it would not be your own body.

In that case, the Tathāgata seeing your face now would also be your body; yet your eyes already perceive this, so your body should not be conscious of it. If you insist that both body and eyes are conscious and must therefore have two separate cognitions, then your single body would become two Buddhas.
Therefore, you should know that your statement—
"seeing darkness is called seeing the internal"— is untenable.
Ānanda said:
"I have often heard the Buddha instruct the fourfold assembly:
'Because the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise;'"
"Because phenomena arise, various kinds of mind are produced.

As I now contemplate, I consider that the very essence of this contemplation is my own mind-nature; wherever it encounters conditions, the mind arises accordingly, yet it does not exist within, without, or in between these three locations.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "As for what you have just said—

that 'various states of mind arise because of dharmas, and wherever they encounter conditions, the mind follows and exists'— if this mind has no substance, then there would be nothing with which it could encounter."
If that which lacks substance could still undergo conjunction, then the nineteen elements would conjoin with the seven objects.
This principle is not so!
If they possess substance, then as when you prick your own body with your hand, does the mind that perceives this emerge from within?
Does it enter from the outside?
Or does it emerge from within and then see the body?
If it were to come from the outside, one should first see its face.
Ānanda said: "To say that 'seeing' is this eye, while the mind knows it is not the eye, would mean that seeing is not its true nature.
The Buddha said:
"If the eye were able to see, would you be able to see while inside a room?
Furthermore, since those who have already died still possess eyes, they should all be able to see objects.
If they could see objects, how could they be called dead?"
Ānanda! Furthermore,
if this mind of yours that perceives and knows must have a substance,
does it consist of a single substance or many substances?
Now, as for this [consciousness] within your body, does it pervade the entire body, or does it not pervade the entire body?
If it were a single entity, then when you prick one limb with your hand, the other four limbs should feel it; if they all feel it, then the location of the prick would be nowhere in particular.
If you possess a single entity, then your own oneness cannot be established.
If you possess many entities, then you would become many people.
Which entity, then, constitutes you?
If it pervades the entire body, it would be the same as what was previously pressed.
If it does not pervade, then when you touch your head, you are also touching your feet; while the head has sensation, the feet should be without consciousness.
"Now you are not so; therefore, you should know that it is impossible for the mind to exist wherever it happens to meet [an object].
Ānanda said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One!"
I have also heard that when the World-Honored One was discussing the true nature of reality with Mañjuśrī and other such Dharma princes, the Buddha likewise said:
"The mind is neither within nor without."
"As I reflect upon this, there is nothing seen within and no mutual cognition between the internal and external. Because there is no cognition within, it cannot be established as being 'inside';
that the body and mind cognize one another as being 'outside' is likewise illogical."
"Now, because you know each other and yet do not see within, you must be in between.
The Buddha said, "As for what you call 'in between,' that which is in between cannot be deluded; it must have a specific location."
Now, as you investigate this "middle," where does the middle reside?
Does it reside in the location,
or does it reside in the body?
If it resides in the body, does it reside at the periphery rather than in the center? If it were in the center, it would be the same as being internal.
If it resides in a location, is that location something that can be indicated, or is it something that cannot be indicated?
The unmanifest (avijñapti) is likewise non-existent; as for the manifest (vijñapti), it lacks fixedness. Why is this?
For example, when a person uses a manifest action to indicate the center, from the perspective of the east it becomes the west, and from the perspective of the south it becomes the north.
"Since the substance of the representation is already confused, the mind ought to be disordered as well.
Ānanda said, "What I have described is neither of these two kinds."
As the World-Honored One has said:
"With the eye and forms as conditions, eye-consciousness arises.
The eye possesses discrimination, while the object of form is devoid of cognition; when consciousness arises between them, it is the mind that resides therein.
The Buddha said:
"If your mind were located between the sense organs and their objects, would this essence of the mind encompass both,
or would it not encompass both?"

If one were to combine both [the knower and the known], the substance of things would become confused; since the object is not the knowing substance, these two would stand as opposing entities—how could this be the Middle?
If the combination of the two is not achieved, then that which is neither knowing nor non-knowing lacks any essential nature; what, then, would be the characteristic of the Middle?
"Therefore, you should know that it would be impossible for this to occur in the interim.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
In the past, I saw the Buddha together with his four great disciples—Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Subhūti, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, and Śāriputra—turning the wheel of the Dharma. He constantly said:
"The nature of the mind that perceives and discriminates exists neither within, nor without, nor in between; it has no location at all."
"Non-attachment to all things is called the mind.
"In that case, is non-attachment to me called the mind?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"You say that the nature of the mind, as well as perception and discrimination, are both non-existent; yet, all things in the world—whether in space, on water, on land, or in flight—all such objects and phenomena are called 'all.'"
If you do not cling, does this non-clinging exist or not?
If it does not exist, it would be like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit; how then could there be non-clinging?

If it exists, that which does not cling cannot be called non-existent. That which lacks characteristics is non-existent, whereas that which is not non-existent possesses characteristics. If characteristics exist, then there is existence; how then can there be non-attachment?
"Therefore, you should know that it is impossible for one who is attached to anything to possess the awakened mind that knows all things as nameless.

At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat amidst the great assembly; he bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "I am the youngest brother of the Tathāgata.

Having received the Buddha’s compassionate love, even though I have now left the household life, I still rely upon his affectionate indulgence. Consequently, although I have heard much, I have not yet attained the state beyond outflows (*anāsrava*). I was unable to subdue the *Sāvitrī* spell and was turned by it, falling into a house of prostitution. This must have been because I did not know where the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) points."

"We only pray that the World-Honored One, out of great compassion and pity, will reveal to us the path of *śamatha*, so that all those of the icchantika class may destroy their Mleccha [barbaric] nature.
Having spoken these words, they prostrated themselves, casting their five limbs upon the ground.
The great assembly likewise leaned forward in eager anticipation, longing to hear his instructions.

At that time, the World-Honored One emitted various rays of light from the gate of his face; these lights shone brilliantly like hundreds of thousands of suns, causing the entire Buddha-world to tremble in six ways. Thus, lands as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions were revealed all at once.

Through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, all these worlds were merged into a single realm, and all the great Bodhisattvas within those worlds remained in their respective lands, joining their palms in reverent attention.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"All sentient beings, from time immemorial, have been subject to various inversions. Their karmic seeds naturally cluster like the *akṣa* fruit; thus, practitioners are unable to attain unexcelled Bodhi, and instead may only become Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, or even become non-Buddhists, celestial beings, Māras, or their followers. All this arises from not knowing the two kinds of fundamental roots and practicing in a confused manner—like boiling sand in the hope of making a fine meal, which, even after passing through kalpas as numerous as dust motes, can never be achieved."
"What are these two kinds, Ānanda?
The first is the root of birth and death from time immemorial, which is that攀緣心 (pān-yuán-xīn— the mind that clings to external objects) you and all sentient beings now take as your own nature."

Second is the fundamentally pure essence of bodhi and nirvana from time immemorial; this is precisely your present consciousness-essence, the original luminosity that can give rise to all conditions, yet remains ungrasped by those very conditions.

Because all sentient beings have neglected this fundamental illumination, they wander through the various realms of existence despite acting throughout their entire lives without realizing it; thus, they enter these destinies in vain. "Ānanda!
If you now wish to know the path of śamatha and desire to transcend birth and death, I shall question you once more."
At that moment, the Tathāgata raised his golden arm and bent his five fingers, saying to Ānanda:
"Do you see this now?
Ānanda replied:
“I see it.
The Buddha asked, “What do you see?”
Ānanda said,
"I saw the Tathāgata raise his arm and bend his fingers into a radiant fist, which illuminated my heart and eyes.
The Buddha said:
“Whom did you see? Ānanda replied,
“I and the great assembly all saw with our own eyes.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Answer me now.
The Tathāgata has formed a radiant fist with his fingers to illuminate your eyes and mind; your eyes are able to see it."
"What do you take to be the mind that shines when my fist is held up?

Ānanda replied, "Since the Tathāgata has now questioned me regarding the location of the mind, I have used my mind to investigate and pursue it; that which is capable of such investigation, I shall take to be the mind."
The Buddha said, "Ho! Ānanda!"
"This is not your mind.
Ānanda, startled, withdrew from his seat, joined his palms, stood up, and addressed the Buddha:
"This is not my mind; what should it be called?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This is the delusive perception of the false characteristics of external objects that confuses your true nature.
Because from time immemorial until this present life you have mistaken a thief for your son, you have lost your original constancy and thus undergo the cycle of rebirth."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

As the beloved younger brother of our Buddha, it was because my heart loved the Buddha that he caused me to leave the household life. Why should my mind be concerned with making offerings only to the Tathāgata? Even as I travel through lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, serving all Buddhas and spiritual friends, and as I give rise to great courage and perform all manner of difficult practices, I do so entirely with this same mind.”
"Even if one were to slander the Dharma and forever lose their roots of goodness, it would still be because of this mind.
If this manifestation were not the mind, I would be without a mind, identical to wood or earth; apart from this awareness, there is nothing else."
Why does the Tathāgata say that this is not the mind?

I am truly alarmed and terrified, and there is no one among this great assembly who is not filled with doubt; we pray only that you will bestow your great compassion and reveal the truth to those who have not yet awakened!

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to cause Ānanda and the great assembly to enter the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), rubbed the crown of Ānanda’s head while seated upon the lion throne and addressed him, saying:
“The Tathāgata has always taught that all dharmas that arise are manifested solely by the mind; the essence of all causes and effects, as well as the atoms of the world, is formed by the mind.”

Ānanda! If all that exists within all worlds—even down to blades of grass, leaves, and strands of thread—when one traces their origins, they all possess a substantial nature; even empty space has its name and appearance. How much more so for the pure, wondrously pure, and luminous mind-nature, which is the essence of all minds—how could it itself lack a substance?

If you maintain that the nature of discernment and deliberation—which you grasp with parsimony—must necessarily be the mind, then this mind should exist as a distinct, complete entity apart from all colors, fragrances, tastes, and tangibles, as well as all sensory objects and activities. Just as you now listen to my teaching, this [listening] involves discrimination based on sound; even if you were to extinguish all seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, and internally maintain a state of profound stillness, it would still be a mere shadow of discrimination regarding mental objects (*dharmaviṣaya*). I am not commanding you to insist that this is not the mind; rather, you must examine the mind minutely: if there is a nature of discrimination that exists apart from the preceding sense-objects, then that is truly your mind.

If the nature of discrimination lacks substance because it is devoid of objects, then these objects are merely shadows of mental discrimination. When objects are not permanent and undergo transformation and extinction, this mind would become like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit; thus, your Dharma-body would be subject to annihilation. Who then could cultivate and realize the patience of non-arising?
At that moment, Ānanda and the great assembly were silent and overcome with despondency.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda:

"All practitioners in the world who have attained the nine successive concentrations in the present life yet fail to achieve the exhaustion of outflows and become Arhats, do so because they cling to these deluded thoughts of birth and death, mistaking them for reality."
"Therefore, although you have now acquired much learning, you have not attained the fruit of sainthood.
Having heard this, Ānanda wept again with deep sorrow; prostrating himself on the ground, kneeling with palms joined, he addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Since I followed the Buddha to leave the household life, I have relied upon the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, constantly thinking to myself that there was no need for me to practice. I presumed that the Tathāgata would bestow samādhi upon me, unaware that body and mind can never substitute for one another. I have lost my original mind; though I have left home in body, my mind has not entered the Way. It is like a destitute son who abandons his father and flees; only today do I realize that although I have much learning, if I do not practice, it is equal to having heard nothing at all—like a person speaking of food who can never be satisfied by the talk alone."
“World-Honored One!
We are now entangled by the two obstacles precisely because we do not know the nature of the mind, which is quiescent and eternal.
We only pray that the Tathāgata, out of compassion for us who are destitute and exposed, will manifest the wondrously luminous mind and open our eye of the Way.”

Immediately, the Tathāgata emitted a precious light from the *svastika* on his chest; this light was brilliant and radiant, possessing hundreds of thousands of colors, which simultaneously pervaded Buddha-worlds as numerous as the motes of dust in the ten directions. It completely drenched the crowns of all the Tathāgatas in all the precious lands throughout the ten directions, and then returned to Ānanda and the great assembly.
He addressed Ānanda, saying:

"I now establish for you the Great Dharma Banner, so as to enable all sentient beings throughout the ten directions to obtain the wondrous, subtle, and secret nature of pure and luminous mind, and to attain the eye of purity."
Ānanda! You previously answered me that you saw the light of my fist; from what cause does this light of the fist arise?
How is it formed into a fist, and by whom do you see it?
Ānanda said:

"Because the Buddha’s entire body is made of Jāmbūnada gold, blazing like a mountain of jewels, and because he is born of purity, he possesses radiance; yet when I actually observe with my own eyes his five fingers at their tips bent and clenched as he shows them to people, there is indeed the appearance of a fist."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“Tathāgata now speaks these true words to you: those who possess wisdom must rely upon parables to attain awakening. Ānanda!
For example, my fist: if there were no hand of mine, my fist would not be formed;
if there were no eye of yours, your seeing would not be formed.
Applying the principle of my fist as an analogy for your faculty of sight, is the meaning not the same?
Ānanda said:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
Since there is no ‘my eye,’ ‘my seeing’ cannot be established; taking my visual faculty as an analogy for the Tathāgata’s fist, the principle and the facts are analogous.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"What you say regarding their similarity is not correct. Why is this so?
Just as a person without hands has no fist because it is ultimately extinguished,
so too, that which lacks eyes does not mean there is a total absence of seeing. Why is this so?
"You should try asking a blind person on the road:
'What do you see?
Those blind people will surely answer you."
"I now see only darkness before my eyes; there is nothing else for me to behold.
Judging by this principle, the external objects themselves are dark; what deficiency could there be in the faculty of vision?
Ānanda said, "The blind see only darkness before their eyes; how can this constitute seeing?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“Is there a difference between the darkness perceived by those who are blind and sightless, and the darkness experienced by one with sight while staying in a dark room?
Or is there no difference?
“It is so, World-Honored One!”
"The person in this darkness and that group of blind men—there is no difference whatsoever when comparing these two types of blackness. "Ānanda!

If a person who has no eyes sees only the blackness before them, and suddenly regains the light of their eyes so as to see various forms within the external objects before them, this is called 'seeing with the eyes'."

That person in the darkness sees only what is black before them; when they suddenly obtain the light of a lamp, they likewise see various forms within those same external objects. This should be called "seeing by the lamp.
If it were seeing by the lamp, then since the lamp possesses the capacity for seeing, it would no longer be called a "lamp"; furthermore, if it is the lamp that observes, how does it concern you?
Therefore, you should know that it is the lamp that can reveal color.
Likewise, the one who sees is the eye and not the lamp; the eye can reveal color. In this same way, the nature of seeing is the mind and not the eye.

Although Ānanda had heard these words, he and the great assembly remained silent with their mouths, yet their minds were not yet enlightened; still hoping for the compassionate voice of the Tathāgata to provide further instruction, they joined their palms, purified their hearts, and waited expectantly for the Buddha’s merciful teaching.
At that time, the World-Honored One extended his hand, which was marked by a web of fine, cotton-like light, and opened his five fingers as he instructed Ānanda and the great assembly:
"When I first attained the Way in the Deer Park, I spoke to Ājñātakauṇḍinya, the five bhikṣus, and you fourfold assembly, saying:
'That all sentient beings fail to achieve Bodhi and Arhatship is entirely due to being misled by adventitious afflictions.'"
"By what means did you all attain awakening at that time, such that you have now achieved the fruit of sainthood?
At that moment, Kauṇḍinya rose and addressed the Buddha:
"I am now the eldest among this great assembly and alone have earned the name 'The Liberated. It was by awakening to the two characters 'guest' and 'dust' that I attained the fruit."
World-Honored One!
It is like a traveler who stays at an inn, either to lodge or to eat; once the tasks of lodging and eating are finished, he packs his bags for the road ahead and has no leisure to remain.
If he were the actual owner of the house, he would have nowhere else to go.
Reflecting thus, that which does not abide is called a guest, and that which abides is called the host; for the meaning of "guest" is precisely that which does not abide.

Furthermore, it is like when after a fresh clearing, the bright sun rises in the sky and its light enters through a crack, revealing the various forms of dust within the air; while the substance of the dust flickers and moves, empty space remains utterly still.
Reflecting thus, he thought: "Stillness and tranquility are called 'emptiness,' while agitation is called 'dust'; for that which is agitated is the very meaning of 'dust.
The Buddha said: "It is so."
At that moment, the Tathāgata, amidst the great assembly, bent his five fingers; having bent them, he opened them again; having opened them, he bent them once more. He then said to Ānanda:
"What do you see now?"
Ānanda said,
"I saw the Tathāgata’s palms, adorned with the wheels of a hundred jewels, opening and closing amidst the assembly.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“Do you see my hand opening and closing within this assembly? Is it that my hand itself has opening and closing, or is it that you perceive opening and closing?
Ānanda replied:
“World-Honored One!
When the hands of the Jewel-Handed One open and close among the assembly, I see it as the Tathāgata’s own hands opening and closing; it is not that the nature of my vision itself opens and closes.
The Buddha said:
"Who moves and who is still?
Ānanda replied, "The Buddha's hand does not remain still, yet my seeing-nature has no stillness even now; so who could be said to be 'not remaining'?"
The Buddha said, "So it is.

Thereupon, the Tathāgata emitted a single jewel-light from the wheel-mark on his palm, which hovered to Ānanda’s right; immediately, Ānanda turned his head to look to the right. He then emitted another light to Ānanda’s left, and Ānanda likewise turned his head to look to the left.
The Buddha asked Ānanda:
"For what reason is your head shaking today?
Ānanda replied:
“I saw the Tathāgata emit wondrous jewel-light coming from my left and right; therefore, as I looked to the left and right, my head moved of its own accord.
“Ānanda! When you followed the Buddha’s light and moved your head to the left and right, was it your head that moved?”
"Or do you see movement?
"World-Honored One!
It is my head that moves, yet the nature of my seeing has no cessation; who, then, could cause it to shake?"
The Buddha said, "It is so. Thereupon,
the Tathāgata addressed the great assembly:

"Furthermore, if sentient beings designate that which moves as 'dust' and that which does not abide as 'guest,' then consider this: Ānanda, you observe your own head moving back and forth, yet your vision remains unmoving; you observe my hand opening and closing, yet your vision neither expands nor contracts. Why is it that you now take movement to be the body and movement to be the environment? From beginning to end, moment by moment, you give rise to and perish with these states, losing the true nature and acting in delusion. Your fundamental nature and mind have become estranged from reality as you mistake external objects for yourself; thus you revolve within this cycle, bringing about your own continuous wandering."

At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly, having heard the Buddha’s instructions, felt their bodies and minds become tranquil and at ease. They reflected that since beginningless time they had lost their original mind, mistakenly identifying with the deluded discriminations of conditioned objects and shadow-like phenomena. Today, their awakening was like a child who has lost its mother suddenly encountering her again. With palms joined, they prostrated to the Buddha and wished to hear the Tathāgata reveal the true and the false within body and mind, and the nature of the two kinds of luminosity—the arising and ceasing before one's eyes and that which is neither arising nor ceasing.
King Prasenajit rose and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In the past, before I had received the instructions of the Buddhas, I saw Kātyāyana and the son of Vairaṭī, both of whom said:
'After this body dies, it is annihilated; this is called Nirvāṇa.'"
"Although I have encountered the Buddha, I still harbor doubts. How can one manifest and realize this ground where the mind is neither born nor extinguished?
May all those in this great assembly who possess outflows (āsrava) likewise desire to hear this."
The Buddha said to the Great King:
"Your body exists now; I ask you again: is this physical body of yours permanent and indestructible like a vajra?"
"Or will it undergo transformation and decay?
"World-Honored One!
This body of mine will ultimately end in transformation and extinction."
The Buddha said, "Great King!
You have never extinguished [the self]; how then can you know extinction?"
“World-Honored One!

Although this body of mine, subject to impermanence and decay, has not yet perished, I observe that it undergoes transformation and passes away from moment to moment; ever-new and never-abiding, it is like fire turning to ash, gradually wasting away and perishing without ceasing. I am certain that this body must eventually come to total extinction.”
The Buddha said, “So it is, Great King!
Your current age has already reached old age; how does your appearance compare to that of your youth?”
“World-Honored One!

In my youth, my skin and flesh were moist and lustrous; as I grew to maturity, my blood and vital energy were full. Now that I am advanced in years and pressed by decrepitude, my appearance is withered and haggard, my spirit is clouded and dim, my hair is white and my face is wrinkled, and I shall not last much longer. How can I be compared to the time when I was in the full vigor of life?”
The Buddha said,
"Great King!
Your physical appearance should not have decayed so suddenly."
The King said, "World-Honored One!
The transformations of conditioned phenomena shift so subtly that I truly do not perceive them; yet, as cold and heat pass by and flow on, they have gradually reached this point."
Why is this? Although I am twenty years old and thus called young, my appearance has already aged compared to when I was ten;
at thirty, I shall again have declined further than at twenty.
Today I am sixty-two years old;
when I was fifty, I appeared as robust as ever.
World-Honored One!

I observe their subtle shifts; though this decay and falling away occurs within the span of ten years, if I were to reflect upon it with minute attention, would the change be limited to merely one or two cycles of twelve years? In truth, it is a change that occurs year by year;
yet it does not stop at changing by the year—it also transforms month by month.
Not only does it transform by the month, it also migrates day by day.

"Reflecting deeply and observing with discernment, I see that from moment to moment, from thought to thought, there is no staying still; therefore, I know that my body will ultimately undergo transformation and perish.
The Buddha said, "Great King!"
"You see that transformations and changes ceaselessly proceed; you realize and know your own extinction.
At the moment of extinction, do you also know that within your body there is something that does not perish?
King Prasenajit joined his palms and addressed the Buddha:
“I truly do not know!
The Buddha said,
“I shall now show you the nature that is neither born nor extinguished.”
"Great King!
At what age did you first see the waters of the Ganges?
The King replied:
"When I was three years old, my compassionate mother took me to visit the deity Jīvaka, and we passed by this stream.
At that moment, I immediately recognized it as the waters of the Ganges.
The Buddha said:
“Great King!

As you have said, one declines from ten years to twenty, and so on until sixty; as days, months, years, and seasons pass, every moment changes. Thus, when you were three years old and saw this river, what was the water like when you reached the age of thirteen?”
The King said, "Just as when I was three years old, it is exactly the same now; even until this year at sixty-two, there has been no difference.
The Buddha said:

"You now see for yourself that your hair has turned white and your face is wrinkled; your face is certainly more wrinkled than it was in your youth. Now, as you look at this Ganges River, is there any difference between the vision you have now and the vision you had when you looked at this river as a child—any distinction between childhood and old age?"
The king said,
“No, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:

"Great King! Although your face has wrinkled, the nature of this essential faculty of seeing has never wrinkled. That which wrinkles is subject to change; that which does not wrinkle is not subject to change. That which changes undergoes extinction; that which is unchanging is fundamentally without birth or death. How could birth and death affect it? Yet you still cite Makkhali Gosāla and others, claiming that after the death of this body, there is total annihilation."

Upon hearing these words, the King believed that after death one leaves this life to take rebirth; together with the great assembly, he leaped for joy and experienced a state of wonder never before known.
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat, prostrated before the Buddha, joined his palms, knelt for a long time, and addressed the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!"
If these seeing and hearing are necessarily neither arising nor ceasing, why does the World-Honored One say that we have lost our true nature and act in a state of perversion?
We pray that you will arouse compassion to wash away our defilements.
Immediately, the Tathāgata extended his golden arm, pointing downward with his wheel-marked hand, and said to Ānanda:
"Do you now see my *mudrā* hand as upright or inverted?"
Ānanda said,
"The sentient beings of the world consider this to be inverted, yet I do not know who is upright and who is inverted.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If worldly people consider this to be inverted, then what do worldly people take to be upright?
Ānanda replied,
"If the Tathāgata raises his arm, with his hand of *tūla* cotton pointing upward toward the sky, that is called upright."
The Buddha then raised his arm and said to Ānanda:

"If this inverted state were such that head and tail were exchanged, and all people of the world looked at it with double the attention, then you would know that your body and the pure Dharma-body of the Tathāgatas could be compared and illuminated against one another. The body of the Tathāgata is called 'Perfect Universal Knowledge' (Samyak-saṃbuddha), while your bodies are termed 'inverted by nature. As you observe your own body and the Buddha’s body, consider where the name 'inversion' applies—if you call your body inverted, at what point is it designated as such?"

At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly gazed fixedly at the Buddha with unblinking eyes, their minds and bodies so overwhelmed by confusion that they did not know where their own inverted perceptions lay.
The Buddha, giving rise to compassion and pitying Ānanda and the great assembly, emitted a voice like the tide and addressed the entire gathering:
"O sons of good family!
I have always said: "The various conditions of form and mind, as well as all dharmas that serve as objects for the mental factors, are manifested solely by the mind.

Your body and your mind are both things manifested within the wondrously bright, true essence of the wondrous mind. Why, then, do you lose this fundamental, wondrous, perfect, and luminous mind—the precious, brilliant, and wondrous nature—and instead recognize delusion within enlightenment? You take the dark obscurity to be empty space; within the darkness of that emptiness, you bind darkness together to form matter. Intermingling matter with false thoughts, you take these conceptualizations to be a self. With internal agitation from gathering conditions and external flight toward objects, you take this state of confused turmoil to be the nature of the mind.

Once deluded, they take this as their mind and are resolutely confused that it resides within the physical body; they do not know that from the physical body outward to the mountains, rivers, empty space, and the great earth, all are objects within the wondrously luminous true mind.

It is like discarding hundreds of thousands of vast, clear oceans and instead clinging to the substance of a single bubble, declaring that this alone constitutes the entirety of the tide and the full extent of the sea.
You all are people who are doubly lost within delusion; you are no different from one who hangs down their own hand [to help themselves up]. The Tathāgata calls such as you objects of pity.
Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s compassionate rescue and profound instruction, wept and, with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Although I have received the Buddha’s such wondrous voice and awakened to the wondrous, luminous mind—the fundamentally perfect and eternally abiding ground of the heart—I nevertheless perceive the Buddha’s currently spoken Dharma-sounds through my conditioned mind (緣心), which I now respectfully gaze upon; thus, while I have attained this mind, I do not yet dare to recognize it as the fundamental, original ground of the heart.”
"I pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will proclaim his perfect voice to uproot my doubts and lead me back to the Unsurpassed Way.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If you and the others still listen to the Dharma with a conditioned mind, this Dharma is itself a condition and not the attainment of the Dharma-nature."
It is like a person pointing at the moon with their finger to show it to another; that person should look at the moon because of the finger.
If, however, they look only at the finger and take it to be the substance of the moon, this person not only loses sight of the lunar orb, but loses the finger as well.
Why is this? Because they mistake the pointing finger for the bright moon.
Not only do they lose the finger, but they also fail to distinguish between light and darkness.
Why is this? Because if the substance of the finger itself were the nature of the moon’s brightness, then the two natures of light and darkness could not be distinguished.
You are just the same: if you take my voice as I preach the Dharma to be your own mind, then this mind should inherently possess the nature of discrimination even apart from the discriminating sound.

It is like a traveler who stays overnight at an inn; having halted for a brief time, he departs and never remains permanently, yet the person who manages the inn goes nowhere and is called the master of the inn.
This is also like that: if it were truly your mind, it would have no place to go.
What is the nature of non-conceptuality apart from sound?

This is not merely the absence of conceptualizing the mind regarding sound; it is the absence of conceptualizing my own appearance as being free from all physical forms (*rūpa*). In this way, even up to the point where all conceptualization is entirely absent, there is neither form nor emptiness.

The people of Kauśāmbī and others mistake ignorance for the ultimate truth (tattva); yet, apart from the conditions of all phenomena, there is no nature of non-discrimination. Thus, your mind-nature has its own respective place of return—how can it be the master?
Ānanda said:
"If my mind-nature each has something to which it returns, then why does the Tathāgata say that the wondrous, luminous, original mind has nothing to return to?
I pray that you will deign to show compassion and explain this for me."
The Buddha told Ānanda: "Furthermore, you see me;

this seeing is the fundamental source of the clarity of vision. Although this seeing is not the wondrous, ultimate, and clear mind, it is like a second moon—it is not a reflection of the moon. You should listen attentively; I shall now show you the ground where there is nothing to be returned."

Ānanda! This great lecture hall opens wide toward the east; when the sun rises in the sky, there is bright radiance. At midnight, under a dark moon shrouded by clouds and mist, it becomes obscure and dim again. Through the gaps of doors and windows, one perceives openness; within the spaces between walls and buildings, one observes obstruction. In places where distinctions are made, one perceives conditions; throughout the midst of solid emptiness, there is everywhere the nature of space. When the appearance of thick mists arises, turbid dust swirls about; when the sky clears and the vapors subside, one again observes purity.
Ānanda! You have all observed these various manifested forms; I shall now each return them to their original causes.
What are these original causes?
Ānanda! These various transformations return their clarity to the solar disc. Why is this?
There is no day that is not bright; brightness depends on the sun, therefore it returns to the sun;
darkness returns to the dark moon;
penetration returns to doors and windows.
Embracing returns to the walls and eaves;
conditions return to discrimination;
stubborn emptiness returns to the void.
When turbid, it returns to dust;
when clear and bright, it returns to a cloudless sky.
Thus, all that exists within the world does not transcend these categories.
As for the eight kinds of objects you perceive, to whom should the luminous nature of seeing itself return? Why is this?

If it were to return to light, then when it is not light, there would no longer be the perception of darkness; yet, although there are various distinctions such as light and darkness, the seeing itself remains without distinction.
All things that can be returned are naturally not you; as for that which cannot be returned by you, if it is not you, who else could it be?
Thus you should know that your mind is fundamentally wondrous, luminous, and pure.

You have become deluded and distressed, losing your original nature and undergoing the cycle of rebirth, constantly drifting and drowning within birth and death; therefore, the Tathāgata calls you pitiable.
Ānanda said:
“Although I recognize that this nature of seeing has no source from which it returns, how can I know that it is my true nature?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"I now ask you this: although you have not yet attained the purity of the outflows-free state, by receiving the Buddha's spiritual power, you see the first dhyāna without obstruction;
Āniruddha sees Jambudvīpa as if looking at an āmalaka fruit in the palm of his hand;
and the various bodhisattvas see hundreds of thousands of worlds."
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions behold all pure lands as numerous as atoms, leaving nothing unseen;
yet sentient beings, though they possess penetrating vision, cannot see beyond the span of a few inches. Ānanda!

Furthermore, let us observe the palaces where the Four Heavenly Kings dwell; in the space between them, we shall survey all that moves upon water, on land, and through the air. Although there are various forms appearing as dark or bright, none of them are anything other than the obstructions left behind by the discriminations of external objects. You should, within this context, distinguish between self and other.
"Now, I shall lead you to discern among these perceptions:
which is my own substance, and which are external objects? Ānanda!"
Exhaustively trace the source of your vision: from the palaces of the sun and moon, these things are not you;
proceed to the seven golden mountains and observe them thoroughly and completely—though they possess various kinds of light, they too are things and not you;

gradually continue further to observe the rising clouds, the flying birds, the moving winds, the stirring dust, the trees, the mountains and rivers, the grasses and weeds, and all humans and animals—all are things and not you.

Ānanda! Although these various natures of things, whether near or far, differ from one another, they are all equally beheld by your pure visual essence. Thus, while the categories of objects possess their own distinctions, the nature of seeing has no difference; this wondrously brilliant essence is truly your own nature of seeing.
If you see this object, can you also see my seeing?
If you see it in the same way as I do, that may be called "seeing me";
but when I am not seeing, why do you not see the place where I am not seeing?
If you see the "not-seeing," it is naturally not that mark of not-seeing;
if you do not see the ground of my not-seeing, it is naturally not a thing—how could it not be you?

Furthermore, at the present moment when you see an object, if the object also sees you, then their essential natures would become confused and intermingled; consequently, neither you, nor I, nor the rest of the world could be established as stable entities.
Ānanda! If, when you see, it is you who see and not I, then since this nature of seeing is all-pervasive, who else could it be but you?
Why do you doubt your own true nature, claiming that your nature is not real and seeking the truth from me?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If this nature of seeing is necessarily mine and not that of others, then when I and the Tathāgata observed the magnificent treasure-palace of the Four Heavenly Kings and resided in the Sun and Moon Palaces, this seeing was all-encompassing, pervading the entire Sahā world.”
Upon returning to the vihāra, I saw only the monastery; when I entered the hall with a purified mind, I beheld only the eaves and corridors.
World-Honored One!

Since this vision was originally all-pervading throughout the entire realm, yet now that I am inside the room it fills only the room—is it that this vision has contracted from being large to being small?
"Should it be caused to be severed by enclosing it with walls and buildings?
I do not now understand the meaning of this matter; I pray that you will bestow your great compassion and expound it for me.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"All the various activities of the world—whether great or small, internal or external—each belong to their respective objective fields (*viṣaya*); one should not say that the seeing itself expands or contracts.
For example, when a square vessel is present, the space seen within it appears square. I ask you again: Is this square space seen within the vessel definitively square?"
Is it of indefinite shape?
If it were of definite shape, then when placed in a separate round vessel, the space within should not be round;
if it were of indefinite shape, then when contained within a square vessel, there should be no square space.
You say that you do not know where this principle resides; yet, since the nature of a principle is such as this, how could it have a location? Ānanda!

If you wish to cause [the space] to enter into a state devoid of squareness or roundness, you need only remove the squareness of the vessel; the substance of space itself has no directionality. You should not say that there is some further location for the directional characteristics of space that must be removed.
If, as you ask, the visual faculty contracts and becomes small when entering a room, then when looking up at the sun, do you pull the faculty upward until it is level with the face of the sun?
Furthermore, if building walls and houses can obstruct and sever the visual faculty, would there not be traces of continuity when a small hole is pierced through them?
This interpretation is not correct.

Since beginningless time, all sentient beings have been deluded about themselves as being external objects; having lost their original mind, they are turned by objects, and thus within this state they perceive the large as small.

If one can turn objects, then one is identical to the Tathāgata: body and mind are perfectly luminous and unmoving within the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), and upon the tip of a single hair, one is able to universally contain the lands of the ten directions.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If this essence of vision is necessarily my wondrous nature, and if this wondrous nature is now present before me, then this seeing must be my true self. What, then, are my current body and mind?”

Now, you claim that there is a real distinction between body and mind. Yet, in your perception, you cannot differentiate my body; if it were truly my mind that enables me to see, and if the nature of seeing were truly my self while the body were not, how would this differ from what the Tathāgata previously refuted:
"How can an object see me?"
“I only pray that you will, out of great compassion, reveal and awaken those who have not yet understood.
The Buddha told Ānanda: “As for what you have just said:”
The statement "it is present before you" is not ultimately real.
If it were truly before you and you were truly seeing it, then this essence of vision would have a specific location and could be pointed out.

Furthermore, as we now sit together in the Jeta Grove, you may survey the groves, the channels, and the halls; looking upward to the sun and moon and facing forward toward the Ganges, you now, before my lion throne, point with your finger and describe these various phenomena: the shaded area is the grove, the bright area is the sun, the obstructed area is the wall, and the unobstructed area is space. In this way, down to the grasses, trees, and even the finest hairs, though they differ in size, as long as they possess form, there is nothing that cannot be pointed out.
If there must be a vision present before you, you should point it out with your hand and state with certainty:
"This is the vision. Ānanda!
You should know that if empty space were the vision, then since it has already become the vision, what would constitute empty space?
If an object is seeing, then since it is already seeing, what constitutes the "object"?

You should minutely peel away and analyze the myriad phenomena to extract the pure, brilliant, and wondrous source of seeing, and point it out to me so that it may be as clearly understood as those other objects, without any doubt.
Ānanda said:

"Right here in this multi-storied lecture hall, reaching as far as the Ganges River, looking up at the sun and moon, wherever my raised hand points or wherever my gaze falls, everything that is pointed at is an object; there is nothing therein that is the faculty of seeing."
World-Honored One!

As the Buddha has taught, how much less could I—a defiled, novice śrāvaka—even a bodhisattva—extract the essential seeing from before the myriad phenomena, such that it exists as a distinct self-nature apart from all things?
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is!
The Buddha then further addressed Ānanda:
"As you have said, if there were no pure seeing and no distinct intrinsic nature apart from all objects, then that which you point to among these objects would not possess this faculty of seeing."
I now tell you again:

you and the Tathāgata shall sit together in the Jeta Grove and further observe the groves and gardens, even down to the sun and moon and their various distinct forms; yet the essence of seeing will certainly not be found to respond to your pointing.
You must then discern, among all these objects, which one is not the seeing itself?
Ānanda said:
"I have indeed seen this entire Jeta Grove; I do not know what within it is not seen. Why is this?"
If the tree is not seeing, how can one see the tree?
If the tree is itself seeing, how can it still be called a tree?
This applies even to space: if space is not seeing, how can there be space?
"If space itself is seeing, how can it be empty?
Furthermore, as I contemplate these myriad phenomena, I find that even their subtlest manifestations are nothing other than seeing.
The Buddha said:

"So it is, so it is! At this, the great assembly—none of whom were yet those beyond training—heard these words from the Buddha and were utterly bewildered, unable to grasp the beginning or end of their meaning; for a moment they were struck with trepidation, losing their composure.
The Tathāgata, knowing that their spirits were trembling with fear, gave rise to compassion and comforted Ānanda and the great assembly:
"O sons of good family!

The Unsurpassed Dharma King speaks words of truth; as he speaks according to reality, he neither deceives nor errs. This is not the fourfold 'Eternalist' discourse of the sophistry of Maskarī Gośālīputra. You should contemplate this carefully, so as not to dishonor your sorrowful longing."

At that time, the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, out of compassion for the fourfold assembly, rose from his seat amidst the great multitude, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

This great assembly has not yet realized the meaning of the Tathāgata’s clarification regarding the two kinds of refined vision—vision of form and vision of emptiness—and the distinction between what is and what is not that vision.
World-Honored One!
If these preceding objects of perception, such as form and emptiness, were themselves the vision, then there should be something that can be pointed out [as being the vision].
If it were not the seer, there would be nothing perceived.

Yet, because we do not know where this principle ultimately leads, we are filled with fear; it is not that our past roots of goodness are meager or slight. We only pray that the Tathāgata, out of great compassion, will clarify what these various objects and this seeing-essence originally are, so that within them there may be neither "is" nor "is not."
The Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī and the great assembly:

“The Tathāgatas and great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, while abiding in their own samādhi, perceive that the seer, the objects of seeing, and all conceived appearances are like flowers in the sky—fundamentally non-existent.”
This seeing and its objects are fundamentally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of bodhi; how could there be "is" or "is not" within them?
Mañjuśrī! I now ask you: apart from you, Mañjuśrī, is there another Mañjuśrī who is Mañjuśrī?
"Is it that there is no Mañjuśrī?
"It is so, World-Honored One!
I am truly Mañjuśrī, yet there is no such thing as Mañjuśrī."
Why is this? If such were the case, there would be two Mañjuśrīs.
However, it is not that I am without Mañjuśrī today; yet within this, there truly are no dual characteristics of "is" and "is not."
The Buddha said:

"This seeing that is wondrously luminous, along with all empty phenomena and sensory objects, is likewise so. It is originally the wondrously luminous, unsurpassed Bodhi—the pure, perfect, true mind. Through delusion, it becomes form and emptiness, as well as hearing and seeing, like a second moon. Which of these is the real moon?"
Furthermore, who is not the moon? Mañjuśrī!
Since there is but one true moon, within it there is naturally neither "this is the moon" nor "this is not the moon."

Therefore, when you now observe the seeing and the objects, the various manifestations thereof are called deluded thoughts; they cannot, within themselves, determine what is and what is not. It is because of this essence of ultimate truth, the wondrously enlightened and luminous nature, that it enables you to transcend the distinction between "pointing" and "not pointing."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Truly as the Dharma King has said, the awareness-condition pervades the worlds of the ten directions; it is profoundly still and eternally abiding, its nature being neither arising nor ceasing. How does this differ from the ‘Ultimate Darkness’ (Tattva) spoken of by the former Brahmin Śāṇḍilya, and from the ‘True Self’ that exists and pervades the ten directions as taught by the various non-Buddhist schools, such as those who smear themselves with ashes?”

The World-Honored One also once expounded this meaning on Mount Laṅkā for the sake of Mahāmati and others, saying: "Those heterodox teachers always speak of spontaneity (*svabhāva*), whereas I speak of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*); it is not within their sphere of experience."

As I now contemplate this nature of awareness, it is spontaneously neither born nor extinguished, and is far removed from all false delusions and inversions; it seems neither a product of causes and conditions nor something spontaneous. How may I instruct others so that they do not fall among the heterodox, but instead attain the wondrously enlightened and luminous nature of the true mind?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"I have now thus revealed these skillful means and truly informed you; yet you still have not awakened to them, remaining deluded by the notion of spontaneity."
Ānanda! If it were necessarily inherent by nature, one must clearly discern what constitutes the essence of that inherent nature.
Observe now, within this wondrously luminous vision: what do you take to be "self"?
Furthermore, does this vision take light as its own nature,
or darkness as its own nature,
or space as its own nature?
Do you consider obstruction to be the self? Ānanda!
If light were the self, one should not perceive darkness.
If, moreover, emptiness were taken as its own essence, one would not perceive obstructions.
Likewise, if even such characteristics as darkness and so forth were taken as its own essence, then when light appears, the nature [of the eye] would be annihilated; how then could it see the light?
Ānanda said: "If this wondrous nature of seeing is certainly not self-originated, I have now clarified that it is of the nature of causes and conditions;
yet my mind is still not clear. I ask the Tathāgata: how does this meaning accord with the nature of causes and conditions?"
The Buddha said:
"You speak of causes and conditions; I shall question you further.
As you now see together, this seeing-nature is manifest before you. Does this seeing exist because of light? Or does it exist because of darkness?"
Is seeing caused by darkness?
Is seeing caused by space?
Or is seeing caused by obstruction?
Ānanda! If it exists because of light, one should not see darkness;
if it exists because of darkness, one should not see light.
In this way, it extends even to the conditions of emptiness and obstruction, which are identical to light and darkness.
Furthermore, Ānanda!
Does this seeing, moreover, exist because it relies upon light?
Is there seeing conditioned by darkness?
Is there seeing conditioned by space?
Is there seeing conditioned by obstruction?
Ānanda! If existence were dependent upon emptiness, one should not perceive obstruction;
if existence were dependent upon obstruction, one should not perceive emptiness.
Thus it continues until one contemplates light or darkness, which are identical to emptiness and obstruction.

You should know that this wondrously bright, essential awareness is neither caused by conditions nor dependent on them; it is neither spontaneous nor non-spontaneous. It is not "not" and yet not "not," it is not "is" and yet not "is. Detached from all marks, it is itself all phenomena.
How can you now apply your mind to this, attempting to make distinctions through the conceptual names and marks of worldly sophistry?
It is like trying to grasp and rub empty space with your palms; it only serves to increase your own weariness!
"How can you grasp at empty space as you do?
Ānanda said to the Buddha,
"World-Honored One!"
If the nature of wondrous enlightenment is neither cause nor condition,

World-Honored One, why do you constantly teach the bhikṣus that the nature of seeing is endowed with four kinds of conditions— namely, depending on space, depending on light, depending on the mind, and depending on the eyes?
"What is the meaning of this?
The Buddha said, "Ānanda!"
I say that the characteristics of the various causes and conditions in the world are not the ultimate truth.
Ānanda! I shall ask you further.
"Ordinary people of the world say, 'I can see. In what sense is this called seeing?
In what sense is it not seeing? Ānanda said:
“Worldly people see various forms by means of the light of the sun, the moon, and lamps; this they call ‘seeing.
If these three kinds of illumination were absent, they would be unable to see.”
“Ānanda! If the state of being without light is called ‘not seeing,’ then one should not see darkness;
yet if one certainly sees darkness, how can it be said that there is no seeing simply because of the absence of light?”
Ānanda! If one does not see light when it is dark, it is called "not seeing";
now, when one is in the light and does not see the appearance of darkness, it is likewise called "not seeing."
Thus, these two aspects are both termed "not seeing.

Furthermore, if these two aspects mutually cancel each other out, it does not mean that your nature of seeing is temporarily absent therein; rather, you should know that both are actually instances of seeing. How then can they be called "not seeing"?
Therefore, Ānanda!
You should now know that when you see light, the seeing is not the light;
when you see darkness, the seeing is not the darkness.
When seeing emptiness, what is seen is not emptiness;
when seeing obstruction, what is seen is not obstruction—thus the four meanings are established.
You should further know that when seeing the act of seeing, that which is seen is not the seeing itself.
Even seeing is already detached from seeing, for seeing cannot reach it.
Why, then, do you speak again of causes and conditions, spontaneity, and the characteristics of combination?

You śrāvakas are narrow-minded, inferior, and lacking in wisdom; you are unable to penetrate the pure true reality. I now instruct you: you should contemplate this well and must not grow weary on the sublime path to Bodhi.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Although the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has expounded for our sakes the nature of causes and conditions as well as spontaneity, and the characteristics of both harmony and disharmony, our minds have still not yet been opened.”
Now, hearing further that "seeing-seeing is not seeing," my confusion and distress increase all the more.
I prostrate myself, entreating Your vast compassion to bestow the eye of great wisdom and reveal to us the clarity and purity of the awakened mind.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with tears of sorrow and accepted the holy command.

At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for Ānanda and the great assembly, and wishing to expound the path of sublime practice consisting of the various *samādhis* of the Great *Dhāraṇī*, addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Although you possess a powerful memory, it only serves to increase your erudition."
Regarding śamatha, your subtle and secret contemplation has not yet reached full realization.
Listen attentively now; I shall now analyze and reveal it for you, so that all those with outflows in the future may likewise attain the fruit of Bodhi.

Ānanda! All sentient beings transmigrate through the world due to the deluded views of dualistic inversion and discrimination; these arise in their very place, and they revolve according to their respective karma.
What are the two kinds of views?
First, the deluded vision resulting from the individual karma of sentient beings;
second, the deluded vision resulting from the common lot of sentient beings.
"What is meant by 'delusory vision caused by individual karma'? Ānanda!
It is like a person in the world who has a red film over their eye; at night, when they see the light of a lamp, they perceive a separate circular shadow with five overlapping colors."
"What do you think?
Is this circular light manifested by the brightness of this night lamp the color of the lamp, or is it the color of what is seen? Ānanda!"
If this were the color of the lamp, why would those who do not suffer from the eye disease not see it as well? Why is it that only those with the disease perceive this circular shadow?
If it were the color perceived by the vision itself, then since vision has already become color, what could be called the "perception of the circular shadow" by those diseased people?
Furthermore, Ānanda!
If this circular reflection existed separately from the lamp, then one should see a circular reflection appear when looking at the side-screens, curtains, tables, and mats;
if it existed separately from the act of seeing, it should not be within the range of the eyes—how then could a person with cataracts see this circular reflection?

Therefore, you should know that form actually resides within the lamp; the visual disorder perceives it as a shadow. Both the shadow and the perception are defects of vision, yet the perception of the defect itself is not a disorder.
Ultimately, one should not say that this is the lamp or that this is the vision, nor that within this there is something that is neither lamp nor vision.
It is like a second moon, which is neither a substantial entity nor a reflection. Why is this?
Because the perception of a second moon is produced by pressing [the eyes].
No wise person should say that this pressing of the root of the sense organ is either form or non-form, or seeing or non-seeing;
