this case is exactly the same. It is produced by a cataract in the eye; now, whom could one name as being the lamp or the seeing? How much less can one distinguish it as being neither lamp nor seeing?
"What is meant by 'common delusory vision'? Ānanda!

In this Jambudvīpa, excluding the great oceans, there are three thousand islands upon the level lands in between. Measuring from east to west across the central great island, there are two thousand three hundred large nations; as for the other small islands within the various seas, they contain perhaps two or three hundred nations, or one or two, up to thirty, forty, or fifty."

Ānanda! Furthermore, if within this there is a small continent containing only two countries, and the people of only one nation collectively experience adverse conditions, then the sentient beings of that land on the small continent will behold all manner of inauspicious phenomena.

Some may see two suns or two moons; within these appearances, there may even be halos, eclipses, rings, crescents, comets, meteors, and flying stars, as well as various evil omens such as the "burdened ear" and rainbows—phenomena seen only in this country, which the sentient beings of other lands have neither seen nor heard of before.
Ānanda! I shall now, for your sake, clarify these two matters by advancing and retreating them together. Ānanda!

Just as those sentient beings, due to the delusive vision of their individual karma, perceive the circular shadow appearing within a lamp’s light; although it appears to be an external object, it is ultimately produced by the cataract in the viewer's own eye. This cataract is simply the exhaustion of seeing and is not created by the color-form itself. Yet, for one who perceives this cataract, there is ultimately no fault in their seeing.

For example, today as you observe with your eyes the mountains, rivers, lands, and all sentient beings, these are all produced by the disease of vision that has existed since beginningless time. Vision and its conditions appear as present objects; yet fundamentally, they are the cataracts within the objective field of my enlightened awareness. Awareness of vision is itself the cataract; the fundamentally enlightened, luminous mind is not the cataract. Awareness of the conditions is not the cataract; it is the object of awareness that is the cataract. When awareness is aware that it is not within the cataract, this is truly the seeing of seeing.
What, then, is meant by "awakening, hearing, knowing, and seeing"?
Therefore, when you now see me, yourself, and all the ten classes of sentient beings in the world, you are all seeing a cataract;
it is not that you see the cataract itself. That which sees the cataract is the true essence of vision, and because its nature is not a cataract, it is not called "seeing."

“Ānanda! Just as those sentient beings share a commonality of deluded vision, consider one person with a distinct karmic condition who experiences that same deluded vision; or one person with diseased eyes who sees the same circular shadow as everyone else in a country. That circular shadow arises from the delusion of a visual disorder (*taimira*), and these inauspicious signs manifested within this commonality of sentient beings arise from the miasmic evils of their collective karma. Both are produced by beginningless deluded vision.”

For example, within the three thousand continents of Jambudvīpa, including the four great oceans of the Sahā world, as well as all the realms of outflows and all sentient beings throughout the ten directions, they are all equally this enlightened, luminous, and untainted wondrous mind; yet through the conditions of the delusory illnesses of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, they falsely arise together in harmony and falsely die together in harmony.

If one can distance oneself from all conditions of conjunction and non-conjunction, then one further eliminates the causes of birth and death; thus, the nature of bodhi—which is beyond arising and ceasing—the pure fundamental mind, and the ever-abiding original enlightenment, will be perfected.

“Ānanda! Although you have previously realized that the wondrous clarity of fundamental enlightenment is by nature neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously, you have not yet clarified that this source of enlightenment is neither born from a combination of factors nor from their non-combination.”
Ānanda! I now ask you again regarding the objects before you.
You still harbor doubts within yourself, based on the deluded imaginings of the entire world, concerning the nature of the combination of all causes and conditions.
As for that which arises through the union of the mind realizing bodhi: does your present wondrously pure essence of seeing conjoin with light,
or does it conjoin with darkness,
or does it conjoin with openness?
Is it a mixture with darkness?
If you say it is a mixture with light, then consider this light: when the light appears before you, where is the vision mixed in?
Since the characteristics of the vision can be distinguished, what form or image would the mixture take?
If it is not the seeing itself, how can it see light?
If it is the seeing itself, how can it see the seeing?
If the seeing were complete in itself, where would there be a conjunction with light?
If illumination were complete, it would not combine with seeing; seeing must be distinct from illumination.
If they were mixed, one would lose the name and nature of that inherent illumination.
If the nature of illumination is lost through such mixing, then the combination of illumination is illogical; the same applies to darkness, penetration, and all various obstructions.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
As for this wondrous, pure essence of seeing that you now possess, does it unite with light?
Or does it unite with darkness?"
Does it unite with what is open?
Or does it unite with what is obstructed?
If it unites with light, then when darkness arrives and the characteristic of light has already ceased, this vision would not unite with the various forms of darkness.
What is meant by seeing darkness?

If, when seeing darkness, one does not conjoin with darkness, then if one were to conjoin with light, one would not be seeing the light; since one does not see the light, how could one conjoin with it?
"Clear awareness is not darkness; that same principle applies to darkness, to openness, and likewise to all various obstructions.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One!"
"As I reflect upon it, is this wondrous source of awakening not non-composite with the various objective conditions, sensory objects, and the mind's thoughts and deliberations?
The Buddha said,
"Now you say again that awakening is non-composite."
I ask you again:
this wondrous seeing-essence is not a product of combination; is it not combined with light?
Is it not combined with darkness?
Is it because of non-penetration that there is no harmony? Is it because of non-obstruction that there is no harmony?
If it is not through clarity that there is harmony, then between seeing and clarity there must necessarily be a boundary.
You should observe closely: where is clarity?
Where is seeing? Within seeing and within clarity, what constitutes their boundary?

Ānanda! If there were necessarily no seer within the limit of light, then [the seer] would not reach it; since one would not know for oneself where the characteristic of light is located, how could its boundaries be established?
It is the same for darkness, light, and all various obstructions.
Furthermore, as for this wondrous seeing-essence, if it is not a product of combination, does it not combine with light?
Does it not combine with darkness?
Is it a union through non-penetration?
Or is it a union through non-obstruction?

If it were a union with light, then the nature of seeing and the nature of light would be mutually contradictory; they would be as distinct from one another as the ear and light, which do not touch at all. Since seeing itself does not even know where the characteristics of light reside, how could it discern whether the principle of union or non-union applies?

The same applies to darkness, light, and all such obstructions. Ānanda! You still do not clearly understand that all these superficial, floating, illusory, and transformative phenomena arise where they are and perish where they are;

they are called "phenomena" only because they are illusory and false, yet their nature is truly the essence of wondrous, enlightened clarity. Thus it is with the five aggregates (*skandha*), the six sense bases (*āyatana*), and from the twelve bases (*āyatana*) to the eighteen realms (*dhātu*): through the conjunction of causes and conditions there is illusory birth, and through the separation of causes and conditions there is illusorily named extinction. One cannot at all know that this arising and ceasing, this coming and going, is fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha—ever-abiding, wondrously clear, immovable, omnipresent, and the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Within this true and eternal nature, if one seeks for coming and going, delusion and enlightenment, or death and birth, nothing at all can be found.
“Ānanda! How are the five aggregates fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness? Ānanda!”

It is like a person with clear vision who gazes at a bright, cloudless sky; there is only a singular, pure emptiness, vast and devoid of anything. For no reason, that person does not move their eyes but stares fixedly until they become fatigued, whereupon they see illusory flowers appearing in the empty space, as well as all manner of other chaotic, unreal forms.
You should know that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is exactly like this.
Ānanda! These illusory flowers do not come from space, nor do they emerge from the eyes.
It is thus, Ānanda!

If it comes from space, then having come from space, it must return to space; if there is coming and going, it is not empty space. If space were not empty, it could not itself accommodate the arising and ceasing of the appearance of flowers, just as Ānanda’s own body cannot accommodate Ānanda himself.

If it emerges from the eyes, then having emerged from the eyes, it must also enter back through the eyes; since this nature of the flower emerges from the eyes, it should necessarily possess the faculty of vision.
If it possesses vision, then as it departs and the flower becomes empty, it should upon returning see the eyes.
If it lacks vision, then having already obscured the space outside, it should upon returning obscure the eyes.
Furthermore, when seeing flowers, the eyes should be free from any obscuration; why then is a clear sky called "clear and bright" vision?
Therefore, you should know that the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is illusory and false, fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.

“Ānanda! Suppose there is a person whose hands and feet are at ease and whose entire body is in harmony; suddenly, as if forgetting his very existence, his nature is free from any sense of opposition or compliance. For no reason, this person rubs his two palms together in the air, and within his hands, various sensations of roughness, smoothness, cold, and heat falsely arise.
You should know that the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) is exactly like this.”
Ānanda! These illusory touches do not come from space, nor do they emerge from the palm.
It is thus, Ānanda!
If it comes from empty space, since it can touch the palm, why does it not touch the body?
Empty space should not be able to choose where to come and touch.
If it emerges from the palm, it should not depend upon the coming together [of the two hands].

Furthermore, since it emerges from the palm, when the hands are joined, the palm perceives it; yet when separated, it enters through the point of contact. If this were so, the arm, the wrist, the marrow, and the bones should likewise perceive the traces of its entry. There must surely be a conscious mind that knows its emergence and its entry, such that there is some distinct entity moving back and forth within the body. Why then wait for the perception upon joining to designate it as "contact"?
Therefore, you should know that the aggregate of sensation is false and illusory; fundamentally, it is neither caused by conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature. "Ānanda!
It is like a person who, upon speaking of a sour plum, has saliva flow from his mouth; or one who, thinking of treading on a precipice, feels a stinging ache in the soles of his feet."
Ānanda, you should know that the aggregate of perception is likewise so.
As it is said, this sourness does not arise from the plum, nor does it enter through the mouth.
Thus it is, Ānanda!
If the plum were to arise [of itself], the plum ought to speak for itself; why wait for someone else to say it?
If it entered through the mouth, the mouth ought to hear it for itself; why need one wait for the ear?
If it were heard by the ears alone, why would this water not emerge from within the ears?
This imagined treading upon a precipice is similar to what was previously explained.
Therefore, you should know that the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) is empty and false; fundamentally, it is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
“Ānanda! Just as the waves of a violent torrent flow in succession, with the preceding and succeeding moments not overstepping one another;
you should know that the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) is likewise.”
Ānanda! This nature of flow does not arise because of space, nor does it exist because of water;
it is neither the nature of water, nor is it separate from space and water.
Thus it is, Ānanda!
If [the world] were born from emptiness, then the inexhaustible emptiness of the ten directions would become an inexhaustible flow, and all worlds would naturally be submerged and drowned within it.
If [the nature of turbulence] exists because of water, then this turbulent stream-nature should not be water; its distinct characteristics should now be manifest.
If it were identical to the nature of water, then when the water is clear and still, it would no longer be the essence of water.
If one were apart from space and water, there would be no space external to water, nor any flow external to it.

Therefore, one should know that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is false and illusory; fundamentally, it is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
“Ānanda! It is like a person who takes a *piṅgala* jar, plugs its two openings, fills it with empty space, and carries it for a journey of a thousand *li* to present as a gift to another country;
you should know that the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is likewise.”
Ānanda! Thus, this space does not come from that direction, nor does it enter here.
It is thus, Ānanda!

If it comes from that direction, then since empty space was already contained within the original bottle when it departed, there should be a deficiency of empty space on the ground where the original bottle stood.
If it enters from this direction, one should see the empty space emerge as the bottle is opened and overturned.
Therefore, one should know that the aggregate of consciousness is empty and false; fundamentally, it is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
*The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Cultivation and Realization of the Secret Causes of the Tathāgata*, Fascicle Two.
The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Tathāgata’s Secret Causes... [and so forth].
The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ten Thousand Practices of the Bodhisattvas, Scroll Three;

also known as the Great Maṇḍala Sūtra of Nālandā in Central India, excerpted from the Abhiṣeka Section for separate circulation, translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Prajñāmitra of the Tang Dynasty. "Furthermore, Ānanda!"
What are the six sense bases that are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness? Ānanda!

That very visual faculty which, when stared fixedly, gives rise to fatigue—both the eye and the fatigue are equally Bodhi. This appearance of fatigue arising from staring is caused by the two kinds of false objects, light and darkness. The faculty of vision arises within them and absorbs these objective images; this is called the "nature of seeing. Yet, apart from those two objects of light and darkness, this seeing ultimately has no substance.
Thus it is, Ānanda!
You should know that this seeing does not come from light or darkness, nor does it emerge from the sense organ, nor is it produced from space. Why is this?
If it comes from light, then darkness would cease along with it, and thus one should not see darkness.
If it comes from darkness, then light would cease along with it, and thus one should not see light.
If it arose from the sense organ, there would necessarily be neither light nor darkness.
Thus, this essence of vision originally has no inherent nature of its own.
If it emerged from empty space, then when one gazes at external objects before one, upon returning one should see the sense organ itself.
Furthermore, emptiness observes itself; how does it concern your sense-base?
Therefore, you should know that the eye-base is illusory, fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor arising spontaneously. "Ānanda!

For example, suppose a person were to tightly plug their ears with two fingers; because the faculty of hearing is strained, a sound arises within the head. Both the ear and the strain are equally Bodhi.

The appearance of fatigue arising from staring is caused by the two kinds of false objects—movement and stillness. When the faculty of hearing arises within the center, it draws in these objective images; this is called the nature of hearing. Yet, apart from those two objects of movement and stillness, this hearing ultimately has no substance.
Thus it is, Ānanda!
You should know that this hearing does not come from movement or stillness, nor does it emerge from the sense organ, nor is it produced from space. Why is this?
If it comes from stillness, movement would immediately cease along with it, and one should not perceive movement.
If it comes from movement, stillness would immediately cease along with it, and one should have no awareness of stillness.
If it were produced from the sense organ, it would necessarily be devoid of movement or stillness.
Thus, this essence of hearing fundamentally lacks intrinsic nature.
If it emerged from empty space, then the existence of hearing would constitute its inherent nature, and it would no longer be empty space.
Furthermore, emptiness hears by itself; what concern is this for your auditory faculty?
Therefore, you should know that the ear-faculty is illusory, fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor of a spontaneous nature. "Ānanda!

For example, suppose a person forcefully pinches their nose; after pinching it for a long time, fatigue arises, and they perceive a sensation of cold within the nose. Based on that sensation, they distinguish between what is open or obstructed, and what is real or unreal. This extends even to various fragrant and foul odors; furthermore, both the nose and the resulting fatigue are equally Bodhi.

The appearance of fatigue arising from staring is caused by two kinds of false objects: penetration and obstruction. When the faculty of hearing arises in the midst of this, it draws in these objective images; this is called the nature of olfactory-hearing. Yet, apart from those two objects of penetration and obstruction, this hearing ultimately has no essence.
You should know that this hearing does not come from the state of being open or obstructed; it does not emerge from the sense organ, nor is it produced from space.
Why is this? If it came from the state of being open, it would naturally cease when the obstruction occurs; how then could one perceive the obstruction?
If [the faculty] exists because of obstruction, then when there is no obstruction, it would not hear; how then could it manifest the perception of fragrance, stench, and other tactile objects?
If it were produced from the sense organ itself, there would necessarily be no such states as obstruction or non-obstruction.
Thus, the essence of hearing fundamentally lacks intrinsic nature.

If smelling were to emerge from space, then that sense of smell would naturally turn back to smell your own nose; since space itself possesses smelling, what concern is it for your faculty of olfaction?
Therefore, you should know that the olfactory faculty is illusory, fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor existing as a spontaneous nature.

“Ānanda! Suppose there is a person who licks their lips with their tongue; by licking repeatedly until it becomes fatigued, if that person is ill, they perceive a bitter taste, whereas a healthy person perceives a slight sweet sensation. It is through this sweetness and bitterness that the nature of this tongue-organ is revealed; when it is not moving, its quality of neutrality is ever-present.”

Furthermore, the tongue and fatigue are both identical to bodhi; yet, due to the two kinds of false objects—sweetness, bitterness, and blandness—the faculty of cognition arises from the state of staring-induced fatigue. Abiding in the midst, it absorbs these objective images, which is termed the nature of knowing taste. This nature of knowing taste, when separated from those three objects of sweetness, bitterness, and blandness, ultimately has no substance.
Thus it is, Ānanda!

You should know that this perception of bitter and bland does not come from the sweet or the bitter, nor does it exist because of the bland; furthermore, it does not emerge from the sense organ, nor is it produced from empty space.
Why is this? If sweetness or bitterness arises, the neutral flavor is known to cease; how then can one know the neutral flavor?
If one emerges from the neutral flavor, sweetness is known to vanish; how then can one know the two characteristics of sweetness and bitterness?
If it were produced from the tongue, there would necessarily be no objects of sweetness, blandness, or bitterness.
Thus, one knows that the root of tasting has no intrinsic nature.

If it were produced from space, then space itself would possess the taste, which your mouth could not know; furthermore, if space knew it for itself, what would it have to do with your faculty of sensation?
Therefore, you should know that the tongue-faculty is illusory; fundamentally, it is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.

"Ānanda! Suppose there is a person who touches a hot hand with a cold hand: if the power of the cold is greater, the hot hand follows the cold; if the efficacy of the heat prevails, the cold becomes hot. In this way, the sensation of contact through their union manifests the cognition of separation. When these forces interact, if a result is formed, it arises from the friction of contact."

Furthermore, both the body and its weariness are equally Bodhi; the appearance of weariness arises from the eyes staring fixedly due to the two kinds of false objects—separation and union. As the faculty of awakening abides in the center and draws in these objective images, it is called the nature of cognition.
This essence of perception, being devoid of those two objects—separation and union, or opposition and compliance—is ultimately without substance.

Thus, Ānanda, you should know that this perception does not come from separation or union, nor does it exist through opposition or compliance; it does not emerge from the sense organs, nor is it born from space.
Why is this? If [the sensation] comes when there is contact, it must have already ceased when there is separation; how then could one perceive separation?
The same applies to the two characteristics of the disagreeable and the agreeable.
If it emerged from the sense organs, there would necessarily be no four characteristics of separation, union, opposition, or compliance;
thus, your bodily cognition would fundamentally lack self-nature.
If it emerged from space, then space itself would possess cognition and awareness; what connection would that have with your sensory faculties?
Therefore, you should know that the body-faculty is empty and false; it is fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature. "Ānanda!

It is like a person who, when weary, falls into deep sleep and then awakens; upon perceiving sensory objects, they remember them, yet the loss of such memory constitutes delusion. This is the cycle of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing, which proceeds through inhalation and exhalation without transgression, and is designated as the faculty of cognition."

Furthermore, both intention and fatigue are identical to Bodhi; yet, due to the two kinds of delusory objects—arising and ceasing—the eyes produce the signs of fatigue. Consciousness gathers within the center and draws in internal dust; seeing and hearing flow against the current until they reach a ground where the flow no longer reaches, which is called the nature of cognitive awareness.
This nature of awareness, being devoid of the two objects of waking and sleeping, or arising and ceasing, ultimately has no substance.

Thus, Ānanda, you should know that this faculty of awareness does not come from waking or sleeping, nor does it exist through arising or ceasing; it does not emerge from the sense organs, nor is it produced from space.
Why is this? If [the dream] comes from the waking state, then upon falling asleep it would immediately perish; what, then, would constitute sleep?
It must exist during the time of birth, yet if it perishes, it becomes non-existent; who then would experience this cessation?
If birth arises from cessation, then birth is simply the absence of cessation; who then could know that which is born?

If it emerges from the sense organs, then its two aspects—waking and sleeping—manifest as the body opens and closes. Apart from these two states, this conscious knower is like a flower in the sky, ultimately devoid of intrinsic nature.
If it were produced from emptiness, it would inherently be the cognition of emptiness; what concern would it have with your faculty of mind?
Therefore, you should know that the mind-faculty is illusory, fundamentally neither arising from causes and conditions nor being of a spontaneous nature.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
How are the twelve bases (āyatana) fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness? Ānanda!"
"You should now observe this Jeta Grove and its various springs and ponds.
What do you think: do these forms arise and are seen by the eye, or does the eye arise with the characteristics of form?"

Ānanda! If it were the visual faculty that produced the appearance of form, then when seeing empty space—which is not form—the nature of form would have to dissolve. If it dissolved, everything would be revealed as utterly non-existent; since the appearance of form would no longer exist, who would perceive the substance of empty space?
Space is also like this.

If the visual consciousness arises from the dust of form to perceive space, then by observing that space is not form, the perception itself vanishes; once it has vanished, it is entirely non-existent—who then can discern space as form?

Therefore, you should know that seeing and the emptiness of form both have no location; thus, the two locations of form and seeing are illusory, fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor arising spontaneously.

“Ānanda! Listen further to this sound within Jeta’s Grove: when the meal is prepared, the drum is struck; when the assembly gathers, the bell is tolled. The sounds of the bell and the drum follow one another in succession.”
"What do you think: does the sound come to the ear, or does the ear go to the place where the sound is?
"Ānanda! [the Buddha said.]

Furthermore, if this sound comes to the vicinity of the ear, then just as I have no "self" when begging for alms in Śrāvastī while staying in the Jeta Grove, so too this sound must come specifically to Ānanda’s ear;
Maudgalyāyana and Kāśyapa would not hear it together, let alone the one thousand two hundred and fifty śramaṇas who, upon hearing the bell, all came together to the place of the meal.

Furthermore, if your ear were to travel to the location of the sound—just as when I reside in the Jeta Grove, there is no "me" in the city of Śrāvastī—then when you hear the sound of a drum, your ear would have already gone to the place where the drum is being struck;
thus, when the bell-sound arises simultaneously, they should not be heard together, let alone the various sounds of elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep within that assembly.
If there is no coming or going, there is likewise no hearing.

Therefore, one should know that both listening and sound have no location; thus, these two—listening and sound—are both illusory, fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor existing as a spontaneous nature.

“Ānanda! You shall further smell this sandalwood in the brazier; if even one *zhu* of this incense were burned, its fragrance would be smelled simultaneously throughout the forty *li* within the city of Śrāvastī.”
What do you think? Does this fragrance arise from the sandalwood tree,
or does it arise from your nose,
or does it arise from space?

Ānanda! If this fragrance were produced in your nose, then as it is said to be produced by the nose, it ought to emerge from the nose; yet the nose is not sandalwood—how then could there be the scent of sandalwood within the nose?
If you claim that smelling occurs when the fragrance enters through the nose, then to say that one "smells" the fragrance as it exits the nose is illogical.

If the fragrance were produced within emptiness, then since the nature of emptiness is eternal, the fragrance should be ever-present; why then do you rely on burning this withered wood in an incense burner?

If this fragrance originates from wood, then its substance must become smoke through combustion; if the nose perceives it, it should be enveloped by the scent of that smoke. Since the smoke rises into the air and has not yet traveled far—how could it be smelled within forty *li*?

Therefore, you should know that the nose and its smelling, along with the act of smelling and the fragrance, are all devoid of a fixed location; these two locations are false and illusory, fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor arising spontaneously.
“Ānanda! You often carry the alms bowl among the assembly at the two times of the day; during that interval, you may encounter ghee, curd, or clarified butter, which are called the finest flavors.
What do you think? Does this flavor arise from empty space?”
Is it produced within the tongue?
Or is it produced within the food? Ānanda!

Furthermore, if this flavor arises in your tongue, and there is but a single tongue within your mouth, then at that time your tongue would already have become the flavor of ghee; upon encountering black rock honey, it should not change. If it does not change, it cannot be called "knowing flavor. If it does change, then the tongue is not a manifold entity; how then can a single tongue perceive multiple flavors?
If it were produced from food, since food does not possess consciousness, how could it know itself?
Furthermore, if food knew by itself, that would be the same as another’s food; what concern would that have for you regarding the knowledge of names and flavors?
If flavor were produced from space, what flavor would you experience when consuming empty space?
If that space were to have a salty taste, then since your tongue would be salty and your face would also be salty, the people of this world would be like sea fish;

being constantly subjected to saltiness, they would not know what fresh water is. If they do not recognize the fresh, they cannot perceive the salty; since they would have no knowledge at all, how could it be called "flavor"?

Therefore, you should know that the sense of taste and the tongue, together with the act of tasting, have no location; thus, both tasting and flavor are equally illusory, fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor existing as a spontaneous nature.
“Ānanda! Every morning you habitually rub your head with your hand.
What do you think? Is that which is known through this rubbing merely the act of touching?”
Is it located in the hand, or is it in the head?
If it were in the hand, the head would be devoid of cognition; how then could there be contact?
If [the sensation of touch] were located only in the head, the hands would be useless; how then could it be called "touch"?
If each part possessed its own [separate sensation], then you, Ānanda, would have two bodies.
If the head and the hands were produced by a single instance of touch, then the hands and the head would constitute a single entity; if they were a single entity, touch could not be established.
If they were two distinct entities, with respect to whom would contact exist?
If it exists in the agent, it does not exist in the object; if it exists in the object, it does not exist in the agent.
It is not logical that space should enter into contact with you.

Therefore, you should know that sensation and touch, together with the body, have no location; both the body and touch are equally illusory, fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor arising from a nature of spontaneity.
“Ānanda! Regarding the three natures—wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate—that you constantly take as objects within your mind, these constitute the principles by which phenomena are produced.
Do these phenomena arise from the mind itself?”
"Does it exist as a distinct location apart from the mind?
Ānanda! If it were identical to the mind, then the dharma would not be an external object; since it would not be an object of the mind's cognition, how could it constitute a sense-field?"
If there were a separate location apart from the mind, would the self-nature of that phenomenon be conscious or unconscious?

If it is conscious, it is named "mind"; it would differ from you yet not be an external object, and being identical to the mental measure (*cittamātra*) of others, it would be both you and the mind itself. How could your mind then be dualistic with respect to you?
If it is not known, and since this object is neither form, sound, fragrance, taste, nor the phenomena of conjunction, disjunction, cold, warmth, or empty space, where then could it possibly reside?

Now, within the emptiness of form, there is no indication whatsoever; it cannot be that there is further emptiness outside of the human realm. Since the mind has no object of perception (*ālambana*), from what could its locus be established?

Therefore, one should know that both phenomena (*dharma*) and the mind have no location; thus, both the mental faculty (*manas*) and phenomena are equally illusory, fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
What are the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) that are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous true nature of Suchness? Ānanda!"

According to what you have clarified, visual consciousness arises with the eye and visible forms as conditions. Does this consciousness arise because of the eye, such that the eye constitutes its constituent element (*dhātu*), or does it arise because of visible forms, such that visible forms constitute its constituent element?
Ānanda! If [consciousness] were produced because of the eye, then since there would be neither form nor space to distinguish, even if you possessed this consciousness, what would you have it serve?
Furthermore, your seeing is not itself blue, yellow, red, or white; having nothing to represent it, from where could its boundaries be established?
If [your consciousness] arises because of form, then when space is devoid of form, your consciousness should cease; how then could you cognize the nature of emptiness?

If form undergoes change, you likewise cognize the shifting and transforming characteristics of that form; yet if your consciousness does not shift, from what basis could the [distinction between] realms be established?
If it changes according to transformation, the characteristics of the realms would naturally cease to exist;
if it does not change, it would be permanent.
Since it arises from form, it should not be able to cognize the location of empty space.

If both types of eyes and forms were to arise together, then when they combine, they would be separated from their center; and when they separate, they would join at both ends. Their essential natures would thus be in chaotic confusion—how could they constitute a "realm" (*dhātu*)?

Therefore, you should know that it is with the eye and form as conditions that the eye-consciousness-realm arises. Since none of these three locations exist [independently], then the eye, the form, and the form-realm—these three—are fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
“Ānanda! Furthermore,
regarding what you have clarified— that the ear and sound act as conditions to give rise to ear-consciousness—
does this consciousness arise because of the ear, such that the ear constitutes its realm?”
"Is it because sound is produced that sound constitutes its realm? Ānanda!

If [hearing] were produced by reason of the ear, then when the two characteristics of movement and stillness are not present before it, the faculty would fail to function as cognition; there would necessarily be nothing known."
If even cognition (*vijñapti*) is not established, what form or appearance could consciousness (*vijñāna*) have?
If one takes "hearing" as the basis, since there is neither motion nor stillness, hearing itself is not established.

How then can the ear’s form, along with the objects of color and touch, be called the "element of consciousness" (*vijñānadhātu*), and from what, then, would the "element of auditory consciousness" (*śrotravijñānadhātu*) be established?
If consciousness arises from sound, and consciousness exists because of sound, then it would have no relation to hearing. Without hearing, the locus of the characteristic of sound would vanish.

If you concede that consciousness arises from sound and that the characteristic of sound exists because of hearing, then hearing should hear the consciousness; yet if it does not hear it, it is not a sensory field (*dhātu*). If hearing were the same as sound, then once consciousness has been heard, who would know the hearing of the consciousness? If there were no knower, one would ultimately be like grass or wood.

One should not allow the auditory faculty and sound to intermingle and form a "middle realm," for there is no such intermediate position within the realms. If that were so, from what would the characteristics of the internal and external arise?

Therefore, one should know that the auditory consciousness-realm arises with the ear and sound as conditions; yet since these three locations are entirely non-existent, the triad of the ear, sound, and the sound-realm are fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.
“Ānanda! Furthermore, regarding what you understand: the nose and fragrance serve as conditions to give rise to nose-consciousness.
Does this consciousness arise because of the nose, such that the nose constitutes its realm? Or does it arise because of fragrance, such that fragrance constitutes its realm?”
"Is it because of fragrance that it arises, and does it take fragrance as its realm? "Ānanda!
If it arises because of the nose, then within your mind, what do you take to be the nose?"
Is it because you grasp at the form of flesh and the appearance of two claws?
Or is it because you grasp at the nature of smelling, knowing, and moving?

If you grasp at the form of flesh, then that fleshy substance is the body; bodily cognition is contact (*spraṣṭavya*), and is thus called the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), not the nose-faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*). What is called contact is an object (*viṣaya*); since even the "nose" lacks a name [in this context], how can a sense-field (*dhātu*) be established?
If you take it to be the sense of smelling, then by what means does your mind know?
If the flesh were the knower, then the knowledge of the flesh would fundamentally be tactile and not olfactory.

If space were the knower, then space would know itself and the flesh would not be perceived; if this were so, then empty space would be you and your body would lack consciousness, such that today, Ānanda, you would have no place of existence.
If you take fragrance as your cognition, then that cognition belongs to the fragrance itself; what concern is it to you?

If the odors of fragrance and stench must arise from your nose, then those two kinds of flowing air—fragrance and stench—would not arise from *eranda* or sandalwood trees. If these two substances do not come to you, you should smell your own nose and tell me whether it is fragrant or foul.

If it were foul, it would not be fragrant; if it were fragrant, it should not be foul. If you could perceive both fragrance and foulness simultaneously, then you, as a single person, would have two noses. Just as there are two Ānandas here before me asking these questions, which of them would constitute your true self?

If the nose were a single entity, then fragrance and stench would not be two distinct things; since stench would already be fragrance and fragrance would again become stench, these two natures would not exist—by what, then, could the sense-field (dhātu) be established?

If consciousness arises because of fragrance and exists because of fragrance, then just as the eye possesses the faculty of seeing yet cannot see itself, so too, because it exists because of fragrance, it should not know fragrance. If it knows it, it has not arisen from it; if it does not know it, it is not consciousness.
If fragrance were not known to exist, the realm of fragrance would not be established;

if consciousness did not perceive fragrance, then the realm could not be established on account of fragrance. Since there is no intermediate state, neither internal nor external can be established; thus, that nature of hearing is ultimately illusory.

Therefore, one should know that the nose-consciousness element arises with the nose and odors as conditions; since these three locations are all non-existent, the triad of the nose, odors, and the odor-element are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
“Ānanda! Furthermore, regarding what you have clarified: with the tongue and flavors as conditions, tongue-consciousness arises.
Does this consciousness arise because of the tongue, taking the tongue as its constituent element?”
“Is it because of taste that [tongue-consciousness] arises, taking taste as its element? “Ānanda!
If it were produced because of the tongue, then all the sugarcane, sour plums, yellow myrobalan, rock salt, fine pepper, ginger, and cinnamon in the world would have no taste at all.”
Taste your own tongue: is it sweet or bitter?
If the nature of the tongue were bitter, who would come to taste it?
Since the tongue does not taste itself, what is there to perceive?
The nature of the tongue is not suffering, and taste does not arise of itself; how, then, can a realm (dhātu) be established?

If consciousness arises because of taste, then consciousness itself would be the taste; being identical to the tongue-organ, it should likewise not taste of itself. How, then, could consciousness discern whether something is a taste or not a taste?

Furthermore, all tastes do not arise from a single substance; since tastes arise from many sources, consciousness should likewise be manifold in nature. If the nature of consciousness were a single entity, it would necessarily arise from taste alone.

When salty, bland, sweet, and pungent flavors combine and arise together, their various changing characteristics would have to become a single taste and thus lack differentiation. If there is no differentiation, it cannot be called "consciousness"; how then could it be termed the "tongue-taste-consciousness element"?
It should not be that space gives rise to your mind-consciousness.
When the tongue and flavors combine, there is fundamentally no self-nature within them; how, then, could a realm arise?

Therefore, you should know that the tongue and flavors serve as conditions to give rise to the tongue-consciousness-realm; yet these three locations are all non-existent. Thus, the tongue, flavors, and the tongue-realm—these three—are fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.
"Ānanda! Furthermore, regarding what you understand: body-contact serves as the condition for the arising of body-consciousness.
Does this consciousness arise because of the body, such that the body constitutes its realm?"
"Is it because it arises from contact that contact constitutes its constituent element? Ānanda!
If it were produced solely by the body, there would necessarily be no joining or parting; with what object of perception and investigation would the two [faculties] perceive the body?"
If it were necessarily produced from contact, there would be no such thing as your body; who then, being bodiless, could perceive union and separation?
Ānanda! Objects do not perceive through contact; it is the body that perceives contact.
To know the body is to know contact; to know contact is to know the body. That which is contact is not the body, and that which is the body is not contact.

The two characteristics of body and contact fundamentally have no location. When conjoined with the body, they constitute the very nature of the body itself; when separated from the body, they are merely phenomena such as empty space. Since neither "inner" nor "outer" can be established, how could a "middle" be posited?
Since internal and external natures do not exist within the middle, from what could the arising of your consciousness establish the realms?

Therefore, you should know that the body-realm arises with body and touch as conditions; yet these three locations are entirely non-existent. Thus, the triad of body, touch, and the body-realm are fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.
“Ānanda! Furthermore, regarding what you understand: with the mind and mental objects as conditions, the mental consciousness arises.
Does this consciousness arise because of the mind, taking the mind as its constituent element?”
"Is it produced because of dharmas, taking dharmas as its boundary? "Ānanda!
If it is produced because of the mind, then within your mind there must be something you are thinking of, which brings forth and clarifies your intention."
If there were no preceding dharmas, the mind would have nothing from which to arise; being devoid of conditions and lacking form, for what purpose would consciousness exist?
Furthermore, is this conscious mind of yours, along with its various modes of deliberation and its nature of discernment, identical to or different from [the preceding dharmas]?
If consent is itself the mind, how can there be that which is produced?
If the mind were different [from what it consents to], they would not be identical, and thus there would be no cognition.
If there is no cognition, how can the mind arise?
If there is something perceived, how can one perceive the mind?
Since neither identity nor difference can be established as two distinct natures, how could the realms (dhātus) be established?
If they arise dependent on dharmas, then all worldly phenomena do not exist apart from the five sense objects.

Observe the dharma of form, as well as the dharmas of sound, fragrance, taste, and touch; their characteristics are distinct and manifest in relation to the five sense organs, and are not subsumed by the mind.
Your consciousness definitely arises in dependence upon dharmas; you should now observe them closely: what is the nature of these dharmas?

If one is separated from form and emptiness, motion and stillness, penetration and obstruction, union and separation, and arising and ceasing—transcending all such characteristics—one ultimately finds nothing at all.

When there is arising, form, emptiness, and all phenomena arise together; when there is cessation, form, emptiness, and all phenomena cease together. Since their cause does not exist, what form or characteristic could consciousness—which arises from that cause—possibly possess?
Since characteristics do not exist, how could a realm arise?

Therefore, one should know that with the mind and dharmas as conditions, the mental consciousness-realm arises; yet these three locations are entirely non-existent. Thus, the mind, dharmas, and the mental realm—these three—are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of spontaneous nature.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The Tathāgata has often taught that all the various transformations in the world arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions; they are all manifested through the combination of the four great elements.”
How is it that the Tathāgata rejects both causes and conditions as well as spontaneity?
I do not yet understand the meaning of this; I only pray that you will take pity on us and reveal to sentient beings the definitive teaching of the Middle Way, free from conceptual proliferation.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:

“Since you have previously grown weary of and detached from the various Hinayana teachings of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and have resolved to diligently seek unsurpassed Bodhi, I shall now reveal the ultimate truth for you.”
Why do you further entangle yourself with worldly conceptual proliferation and the causes and conditions of deluded thoughts?

Though you are learned, you are like a man who knows how to describe medicine but cannot distinguish it when the actual medicine appears before him; the Tathāgata says such a person is truly to be pitied.
"Listen attentively now; I shall analyze and reveal this for you, so as to enable those who will practice the Mahāyāna in the future to penetrate the true reality.
Ānanda remained silent, receiving the Buddha’s sacred instruction.
“Ānanda! It is as you have said: the four great elements combine to manifest the various transformations of the world. Ānanda!”
If the essence of those great elements were not a composite, they could not intermingle with one another, just as empty space does not mix with material forms.

If they were composites, they would be like transformations, beginning and ending in mutual dependence, arising and ceasing in continuous succession—birth and death, death and birth, birth and death, death and birth—like a whirling firebrand that never rests.
Ānanda! Just as water turns into ice and ice returns to water, you should contemplate the nature of earth:

that which is coarse becomes the great earth, and that which is subtle becomes fine dust. Even when analyzing those ultimate atoms down to the *paramāṇu*, the characteristic of the limit of form is composed of seven parts; if one further analyzes the *paramāṇu*, it is in truth the nature of emptiness.
Ānanda! If these atoms were analyzed until they became space, you should know that space gives rise to the appearance of form.
As for what you have now asked:
"Through conjunction, the various transformative appearances of the world are produced.
Observe, for a moment, this single atom: by the conjunction of how much space does it exist?
Atoms should not combine to form atoms.
Furthermore, if an atom is analyzed and enters into emptiness, by means of how many material characteristics (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) is empty space formed?
If it were formed by the combination of material elements, then that which is combined would not be empty space.
If there were a conjunction with space, then that which conjoins with space would not be form.
Since form can still be analyzed, how could space possibly conjoin?

You fundamentally do not know that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of form is true emptiness and the nature of emptiness is true form; it is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
In accordance with the minds of sentient beings and corresponding to the measure of what they know, these phenomena manifest according to their karma.

The ignorant of the world delude themselves by regarding them as having causes and conditions or as being of a spontaneous nature; all such views are merely the conceptual calculations of the discriminating consciousness. They consist only of verbal expressions and possess no real meaning whatsoever.
“Ānanda! The nature of fire is without self; it depends upon various conditions.
Observe those households in the city that have not yet eaten: when they wish to cook, they hold a magnifying lens in their hands and seek fire from the sun.

Ānanda! That which is called a "congregation" is like myself and you, these one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, who now constitute a single assembly. Although the assembly is one, if one examines its fundamental basis, each has his own body; all have their respective lineages and names of birth, such as Śāriputra of the Brahmin caste, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa of the Kāśyapa caste, and even Ānanda of the Gautama clan.
Ānanda! If this nature of fire exists because of a combination of conditions, then when that hand holds a mirror toward the sun to seek fire, does this fire emerge from within the mirror?
Does it come from the mugwort?
Or does it come from the sun? Ānanda!
If it comes from the sun, it should naturally burn the moxa in your hand; furthermore, all the trees and forests where it comes from should likewise be consumed by fire.
If it emerges from within the mirror, it should naturally emerge from the mirror to ignite the moxa; why then does the mirror not melt?
When you wrap your hand around it, there is not even the appearance of heat; how then could it melt?
If fire were produced from the tinder itself, why would it depend on the sun, a mirror, and the meeting of their light before the fire arises?
You should further observe closely: the mirror is held by the hand, the sun comes from the heavens, and the moxa grows from the earth; from what direction does the fire travel here?
The sun and the mirror are far apart, neither merging nor uniting; it cannot be that the fire-light exists of itself without a source.
You still do not know that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of fire is true emptiness and the nature of emptiness is true fire;
it is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm, responding to the minds of sentient beings according to the measure of their cognitive capacity.
Ānanda, you should know this!

When people hold a mirror in one place, fire arises in that one place; when they hold it throughout the entire Dharma-realm, it arises filling the whole world. Since its arising pervades the entire world, how could it have a fixed location? It manifests according to karma.

The world is ignorant and deluded regarding causes and conditions as well as the nature of spontaneity; these are all merely conceptual constructions and calculations of the discerning mind. They exist only as verbal expressions and possess no real meaning whatsoever.
“Ānanda! The nature of water is not fixed; its flowing and ceasing have no constancy.

For instance, in the city of Śrāvastī, there were the great illusionists Kapila Rishi, Cakravāka Rishi, Padma, and Mahasattva, who sought the essence of the moon to compound their magical elixirs. These masters, during the daytime of the bright fortnight, would hold a *fangzhu* (a concave mirror) in their hands to catch the water from the moon.”
Does this water emerge from within the jewel?
Does it exist of its own accord in space?
Or does it come from the moon?

Ānanda! If [the moon] were to come from the moon itself, it would still be able to cause water to emerge from the pearl even from afar; all the trees and forests it passes through should likewise discharge flowing streams.
If they do flow, why wait for the pearl to appear in a specific direction?
It does not flow, clarifying that water does not descend from the moon.
If it were to emerge from the pearl, then this pearl should constantly produce flowing water; why then wait for the middle of the night to receive the white moonlight?

If it were produced from space, then since the nature of space is boundless, water would likewise have no limit; from humans to devas, all would be submerged together. How, then, could there still be those who travel by water, on land, or through the air?

Examine this further with careful attention: the moon ascends from the heavens; the pearl is held by the hand; the basin for receiving the pearl was set out by a person; but from what direction does the water flow here?
The moon and the jewel are far apart; they are neither conjoined nor fused. It is not possible that the water-crystal arose spontaneously from nowhere.
You still do not understand that within the Tathāgata-garbha, the nature of water is true emptiness and the nature of emptiness is true water—pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.

According to the minds of sentient beings and the capacity of their cognition, if one person grasps the jewel in one place, water appears in that place; if it is grasped throughout the Dharma-realm, water arises filling the Dharma-realm. Since its arising fills the entire world, how could it have a fixed location? It manifests according to karma.

The world is ignorant, deludedly regarding things as being caused by conditions or arising spontaneously; these are all merely conceptualizations and calculations of the conscious mind, consisting only of verbal expressions and lacking any real meaning whatsoever.
“Ānanda! The nature of wind has no substantial body; its movement and stillness are not constant.
When you regularly adjust your robes to enter the great assembly, if a corner of your saṃghāṭī moves and touches a person nearby, a subtle breeze will then brush against that person’s face.”
Does this wind emerge from the corner of the *kāṣāya*,
arise from empty space,
or originate from that person's face?
Ānanda! If this wind were to emerge from the corner of my *kāṣāya*, you would be wearing the wind; the garment would flutter and fly away, separating from your body.
Now as I preach the Dharma, I have let my robe hang within the assembly; look at my robe—where is the wind?
There should be no space within your garment where wind can reside.
If it were produced from empty space, then while your garment remains motionless, for what reason would there be no breeze?
Since the nature of emptiness is eternally present, the wind ought to be constantly produced.
If there were no wind, space would have to perish.
While the perishing of wind can be seen, what would the state of the perishing of space be like?
If there were arising and perishing, it could not be called "space."
It is called empty space; how then could wind emerge from it?

If the wind were produced spontaneously from that face which you are brushing, then it should brush you as it arises from that face. Since you yourself are straightening your robe, why do you brush it in the opposite direction?

Examine this carefully: the adjustment of your robe belongs to you, while your face belongs to that person; empty space is tranquil and does not participate in movement—so from which direction does the wind stir and come here?
Wind and emptiness are neither blended nor conjoined; yet it cannot be that the nature of wind exists spontaneously without a source.

You simply do not realize that within the Tathāgata-garbha, the nature of wind is true emptiness and the nature of emptiness is true wind—pure and fundamental from the beginning, pervading the entire Dharma-realm, responding to the minds of sentient beings according to the measure of what they know.

Ānanda! Just as when you alone slightly move your robe, a subtle breeze arises; this breeze pervades the Dharma-realm, sweeps through the entire land, and extends throughout the world—how could it have a fixed location? It manifests according to karma.

The world is ignorant, deludedly taking [phenomena] to be caused by conditions or to possess a nature of spontaneity; these are all merely conceptualizations and calculations of the discerning mind, consisting only of verbal expressions and entirely devoid of real meaning.
“Ānanda! Emptiness has no form; it is manifested through matter.

For example, in the city of Śrāvastī, at a place far from the river, various Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, as well as Purohitas, Caṇḍālas, and others, have newly established a dwelling and dug a well to seek water. When one foot of earth is removed, there is one foot of empty space within; likewise, when ten feet of earth are removed, one obtains ten feet of empty space in between. The depth of the empty space corresponds exactly to the amount of earth that has been excavated.”
Is this emptiness produced by the earth?
Is it due to the act of digging?
Or does it arise spontaneously without a cause?

Ānanda! If this space were produced spontaneously without cause, why was it not unobstructed before the earth was excavated? Why did one see only the great earth, with no passage or penetration at all?

If space emerges because of earth, then when the earth emerges, one should see space entering; if the earth emerges first without space entering, how can it be said that space emerges because of earth?

If there were no coming forth or entering, then empty space and the earth would fundamentally have no distinct causes; being non-distinct, they would be identical. If they are identical, then when the earth comes forth, why does space not come forth as well?
If it is due to digging that [space] comes forth, then it is the digging that brings forth space, and it should not be the case that the earth comes forth?
It does not emerge because of the digging; rather, the digging itself emerges from the earth. How, then, can you speak of "seeing emptiness"?

You should examine this more carefully, scrutinizing it with the utmost precision: the digging follows the hand as it moves in various directions, and the earth shifts according to the ground. In this way, from what source does this empty space emerge?
The void and the solid are distinct and do not function for one another; they are neither blended nor conjoined. It is illogical that the void should emerge from nowhere on its own.

If this void is by nature perfect and all-pervading, fundamentally unmoving, you should know that the earth, water, fire, and wind present before you are likewise called the five great elements. Their natures are truly interfused and harmonious; all are the Tathāgatagarbha, fundamentally without arising or ceasing.

Ānanda! Your mind is clouded and deluded; you do not realize that the four great elements are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha. You should contemplate whether space comes forth or enters, or whether it neither comes forth nor enters.

"You do not know at all that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of awareness is true emptiness and the nature of emptiness is true awareness; it is pure by its very essence, pervading the entire Dharma-realm, responding to the minds of sentient beings according to the measure of what they can know."

“Ānanda! Just as one well has space within it, so too is the space of the ten directions; it completely fills the ten directions. How could it have a specific location? It manifests according to karma.”

The world is ignorant, deludedly taking [phenomena] to be caused by conditions or to possess a nature of spontaneity; these are all merely conceptualizations and calculations of the discerning mind, consisting only of verbal expressions and lacking any real meaning whatsoever.
“Ānanda! Seeing and cognition are themselves devoid of knowledge; they exist only because of form and space.
It is as you experience now in the Jeta Grove: bright in the morning and dark by evening.”
Suppose it is midnight; if the moon is bright during the waxing phase and dark during the waning phase, then brightness and darkness are distinguished through perception.
Is this seeing then identical in substance with the light, the darkness, and the great void, or is it not of one substance?
Is it identical or not identical?
Is it different or not different? Ānanda!
If this seeing were fundamentally one with light, darkness, and space, then light and darkness—these two entities—would mutually negate each other. When it is dark, there is no light;
when it is light, it is not dark. If seeing were one with darkness, then seeing would vanish when there is light;
if it were necessarily one with light, then seeing would cease when it is dark. If it ceases, how could one see light or see darkness?
If seeing is without arising or ceasing, how can it be singular when darkness and light are distinct?

If this essence of seeing is not of one substance with darkness and light, then when you are separated from light, darkness, and empty space, what form or appearance would you discern as the fundamental source of seeing?
Detached from light, detached from darkness, and detached from empty space, this seeing is fundamentally the same as the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit.
Since light, darkness, and empty space—these three things—are all distinct, from what could seeing be established?
Light and darkness are mutually opposed; how could they ever be the same?
Apart from these three, nothing exists; how could they ever be different?
Space and vision are fundamentally without boundaries; how could they not be the same?
When you see darkness and see light, the nature [of seeing] does not shift or change; how then could it not be non-different?

You should examine this further—examine it minutely, examine it in detail, and examine it with precision: observe that light comes from the sun, darkness follows the dark moon, openness belongs to empty space, and obstruction returns to the great earth; from what source, then, does this essence of seeing arise?
Seeing and cognition are empty and inert; they are neither a composite nor a union. Thus, it cannot be that the essence of seeing emerges from nowhere on its own.

If seeing, hearing, and knowing are by nature perfectly pervasive and fundamentally unshakable, you should know that boundless, unmoving space and all its movements, as well as earth, water, fire, and wind, are collectively termed the Six Great Elements. Their natures are truly and perfectly interfused; they are all the Tathāgata-garbha, fundamentally without birth or extinction.

Ānanda! Your nature is submerged and you do not realize that your seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha. You should observe this seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing: do they arise, or do they perish?
Are they the same or different?
Are they beyond arising and ceasing?
Are they neither the same nor different?

You have never known that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of seeing and the clarity of awareness, as well as the essence of awareness and the clarity of spirit, are fundamentally pure and pervade the entire Dharma-realm, responding to the minds of sentient beings according to the measure of what they know.

Just as when the faculty of sight perceives, it pervades the entire Dharma-realm; so too with hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and the cognition of tactile sensations—their wondrous virtue is brilliantly pure and pervades the entire Dharma-realm, filling the ten voids of space. How could they have any fixed location? They manifest according to one's karma.

The world is ignorant, deludedly regarding things as being caused by conditions or arising from spontaneity; these are all merely conceptualizations and calculations of the discriminating mind, consisting only of verbal expressions and lacking any real meaning whatsoever.
"Ānanda! The nature of consciousness has no source; it arises falsely due to the six kinds of faculties and objects.

Now, survey this assembly of noble ones all around you, scanning them with your eyes. As your eyes look about, they are merely like reflections in a mirror, without further analysis. Yet your consciousness sequentially identifies them, pointing out: 'This is Mañjuśrī,' 'This is Pūrṇa,' 'This is Maudgalyāyana,' 'This is Subhūti,' and 'This is Śāriputra.'"
Does this consciousness cognize as being produced from seeing,
or as being produced from forms,
or as being produced from space?
Or does it emerge suddenly without any cause? Ānanda!

If the nature of your consciousness were born from within seeing, then in the absence of darkness, light, form, and emptiness—these four conditions—there would fundamentally be no seeing for you; if the nature of seeing itself did not exist, from what could consciousness arise?

If the nature of your consciousness arises from within the objective form and not from the faculty of seeing, then you would neither perceive light nor darkness; since light and darkness are not beheld, there would be neither form nor emptiness. If those forms do not even exist, from what could consciousness arise?

If it were produced from emptiness, it would be neither a characteristic nor a perception. Without perception, there would be no discernment; it could not, of its own accord, know light, darkness, form, or emptiness. Since it is not a characteristic, conditions would cease; since it is not a perception, seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing would have no place to be established.

Abiding in this state where both are negated, emptiness is not the same as non-existence, and existence is not the same as material objects; even if you were to activate your consciousness, what would you have to differentiate?
If it were to emerge suddenly without any cause, why would you not perceive the bright moon at midday?

You should examine this more closely, scrutinizing it with extreme care: when the seeing relies upon your pupils and projects toward external objects, it can be characterized as existing; it cannot be characterized as non-existent. Thus, from what source does this consciousness arise as its condition?

The movement of consciousness and the clarity of vision are neither a union nor a combination; the same applies to hearing, listening, sensing, and knowing. It should not be that these arise from the conditions of consciousness or emerge from nowhere.

If this conscious mind originally has no source, one should know that the capacity for discerning, seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing is perfect, tranquil, and its nature does not originate from anything external. Together with space, earth, water, fire, and wind, these are all called the Seven Great Elements; their nature is truly interfused and perfectly harmonious, and they are all the Tathāgata-garbha, fundamentally free from arising and ceasing.
Ānanda! Your mind is coarse and restless; you have not realized that the clarity and comprehension arising from seeing and hearing are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha.
You should observe these six sense-consciousnesses: are they the same as it, or are they different?
Is it empty? Is it existent?
Is it neither identical nor different?
Is it neither empty nor existent?

You originally did not know that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature-consciousness is luminous awareness and the true consciousness of awakened clarity; this wondrous awakening is profound and still, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. It contains and emits the ten voids—how could it have a fixed location? It manifests according to karma.

The world is ignorant, deludedly regarding [phenomena] as being caused by conditions or arising spontaneously; these are all merely conceptualizations and calculations of the discerning mind, consisting only of words and lacking any real meaning.

At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly, having received the subtle and wondrous instruction of the Buddha-Tathāgata, found their bodies and minds completely cleared, attaining freedom from all obstructions.

Each member of the assembly realized for themselves that their own mind pervaded the ten directions; they saw the emptiness of the ten directions as clearly as looking at a leaf held in the palm of one’s hand. They perceived that all things existing within every world were none other than the wondrously luminous, original mind of Bodhi; the essence of this mind was perfectly pervasive and encompassed the ten directions.

Looking back upon the body born of their parents, it appeared like a single mote of dust blown into the empty space of the ten directions—sometimes present, sometimes gone—or like a single bubble floating on a vast, tranquil ocean, arising and ceasing without a trace.

Clearly realizing that he had attained his own fundamental, wondrous mind, which is eternally abiding and indestructible, he prostrated to the Buddha, joined his palms, and experienced what he had never known before. In the presence of the Tathāgata, he spoke these verses in praise of the Buddha:

“O Wondrous, Profound, All-Holding, Immovable Honored One! The King of Śūraṃgama Samādhi, rare in the world, Has eliminated my inverted thoughts of billions of kalpas, And allowed me to attain the Dharma-body without passing through the aeons of saṃgha.”
May I now attain the fruit and become a Treasure King, Returning to deliver as many beings as there are sands in the Ganges;
Dedicating this profound mind to every atom and land— This is what is called repaying the Buddha’s kindness.
I prostrate and entreat the World-Honored One to bear witness: I vow to enter first into the evil world of the five turbidities;
so long as even a single sentient being has not attained Buddhahood, I shall never take *nirvāṇa* here.
O Great Hero, Possessor of Great Power and Great Compassion, I pray that you will further examine and eliminate my subtle delusions.
May I swiftly ascend to supreme enlightenment, And sit at the site of awakening throughout the worlds of the ten directions;
Though the nature of śūnyatā might perish, My vajra-mind shall never waver.

The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Tathāgata’s Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization, Definitive Meaning of the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas’ Śūraṅgama, Volume Four; also known as the Nālandā [Sūtra] from Central India.

At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O World-Honored One of Great Majestic Virtue!..."
"You skillfully expound for the sake of sentient beings the Tathāgata’s ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

World-Honored One, you have always ranked me as the foremost among those who preach the Dharma; yet now that I hear the subtle and wondrous sound of the Tathāgata’s Dharma, it is like a deaf person trying to listen for the sound of a mosquito from more than a hundred paces away—what they originally cannot see, how much less can they hear?"

Although the Buddha has proclaimed and clarified this for me so that I might eliminate my delusions, I still have not yet fully understood the ultimate meaning of these principles to reach a ground free from doubt.
World-Honored One!
Those such as Ānanda, though they have attained awakening, have not yet eliminated their habitual outflows.

"Among those of us in this assembly who have attained the state beyond outflows, although we have exhausted all taints, upon hearing the sound of the Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata, we still feel lingering doubt and regret.
World-Honored One!"

Furthermore, if all the faculties, objects, aggregates, bases, and elements of the world are the Tathāgatagarbha, pure and fundamental from the beginning, how is it that the various conditioned phenomena of mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise, undergoing successive transformations and returning again and again to the beginning?
Furthermore, as the Tathāgata has said, the natures of earth, water, fire, and wind are perfectly interfused, pervading the Dharma-realm and abiding serenely and eternally.
World-Honored One, if the nature of earth is all-pervasive, how can it accommodate water?

Since the nature of water is all-pervasive, fire cannot arise; how then can you clarify that the two natures of water and fire both pervade empty space without mutually displacing or extinguishing one another?
World-Honored One!
The nature of earth is obstructive, while the nature of space is void and pervasive; how can these two both pervade the entire Dharma-realm?
I do not understand the meaning of this matter; I only pray that the Tathāgata will let forth his great compassion to dispel the clouds of delusion for me and for the great assembly.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, thirsting for the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed compassionate instruction.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Pūrṇa and all the Arhats in the assembly who were free from outflows and beyond training:

"Today, the Tathāgata shall universally proclaim for this assembly the true nature of the ultimate meaning within the ultimate meaning, so that the śrāvakas of fixed nature in this assembly, as well as all those Arhats who have not yet attained the two kinds of emptiness and have turned toward the Mahāyāna, may all obtain the site of the quiescent cessation of the One Vehicle—the true place for the correct practice of *araṇya*."
"Listen attentively now, and I shall speak for you.
Pūrṇa and the others, revering the Buddha’s voice of Dharma, listened in silence.
The Buddha said:
“Pūrṇa! As you have said, if it is fundamentally pure and serene, how could mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise?
Have you not constantly heard the Tathāgata proclaim that the nature of awareness is wondrously luminous, and that fundamental awareness is luminously wondrous?”
Pūrṇa said: “Indeed, World-Honored One!
I have often heard the Buddha proclaim this meaning.”
The Buddha said:
"When you refer to 'awakened clarity,' does this mean that the nature itself is luminous and is thus called 'awakening'?
Or does it mean that awakening is not inherently luminous, and is therefore designated as 'luminous awakening'?"
Pūrṇa said: "If this lack of illumination were called awakening, then there would be nothing illuminated.
The Buddha said:

"If there were nothing to be illumined, then there would be no awakening through illumination. To have something is not awakening; to have nothing is not illumination. Furthermore, non-illumination is not the nature of profound, clear illumination.
The nature of awakening is necessarily luminous; it is through delusion that one creates 'illumination-awakening.
Awakening is not something to be illumined, yet because of illumination, an object is established."
Once the "object" has been falsely established, your false "subjective capacity" arises;
