within that which is neither identical nor different, a blazing diversity is formed, and by contrast to that which is different, identity is established through that very difference. As identity and difference manifest, one further establishes "neither identity nor difference."

Thus, through such mutual disturbance, weariness arises; when this weariness persists for a long time, it gives rise to dust, which becomes turbid by its own nature. From this, the afflictions of worldly toil are incited, and their arising constitutes the world.
When stillness becomes emptiness, emptiness is the same while worlds are different; yet in that state, there is neither sameness nor difference among truly conditioned dharmas.
When awakened clarity and empty dullness interact, they produce agitation, and thus the wind-circle arises to support the world.

From emptiness, agitation is born, and from the firm clarity, obstruction is established; as for those golden treasures, it is because awakened clarity establishes firmness that the gold-circle exists to maintain the land.

The solid essence of the jewel-essence was formed, and the radiant wind emerged from it. Because the wind and gold rubbed against each other, there was the nature of transformative fire. The radiance of the jewel produced moisture, and the fire-light steamed upward; thus, a water-wheel arose, containing the worlds of the ten directions. Fire ascended and water descended, their interaction establishing solidity:

the moist became the great oceans, and the dry became the continents and islands. For this reason, within those great oceans, fire-light constantly arises; within those continents and islands, rivers and streams constantly flow. Where the power of water is inferior to that of fire, it solidifies into high mountains; therefore, when mountain rocks are struck, they produce flames, and when melted, they become water. Where the power of earth is inferior to that of water, it is drawn up as vegetation; therefore, when forests and thickets encounter fire, they turn to soil, and when subjected to pressure, they turn to water.
The interaction of delusions gives rise to them, each serving as the seed for the other; through these causes and conditions, the world continues in succession.
Furthermore, Pūrṇa, this delusion of clarity is not caused by another;
the fault lies in the very act of awakening to clarity.
Once what is falsely imagined has been established, the principle of clarity cannot transcend it. By these causes and conditions, hearing does not go beyond sound and seeing does not exceed form.
Thus, the six delusions of form, fragrance, taste, touch, and so forth are accomplished. From this, seeing, perceiving, hearing, and knowing are divided;

through the mutual entanglement of similar karma, their union and separation bring about transformation. Seeing gives rise to light, and light gives rise to form; from the manifestation of light, the perception of form is formed.
Divergent views give rise to aversion, while shared perceptions give rise to affection. Affection flows as the seed, and perception is received as the womb.
Through their union, birth occurs, drawing together those of similar karma; thus, by means of causes and conditions, there arise the *kalala*, *arbuda*, and so forth.

Whether born from a womb, an egg, moisture, or transformation, each follows its appropriate course: those born from eggs are produced solely through perception, while those born from a womb depend upon emotional attachment.
Moisture corresponds through union, while transformation responds through separation; as feelings and perceptions unite and separate, they undergo mutual change.
All karmic retributions follow their respective ascent or descent; by these causes and conditions, sentient beings continue in succession.

"Pūrṇa! When the bonds of perception and craving are joined together, and craving cannot be severed, then the succession of parents and children throughout the world continues without end; these are rooted in the craving for sensual desire.

When greed and craving nourish one another, and greed cannot be halted, then all beings in the world—whether born from eggs, transformed, from moisture, or from wombs—devour one another according to their relative strength and weakness; these are rooted in the craving for killing."

When humans eat sheep, the sheep die and become humans; when humans die, they become sheep. In this way, through ten successive births, they die and are born again, preying upon one another. These evil karmas arise together and persist until the end of the future; such beings take the greed for theft as their foundation.
"You owe me my life, and I shall repay you with my debt; by reason of these causes and conditions, we have remained constantly in birth and death for hundreds of thousands of kalpas.

You loved my heart, and I cherished your form; by reason of these causes and conditions, we have remained constantly bound in entanglement for hundreds of thousands of kalpas. Killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct are the three roots; by reason of these causes and conditions, the fruits of karma continue in succession."

Pūrṇa! These three kinds of inverted continuities are all the nature of the luminous clarity of awareness that clearly cognizes; because of this cognition, appearances arise, and from deluded vision, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth are produced. All conditioned phenomena flow on in succession, and through these falsehoods, they end and begin again.

Pūrṇa said: "If this wondrous enlightenment—originally wondrously enlightened and luminous—is neither increased nor diminished compared to the Tathāgata’s mind, then why did the various conditioned phenomena of mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise without cause?

Now that the Tathāgata has attained the wondrous, empty, and luminous enlightenment, when could the habitual outflows of the conditioned world of mountains, rivers, and the great earth ever arise again?"
The Buddha told Pūrṇa:
"Suppose a person who is lost mistakes south for north in a certain village. Does this delusion exist because of delusion?"
"From what does this awakening arise? Pūrṇa replied,
"Such a deluded person arises neither because of delusion nor because of awakening."
Why is this? Delusion originally has no root; how can it arise because of delusion?
Awakening does not produce delusion; how can it arise because of awakening?
The Buddha said:
"When that deluded person is in the midst of confusion, suddenly there is an enlightened person who points it out and causes him to awaken. Pūrṇa!..."
"What do you think? Even though this person is deluded, would he become further deluded regarding this village?
"No, World-Honored One. "Pūrṇa!
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions are likewise thus.

This delusion has no fundamental source; its nature is ultimately empty. Originally there was no delusion, yet it appeared as if there were a perception of delusion. When awakening perceives delusion, the delusion is extinguished; once awakened, delusion does not arise again.
It is also like a person with cataracts seeing flowers in the sky; when the disease of the cataracts is removed, the flowers vanish from the sky.
Suppose there were a foolish person who, at that spot in the empty space where the flowers had vanished, waited for the flowers to grow back.
"Do you consider this person to be foolish or wise?
Pūrṇa replied:
"Empty space originally has no flowers; it is through deluded vision that they appear and disappear. To see the flowers vanish and perceive them as empty space is already an inversion;
to command them to reappear is truly madness."
"How can such a madman be called either foolish or wise?
The Buddha said:
"According to what you understand, why do you ask:
'Since the Buddhas and Tathāgatas possess wondrous, enlightened, luminous emptiness, when will mountains, rivers, and the great earth ever emerge again?'"

"Furthermore, it is like gold ore mixed with refined gold; once that gold has become pure, it can no longer be made impure again. Just as wood turned to ash cannot become wood again, so too is the bodhi and nirvāṇa of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas."
"Pūrṇa! Furthermore, regarding what you asked:

'The fundamental natures of earth, water, fire, and wind are perfectly interfused and pervade the Dharma-realm; yet I have doubts that the natures of water and fire would not mutually overcome and extinguish one another.'"
"Furthermore, if one examines empty space and the great earth, both pervade the dharma-realm and thus cannot coexist within one another.
"Pūrṇa! It is like empty space, whose essence is not composed of manifold characteristics, yet which does not obstruct the manifestation of those various characteristics."
Why is this so? Pūrṇa!

In that great void, when the sun shines it becomes bright; when clouds gather it becomes dark; when the wind stirs it becomes moving; when the sky clears it becomes pure; when vapors condense it becomes turbid; when dust accumulates it becomes a haze; and when water settles it becomes translucent.
"What do you think? Regarding these various conditioned marks in different directions, are they produced because of those [objects], or do they exist as emptiness?
If they are produced because of those, Pūrṇa!"

Furthermore, if the time of sunlight were itself the brightness of the sun, then the worlds of the ten directions would all share the same solar color; how then could a round sun still be seen in the sky?
If it were the brightness of space itself, then space should illuminate itself; why then does it not produce radiance during the dead of night or amidst clouds and mist?
You should know that this luminosity is neither the sun nor space, yet it is not distinct from space and the sun.

When one contemplates their essential characteristics, they are fundamentally false and cannot be pointed out or described; it is like seeking to tie empty flowers together to form an empty fruit—how can one then question the meaning of their mutual interference and cessation?

Contemplate that the fundamental nature of things is solely wondrous, enlightened clarity; this mind of wondrous, enlightened clarity was originally neither water nor fire—how, then, can you ask why they are mutually incompatible?
True, wondrous, enlightened clarity is likewise so.

If you manifest through clarity in emptiness, then emptiness appears; if you manifest through clarity in earth, water, fire, or wind individually, then each appears individually; if you manifest through clarity in them all together, then they all appear together. How do they appear together?

Pūrṇa! It is like the reflection of the sun appearing in a body of water; when two people look together at the sun in the water and walk in opposite directions—one to the east and one to the west—each perceives his own sun following him. Since there was originally no fixed standard [of a single sun], one should not raise the objection:
"This sun is one; how can it go in different directions?"
"Since each day is already dual, how can one appear?
This is a circular falsehood with nothing upon which to rely. "Pūrṇa!..."

You attempt to overturn and supplant one another by means of the characteristics of form and emptiness within the Tathāgatagarbha; yet the Tathāgatagarbha accordingly manifests as form and emptiness, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. Therefore, within it there is the movement of wind, the clarity of space, the brightness of the sun, and the darkness of clouds. Sentient beings become bewildered and distressed, turning their backs on awakening and uniting with the dust of the senses; thus they give rise to worldly afflictions and the appearances of the mundane world.

I unite my wondrous clarity—which is neither extinguished nor born—with the Tathāgata-garbha; and since this Tathāgata-garbha is solely wondrous, enlightened clarity that perfectly illumines the Dharma-realm, within it one becomes many and many become one. Within the small, the large appears; within the large, the small appears. Without moving from the site of enlightenment, I pervade the worlds of the ten directions; my body contains the infinite space of the ten directions. Upon the tip of a single hair, I manifest jeweled king-lands; sitting within a mote of dust, I turn the Great Wheel of Dharma. Because I have extinguished the dust and merged with enlightenment, I give rise to the wondrous, enlightened clarity of the nature of True Suchness.
Yet the Tathāgatagarbha is the fundamentally wondrous and perfect mind; it is neither mind nor emptiness;
it is neither earth, nor water, nor wind, nor fire;
it is neither the eye, nor the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
It is neither form, nor sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental objects;
it is neither the element of eye-consciousness, and so on up to neither the element of mind-consciousness;
it is neither clarity nor ignorance, nor the exhaustion of clarity and ignorance; and so on up to it is neither old age nor death, nor the exhaustion of old age and death.
It is not suffering, not its origin, not its cessation, and not the path;
it is not knowledge, nor attainment;
it is not dāna, not śīla, not vīrya, not kṣānti, not dhyāna, not prajñā, and not pāramitā.
In this way, it extends even to being neither a Tathāgata, nor an Arhat, nor a Samyaksaṃbuddha;
it is not Great Nirvāṇa, and it is neither permanent, nor blissful, nor self, nor pure, because these are all neither mundane nor supramundane.
That is to say, the Tathāgatagarbha is the primordial luminosity of the wondrous mind;
it is the mind itself and it is emptiness; it is earth, water, wind, and fire;
it is the eye, and likewise the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
It is form, it is sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental phenomena;
it is the eye-consciousness element, and so on, up to the mind-consciousness element;
it is clarity and ignorance, and the exhaustion of clarity and ignorance; and so on, up to old age and death, and the exhaustion of old age and death.
It is suffering, it is the origin, it is cessation, and it is the path;
it is wisdom, it is attainment;
it is dāna, it is śīla, it is vīrya, it is kṣānti, it is dhyāna, it is prajñā, and it is the pāramitās.
In this way, it extends even to being the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha;
it is Great Nirvāṇa, it is Permanence, it is Bliss, it is Self, and it is Purity, because these are identical with both the mundane and the supramundane.

This is the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrously luminous source of the mind, which is beyond both identity and difference, and is both identical and non-identical. How can sentient beings within the three realms of existence, as well as world-transcending Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, use their minds of limited knowledge to speculate upon the unsurpassed Bodhi of the Tathāgata, or employ worldly language to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision?

For example, although lutes, harps, *konghou*, and *pipa* possess exquisite sounds, they can never produce them without skilled fingers; you and all sentient beings are just the same. The precious, awakened true mind is fully complete in each and every one of you, just as when I press my finger, the Sea-Seal manifests its radiance.

"As soon as you raise your mind, the dust of worldly toil arises first; this is because you have not diligently sought the unsurpassed path of enlightenment, but instead cherish the Lesser Vehicle and consider a small attainment sufficient.

Pūrṇa said, "My precious, enlightened, perfect, and luminous true, wondrous, pure mind is no different from that of the Tathāgata’s perfect fullness. Yet, in the past, I encountered beginningless delusions and have long remained in saṃsāra; though I have now attained the Holy Vehicle, I am still not yet ultimate."
World-Honored One!

All delusions are completely extinguished, leaving only the wondrous, true, and eternal. I venture to ask the Tathāgata: for what reason do all sentient beings possess delusion, thereby obscuring their own wondrous clarity and undergoing this drowning?
The Buddha told Pūrṇa:
"Although you have removed your doubts, other delusions remain unresolved.
I shall now question you again regarding various matters manifest in the world."

Have you not heard how, in the city of Śrāvastī, the man named Yan-liao-da-duo suddenly one morning looked at his face in a mirror; he became attached to the head in the mirror whose features were clearly visible, yet grew resentful that his own head could not see its own face and features, and thus, perceiving it as a shapeless ghoul, he ran about wildly in madness.
"What do you think? For what reason does this person run about madly?
Pūrṇa replied, "This man’s mind is deranged; there is no other cause."
The Buddha said:
"The wondrous awakening is perfect and bright; its fundamental nature is perfect, bright, and wondrous. Since it is designated as 'delusion,' how could it have a cause?
If it had a cause, how could it be called delusion?"

From the mutual causation of various deluded thoughts, one has accumulated confusion upon confusion throughout countless kalpas; though Buddhas have clarified the truth, they cannot turn one back. Thus, the cause of delusion exists because of delusion itself. When one recognizes that delusion has no cause, then the false has nothing to rely upon; since there is not even birth, what is there to be extinguished?

One who has attained Bodhi is like a person upon waking who recounts events from a dream; though their mind may be sharp and clear, for what cause or condition could they seek to grasp objects within that dream? How much more so when, fundamentally, there were no such things to begin with?

Just as that person in the city, Yanjadatta, had no cause or condition for suddenly fearing his own head and running away; once his madness suddenly subsides, the head is not obtained from without, and even if his madness has not yet subsided, what has he actually lost?
Pūrṇa! Such is the nature of delusion; by what cause does it exist?

You need only refrain from following the threefold continuity of the world, karmic results, and sentient beings through your discrimination. When these three conditions are severed, the three causes will not arise. Then the madness of your inner *yadṛcchā* (Evil Desire) will naturally subside. This subsiding is itself Bodhi—the supremely pure and luminous mind that has always pervaded the Dharma-realm. It is not obtained from others; why rely on arduous toil or laborious cultivation and realization?

"It is like a person who has tied a wish-fulfilling jewel within his own garment, yet remains unaware of it; wandering through foreign lands in poverty and destitution, begging for food, he is truly impoverished though the jewel has never been lost. Suddenly, a wise person points out the jewel to him, and his every wish is fulfilled according to his heart, bringing about great wealth and abundance; only then does he realize that the divine jewel was not obtained from without."
At that moment, Ānanda rose from among the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!

You have just explained that through the severance of the three conditions for the karmas of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, the three causes do not arise; thus, the madness of Citta naturally subsides within the mind. This subsiding is itself Bodhi, which is not obtained from others.”
Thus, the principle of causes and conditions is clear and evident; why would the Tathāgata suddenly discard it?

It was through causes and conditions that I attained awakening of mind. World-Honored One, is this truth intended only for us young śrāvakas still in training? Here in this assembly, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Śāriputra, Subhūti, and others, having heard the Buddha’s teaching on causes and conditions from an elderly brahmin, resolved their minds, attained awakening, and achieved the state of being without outflows.

If you now state that bodhi does not arise from causes and conditions, then the doctrine of spontaneity (*svayambhū*) taught by Kauṣṭhila and others in Rājagṛha would constitute the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
We pray that you will deign to show great compassion and dispel our confusion.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"Just as in the case of the youth Yanjadatta within the city, if the causal conditions for his madness were to be extinguished, then his non-mad state would naturally emerge; the principle of naturalness regarding causal conditions reaches its ultimate limit here."

Ānanda! The head of Śaśaviṣāṇa was originally natural; it was originally so of itself, and there was no "not-so" that was not itself. For what reason and by what conditions did he become terrified of his own head and run about madly?
If madness occurs due to natural causes, why does one not likewise lose [one's head] due to natural causes?
Your original head has never been lost; it is only through deluded fear that madness arises. Since there has never been any change, what need is there for external conditions?
Madness is natural to the fundamental; fundamentally there is madness and fear. Before one was mad, where did this madness lie hidden?
Non-madness is natural; the head is fundamentally without delusion—why then do you run about in a frenzy?

If one awakens to the original head and recognizes that the frantic running was caused by conditions, then both the causes and conditions are seen as natural and merely conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Therefore, I say that when the three conditions are severed, that is itself the bodhicitta.
When the bodhicitta arises, the mind of arising and ceasing ceases; this is merely arising and ceasing. When both ceasing and arising are exhausted, there is the path of non-effort (*anābhoga*).

If there were such a thing as spontaneity (*svabhāva*), then it would follow that a spontaneous mind arises and the mind of arising and ceasing ceases—this too would be arising and ceasing. That which is without arising and ceasing is called spontaneity.

Just as in the world, when various phenomena are mixed and blended into a single entity, it is called "the nature of combination" (*saṃyoga-svabhāva*); that which is not combined is termed "the nature of suchness" (*tathatā-svabhāva*).

Suchness is not suchness, and combination is not combination; when both combination and suchness are left behind, and both leaving behind and combining are negated—only this phrase is called the "Dharma free from conceptual proliferation" (*niṣprapañca-dharma*).

Enlightenment and nirvana still lie far beyond you; they cannot be realized through the arduous cultivation and verification of kalpas. Even if you were to memorize and uphold the twelve divisions of the sutras of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, with their pure and wondrous principles as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, it would only serve to increase your frivolous arguments.

Although you have discoursed upon causes and conditions with such clarity and certainty that people of the world acclaim you as foremost among the learned, yet despite this long eon’s habituation through extensive learning, you could not escape the peril of the Mātanga woman. For what reason did you wait for my Buddha-peak divine mantra, whereby the fire of lust in the Mātanga woman’s heart was suddenly extinguished, she attained the stage of Anāgāmin, became a forest of diligence within my Dharma, the river of craving was dried up, and you were thereby liberated?
Therefore, Ānanda!

Although you have for kalpas memorized and upheld the Tathāgata’s secret and wondrous adornments, it would not equal a single day of cultivating untainted karma (*anāsrava-karman*) to remain far removed from the two sufferings of worldly hatred and love.

Take, for example, Mātanga, who was formerly a courtesan; through the power of the divine mantra, her lustful desires were dissolved. She is now known within the Dharma as the Bhikṣuṇī Śrīmatī, and together with Yaśodharā, the mother of Rāhula, she has realized their past causes. Knowing that throughout successive lives they suffered because of craving and attachment, and because they cultivated untainted goodness for a single thought-moment, some have escaped the entanglements while others have received predictions of enlightenment.
"How can you deceive yourself, still lingering in sight and hearing?

When Ānanda and the great assembly heard the Buddha’s instruction, their doubts were dispelled and they realized the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*). Their bodies and minds became light and serene, attaining a state never before experienced. Weeping again with sorrow, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"O Unsurpassed One of Great Compassion, King of Pure Jewels, you have skillfully opened our minds. By means of such various causes, conditions, and expedient means, you have exhorted and uplifted us, leading those submerged in darkness out of the sea of suffering."
“World-Honored One!

Although I have now received such a Dharma sound and know that the Tathāgatagarbha—the wondrous, enlightened, and luminous mind—pervades the worlds of the ten directions, containing and nurturing the pure, jewel-adorned lands of the Wondrous Enlightened Kings throughout the Buddha-lands of the ten directions;
yet the Tathāgata further rebukes me for my lack of merit in mere learning and my failure to engage in cultivation.”
I am now like a traveler who has suddenly been granted a magnificent mansion by the Heavenly King; though I have obtained this great residence, I must enter it through its gates.

I only pray that the Tathāgata will not abandon his great compassion, but will show me—and all those in this assembly who are still obscured by darkness—how to relinquish the Lesser Vehicle and fully attain the path of the Tathāgata’s original aspiration toward Nirvana without remainder. May those in training learn how to subdue their former attachments to external objects, obtain *dhāraṇī*, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground and stood with single-minded devotion before the assembly, awaiting the Buddha’s compassionate instruction.

At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for the pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas in the assembly who had not yet attained mastery over the bodhicitta, and for the sake of sentient beings in the future Dharma-ending age who shall resolve to attain bodhicitta after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, revealed the path of sublime practice of the Unsurpassed Vehicle and declared to Ānanda and the great multitude:
"You who have resolutely resolved to attain bodhicitta and do not grow weary of the Tathāgata’s wondrous samādhi, should first clarify the two definitive meanings of the initial mind that awakens."
How are the two meanings of the initial mind determined? "Ānanda! Regarding the primary meaning:

if you wish to cast aside the vehicle of the Śrāvakas and cultivate the Bodhisattva vehicle to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, you should carefully examine whether the mind generated at the stage of the causal ground is identical with the awakening at the stage of the resultant ground."
Or is it different? Ānanda!

If, during the stage of the causal ground, one takes a mind subject to arising and ceasing as the fundamental cause for practice, yet seeks the Buddha-vehicle of non-arising and non-ceasing, such a thing is impossible.
For this reason, you should illuminate the vessel-world: all conditioned phenomena are subject to transformation and extinction.
Ānanda! Observe the world: among all conditioned phenomena, which one does not decay? Yet, one never hears of empty space rotting or decaying.
Why is this? Emptiness cannot be created, for it is without destruction or cessation from beginning to end.

Thus, within your body, solidity is earth, moisture is water, warmth is fire, and movement is wind. By means of these four entanglements, your profoundly still, perfect, wondrously enlightened, and luminous mind is partitioned into seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing; from beginning to end, it has become fivefold turbid.
"What constitutes turbidity? Ānanda!

It is like clear water, which is inherently pure and pristine; yet when dust, soil, ash, or sand—substances that are by nature obstructive—are introduced, these two entities naturally do not accord with one another. When people of the world take that soil and dust and cast it into the pure water, the soil loses its obstructive nature and the water loses its clarity; their appearance becomes turbid, and this is what we call 'turbidity. Your fivefold turbidity is likewise thus."
“Ānanda! You see the empty space pervading the worlds of the ten directions, yet the emptiness and the seeing are not distinguished.
There is emptiness without substance, and there is seeing without cognition; these interweave through delusion to form this first layer, which is called the *kalpa-turbidity*.”

Your body currently manifests as a composite of the four great elements; seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are congested and obstructed, while water, fire, wind, and earth revolve to produce these perceptions. These interweave to falsely form this body; this second layer is called the turbidity of views.

Furthermore, within your mind, the nature of recollection, cognition, and repeated study gives rise to knowing and seeing, which manifests as the six sense objects; yet apart from these objects there is no form, and apart from awareness there is no nature. These characteristics interweave to form delusion; this is the third layer, called the turbidity of afflictions.

Furthermore, you arise and perish morning and evening without ceasing; your perceptions and insights constantly desire to remain in this world, while the movement of karma perpetually shifts the lands. These factors interweave to form delusion; this is the fourth turbidity, called the turbidity of sentient beings.

Your seeing and hearing originally possess no distinct natures; yet the various sensory objects are separated and obstructed, appearing as if they were distinct productions. In their essential nature they know one another, but in their functional operation they oppose one another. The standards for identity and difference are lost, and through mutual entanglement they falsely come into being. This fifth layer is called the turbidity of life.

“Ānanda! If you now wish to cause your seeing, hearing, awareness, and cognition to accord distantly with the Tathāgata’s permanence, bliss, self, and purity, you should first select the root of birth and death, and establish yourself upon the nature of the unarisen and undying, the perfect and profound stillness. By means of this stillness, you should revolve back against the false and extinguish arising and ceasing; thus you will subdue the returning original awakening and attain the originally luminous awakening. Taking this nature free from arising and ceasing as the mind for the ground of practice, you may thereafter perfectly accomplish the cultivation and realization of the ground of fruition.”

It is like turbid water settled in a clean vessel; when it is still, deep, and unmoving, the sand and silt naturally sink and clear water appears before one—this is called the initial subduing of adventitious afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa*).
When the mud is removed and only pure water remains, this is called the eternal severance of fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*).

When the marks of clarity are pure and refined, all transformations and manifestations do not become afflictions; they all accord with the wondrous virtue of the purity of Nirvana. "The second meaning is this:

if you truly desire to resolve upon Bodhicitta and give rise to great courage and vigor within the Bodhisattva Vehicle, you must resolutely abandon all conditioned marks. You should carefully examine the root of afflictions: who created these that have, since beginningless time, initiated karma and moistened rebirth?"
Who experiences [this]? Ānanda!
If you cultivate bodhi without carefully examining the root of afflictions, you will be unable to know the false roots and sense objects.
If you do not even know where the inversion lies, how can you subdue it and attain the rank of Tathāgata?
Ānanda! Observe those in the world who untie knots: if they do not see what has been knotted, how can they know how to untie it?
I have not heard of space being shattered or torn asunder by you. Why is this?
Because space is without form or characteristic, and thus possesses neither bondage nor liberation.

Thus, your present eyes, ears, nose, tongue, as well as your body and mind—these six acting as intermediaries for thieves who plunder the family’s treasures—cause sentient beings to be bound from beginningless time; therefore, you are unable to transcend the physical world.
“Ānanda! What is meant by the world of sentient beings?
‘World’ (loka) refers to the constant flux of time, while ‘realm’ (dhātu) refers to spatial orientation.”

You should now know that east, west, south, north, southeast, southwest, northeast, northwest, above, and below constitute the directions (dis); the past, future, and present constitute the times (adhvan).
Thus, there are ten positions of direction and three flows of time.
All sentient beings weave their delusive appearances together, such that within their bodies there is exchange and movement, and worlds intersect one another.

Although the nature of these realms might be clearly defined by fixed positions throughout the ten directions, in the mundane world we only perceive east, west, south, and north; as for above and below, they have no fixed position, and as for the center, it has no fixed direction. These four numbers must be clearly established as they intersect with the world: three times four and four times three result in twelve; through further transformation and multiplication, this becomes thirty, then one hundred, then one thousand. When all these stages are summarized within the six sense faculties, each possesses its own merit of one thousand two hundred.

“Ānanda! You must further determine the relative superiority and inferiority among these faculties. For instance, when the eye looks out, it sees darkness behind and light before; the area directly ahead is entirely bright while the area directly behind is entirely dark; and when looking to the left and right, it perceives only two-thirds of the field. In sum, the merit produced by the eye is incomplete; if one-third of its function is considered a merit, then one-third lacks such merit. Thus, you should know that the eye possesses only eight hundred merits.

As for the ear, it hears in all ten directions without omission; whether sounds are near or far, it discerns them without limit. You should know that the faculty of the ear is complete with twelve hundred merits.”

Just as the nose’s sense of smell functions through the inhalation and exhalation of breath—wherein there is an out-breath and an in-breath, yet the intermediate junction is missing—it can be verified that the nose-faculty lacks one-third of its parts; thus, one should know that the nose possesses only eight hundred merits.

Just as the tongue proclaims all mundane and supramundane wisdom, such that its expressions have distinct boundaries while its principles are inexhaustible, one should know that the tongue-faculty is complete with twelve hundred merits.

Just as the body perceives touch and cognizes the disagreeable and the agreeable, it can perceive when in contact but does not know when separated; since separation constitutes one part and contact constitutes two, it can be verified that the body-faculty lacks one-third of its parts; thus, one should know that the body possesses only eight hundred merits.

The faculty of intention silently accommodates all mundane and supramundane phenomena throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time; from the sages to the ordinary beings, there is nothing it does not encompass, reaching to the very limits of existence. You should know that this faculty of intention is endowed with one thousand two hundred merits in their full perfection.

“Ānanda! If you now wish to go against the current of the flow of birth and death, and trace it back to its root until you reach that which is neither born nor extinguished, you must examine these six faculties of sensory experience: which one is the source?”
Who is liberated?
Who is deep?
Who is shallow?
Who possesses perfect penetration? Who lacks it?

If you can awaken to the faculty of perfect penetration herein, you will turn back the beginningless flow of delusory karma and follow the path of perfect penetration; compared to those with imperfect faculties, your progress will be many times greater than that of eons. I shall now fully reveal the six kinds of profound, perfect luminosity and the measure of their inherent merits as they are. You may carefully examine and choose whichever one you find suitable for entry, and I shall clarify it for you so that you may advance.

The Tathāgatas of the ten directions have all practiced within each of the eighteen realms and attained the perfect, unsurpassed Bodhi; among these, there is no distinction of superiority or inferiority.

However, because you are of inferior capacity and have not yet attained the perfectly sovereign wisdom therein, I proclaim this method so that you may enter deeply through a single gate. Once you have entered one without delusion, the six faculties of cognition will simultaneously become pure.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
How can one flow against the current and enter deeply through a single gate, thereby enabling all six faculties to become pure simultaneously?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“You have now attained the fruit of *srotāpanna* and have already extinguished the delusions of the world of sentient beings within the three realms that are abandoned through insight; yet you still do not know the beginningless, empty habitual tendencies accumulated within the faculties throughout successive births. Those tendencies must be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), so how much more so the various divisions and enumerations of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing within them?”
"Now, you should observe for yourself these six faculties present before you:
are they one, or are they six? Ānanda!"
If you say they are one, why does the ear not see, why does the eye not hear, why does the head not tread, and why do the feet not speak?
If these six faculties were definitively established as six, then when I now proclaim this subtle and wondrous Dharma-door to you in this assembly, which of your six faculties comes to receive it?
Ānanda said, “I hear with my ears.
The Buddha said:
"You hear with your own ears; what concern is this for your body or speech?

Your mouth comes to inquire about the meaning, while your body arises to show reverence and acceptance. Therefore, you should know that it does not end as one but culminates in six, nor does it end as six but culminates in one; ultimately, your faculties are neither fundamentally one nor fundamentally six."

Ānanda! You should know that these faculties are neither one nor six. Due to the inversion and vicissitudes since beginningless time, the notions of "one" and "six" have arisen within the perfect and湛 (zhan—profoundly still) nature. Although you, as a Srotāpanna, have attained the dissolution of the six, you have not yet eliminated the "one. It is like the great void of space which, when combined with various vessels, is called "different spaces" because the shapes of the vessels differ; yet when the vessels are removed and one contemplates the space, one speaks of space as being "one. How could that great void of space be either the same or different for you?
How much less could one say that they are either identical or different?
Thus, your understanding of the six faculties of sensory reception is also like this.

Due to the mutual contrast between the two—light and darkness—within the wondrously perfect [nature], the stillness becomes adhered to, giving rise to vision. The essence of vision reflects forms and, by binding with forms, constitutes the faculty. The source of this faculty is termed the "pure four great elements"; therefore, the substance of the eye is named after its shape as a cluster of grapes. This floating root, amidst the four sense-objects, flows outward and rushes toward forms.

Through the mutual striking of the two conditions of movement and stillness, within the wondrous perfection, the clarity is adhered to and hearing is activated. The essence of hearing reflects sound and, by coiling in upon sound, forms the faculty; this fundamental source is termed the "pure four great elements," and thus the substance of the ear is named after a newly curled leaf. The floating faculties and the four objects flow outward in pursuit of sound.

Through the mutual activation of the two conditions of penetration and obstruction, within the wondrous perfection, the clarity is adhered to and smelling is activated. The essence of smelling reflects fragrance and, by receiving fragrance, forms the faculty; this fundamental source is termed the "pure four great elements," and thus the substance of the nose is named after a pair of hanging claws. The floating faculties and the four objects flow outward in pursuit of fragrance.

Through the intermingling of the two aspects of stillness and change, within the wondrous perfection, the clarity adheres to the stillness to produce tasting. The essence of tasting reflects flavors, and by coagulating flavors, it forms the sense organ; the root of this organ is termed the "pure four great elements," and for this reason the substance of the tongue is said to be like a half-moon, while the floating organ’s four objects flow outward in pursuit of flavors.

Through the friction of the two aspects of separation and union, within the wondrous perfection, the clarity adheres to the stillness to produce sensation. The essence of sensation reflects touch, and by striking against touch, it forms the sense organ; the root of this organ is termed the "pure four great elements," and for this reason the substance of the body is said to be like the head of a waist-drum, while the floating organ’s four objects flow outward in pursuit of touch.

Due to the two kinds of continuity—arising and ceasing—within the wondrous perfection, the stillness becomes adhered to, giving rise to cognition. This essence of cognition reflects phenomena and, by apprehending them, forms the sense organs. The fundamental source of these organs is termed the "pure four great elements. Consequently, they are named the "mental faculty," like seeing within a dark chamber; the floating roots and the four sensory objects flow outward in distraction, rushing toward phenomena.

“Ānanda! Thus, regarding these six faculties: from that awakened clarity (*jñāna-prakāśa*), there arises clarity within clarity and awakening within awakening. Having lost that essential discernment, they become stuck in delusion and emit light. Therefore, now that you are removed from darkness and removed from light, the substance of seeing does not exist; removed from motion and removed from stillness, the essence of hearing fundamentally does not exist; without penetration and without obstruction, the nature of smelling does not arise; neither changing nor tranquil, tasting has no outlet; neither separated nor joined, the perception of touch is fundamentally non-existent; without cessation and without arising, where could the faculty of cognition find its resting place?”

If you simply do not follow after these twelve characteristics of conditioned existence—motion and stillness, union and separation, tranquility and change, penetration and obstruction, birth and death, darkness and light—but instead pluck out one sense-faculty to detach from its clinging and settle inwardly, then that settling will return to the original reality and give rise to the fundamental radiance of clarity.

Once this nature of radiance has manifested, the remaining attachments of the other five faculties will be spontaneously and completely severed; your cognition will no longer arise from external objects, and clarity will manifest by relying on the faculties without following them. Thus, the six faculties will function interchangeably for one another.
“Ānanda! Do you not know that within this assembly, Aniruddha sees though he has no eyes;
and the Naga Bhadrananda hears though he has no ears?
The Goddess of the Gaṅgā does not perceive fragrance with her nose;
Gavāmpati perceives flavors with his tongue;

and the Śūnyatā-deva has no body yet possesses the sense of touch, appearing for a moment when reflected within the light of the Tathāgata, yet having the nature of wind, his substance is fundamentally non-existent.

Śrāvakas who have attained the tranquility of the various meditative absorptions of cessation, such as Mahākāśyapa here in this assembly, have long since extinguished the faculty of mind, yet they possess a perfect and clear understanding that does not depend on mental ideation.

Ānanda! Now, if your sense-faculties are completely uprooted and their inner clarity radiates light, then these superficial phenomena and the various changing appearances of the vessel-world will be like ice melting in hot water; at that very thought, they shall transform into supreme awareness.

Ānanda! It is like those people of the world who perceive with their eyes: if they were to close them suddenly, the appearance of darkness would manifest before them; the six sense organs would become dark, and head and feet would appear indistinguishable. If someone were to run their hand over the outside of their body, although they do not see it, they can distinguish head from foot, and their perception remains the same. Because seeing depends on light, when there is darkness, seeing becomes non-seeing; yet if light were absent and seeing arose spontaneously, then all appearances of darkness could never obscure it. Since the faculties and their objects have already been dissolved, how could the clarity of awareness not be perfectly wondrous?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, if one seeks the permanently abiding state through the mind of awakening on the causal ground, it must correspond with the designations of the resultant stage.”
World-Honored One!

If, within this state, bodhi, nirvana, true thusness (tathatā), buddha-nature, the amala-consciousness, the empty tathāgatagarbha, and the great perfect mirror-wisdom—though these seven names and designations are distinct—their pure and perfect essence is firm and solid, like a diamond-king, eternally abiding and indestructible;

yet if this seeing and hearing were devoid of darkness and light, motion and stillness, penetration and obstruction, and ultimately lacked any substance, being like the thinking mind which, apart from external objects, originally has no existence, how could one take this ultimate annihilation as the cause for cultivation, desiring to obtain the Tathāgata’s seven fruits of eternal abiding?
World-Honored One!

If one is free from light and darkness and perceives ultimate emptiness, then—just as when there are no external objects, thoughts of self-nature cease—one may advance and retreat, circling through subtle investigation, and find that fundamentally there is neither a self-mind nor mental factors associated with a self. With whom, then, shall one establish a cause to seek unsurpassed enlightenment?
If the Tathāgata previously taught that [the nature of reality] is profound, pure, perfect, and eternal, yet now contradicts those sincere words, it would ultimately become mere frivolous discourse.
How can the Tathāgata be said to be one who speaks the truth?
I pray only that you will bestow great compassion and dispel my ignorance and parsimony.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“Though you have studied much and possess great learning, you have not yet exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*). In your mind, you merely know the causes of inversion, but when true inversion actually manifests before you, you truly cannot recognize it. Fearing that your sincere heart may still not be convinced and submissive, I shall now test you with mundane matters to remove your doubts.”
Immediately, the Tathāgata commanded Rāhula to strike the bell once and asked Ānanda,
"Do you hear it now?
Ānanda and the great assembly replied together:
“I hear it.
When the bell had ceased and there was no sound, the Buddha asked again:
“Do you hear it now?”
Ānanda and the great assembly all replied,
"We did not hear it.
Then Rāhula struck once more, and the Buddha asked again:
“Did you hear it just now?
Ānanda and the great assembly replied,
“We all heard it.”
The Buddha asked Ānanda:
"How do you hear? How do you not hear?"
Ānanda and the great assembly together addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If the bell is struck, we hear its sound; once the striking has ceased and the sound has faded until both resonance and echo are utterly cut off, that is called 'no hearing'."
The Tathāgata again commanded Rāhula to strike the bell and asked Ānanda,
"Do you hear the sound now?
Ānanda replied:
"Sound. After a short while, the sound vanished, and the Buddha asked again:
"Do you have sound now?"
Ānanda and the great assembly replied,
“There is no sound.
After a short while, Rāhula came again to strike the bell, and the Buddha asked once more:
"Can you hear the sound now?
Ānanda and the great assembly all replied,
"We can hear it."
The Buddha asked Ānanda:
"What do you mean by 'sound,' and what do you mean by 'no sound'?"
Ānanda and the great assembly together addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If the bell is struck, it is called 'having sound. When the striking has ceased and the sound has faded until both resonance and echo are utterly extinguished, it is called 'being without sound.'"
The Buddha said to Ānanda and the great assembly:
"Why do you now speak with such deceptive confusion?
The great assembly and Ānanda then asked the Buddha together:
"How is it that I am now called evasive?
The Buddha said,
"When I asked you whether you had heard [the Dharma], you replied that you had heard."
He asked again, "Regarding 'your voice,' you then say 'voice.
Since the responses regarding 'hearing' and 'sound' are not fixed, how is this not called evasive equivocation? Ānanda!"

When the sound has vanished and there is no resonance, you say there is no hearing. If, in reality, there were no hearing, the nature of hearing would have already ceased and would be like a withered tree; when the bell is struck again, how could you know it?

To know existence and non-existence is simply because the sensory object of sound is either present or absent; how could that nature of hearing itself be subject to existence or non-existence for you?
If hearing were truly non-existent, who would be there to know its non-existence?
Therefore, Ānanda!

Sound undergoes its own arising and ceasing within the faculty of hearing; it is not that the sound you hear arises and ceases, thereby causing your nature of hearing to become either existent or non-existent.
If you are still deluded by inversion, mistaking sound for hearing, how can you not find it strange that you are so confused as to take the permanent to be intermittent?
You must never say that hearing has no inherent nature apart from movement and stillness, or closure and openness.

It is like a person in a deep sleep, lying comfortably on a bed with a soft pillow. While he sleeps, someone in his house pounds silk or husks rice. In his dream, the man hears the sound of pounding and husking, yet misinterprets it as something else—perhaps the beating of a drum or the striking of a bell. During the dream, he wonders to himself why the bell sounds like wood or stone. Suddenly waking up, he immediately recognizes the sound of the pestle and tells his family:
"While I was dreaming, I was confused by this sound of pounding and took it for the sound of a drum."

"Ānanda! In that person's dream, how could they recall stillness or movement, opening or closing, penetration or obstruction? Although their body is asleep, the nature of hearing is not darkened. Even if your body were to dissolve and the light of life were to pass away, how could this nature be extinguished by you?"

Because all sentient beings, from time immemorial, have followed after forms and sounds, flowing with their thoughts, they have never awakened to the nature that is pure, wondrous, and eternal. Instead of following what is constant, they pursue birth and death; thus, life after life, they wander through defilement.

If you abandon birth and death and maintain the true eternity, the light of constancy will manifest before you, and the objects, the faculties, the consciousness, and the mind will fall away at once. When both the dust of conceptual appearances and the grime of cognitive emotions are removed, your Dharma-eye will become clear and bright at that very moment; how could you then fail to achieve unsurpassed perfect enlightenment?
The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Sūtra on the Myriad Practices of Śūraṅgama, Scroll Four.

The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Tathāgata’s Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization, the Definitive Meaning of the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas’ Śūraṅgama, Scroll Five. Also known as: The Great Path of Nālandā in Central India.
From the *Sūtra on the Site*, excerpted from the *Abhiṣeka Section* and circulated separately, translated by the Tang dynasty Indian śramaṇa Prajñāmitra: Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

Although the Tathāgata has explained this secondary approach, when I observe those in the world who attempt to untie knots, if they do not know the origin from which the knot was tied, I believe such people will ultimately never be able to untie it.
“World-Honored One!

It is the same for me and the śrāvakas in this assembly who are still in training: from beginningless time, we have been subject to the simultaneous arising and ceasing of various forms of ignorance. Although we have attained such roots of goodness through extensive learning and are called ‘those who have left the home life,’ we remain like those afflicted by quotidian malaria.”
I only pray that you, out of great compassion, will take pity on those submerged in the depths of suffering. Today, what constitutes bondage for body and mind, and from what is liberation named?
Furthermore, may sentient beings facing future hardships be enabled to escape saṃsāra and not fall into the three realms of existence.

Having spoken these words, Ānanda and the entire assembly prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground, shedding tears and raising their hearts in sincere devotion, awaiting the unsurpassed instruction of the Buddha-Tathāgata.

At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for Ānanda and all those in the assembly who were still in training, and also to serve as a cause for transcendence and as eyes for the future for all sentient beings, rubbed the crown of Ānanda’s head with his hand of Jambūnada purple-gold light. Immediately, the worlds of the Buddhas throughout the ten directions shook in six ways. From the crowns of the pores of all the Tathāgatas dwelling in those worlds, precious lights issued forth; simultaneously, these lights came from those worlds to the Jeta Grove and drenched the crown of the Tathāgata’s head, a sight never before seen by this great assembly.
Thereupon Ānanda and the great assembly together heard the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, speaking with one voice:
"Excellent, Ānanda!"

If you wish to recognize and understand the co-nascent ignorance that causes you to revolve in birth and death as the root of bondage, it is none other than your six sense faculties; there is no other thing.

Furthermore, if you wish to know unsurpassed Bodhi, which enables you to swiftly ascend to the blissful liberation of quiescent, wondrous, and eternal stillness, it is likewise your six sense faculties and nothing else.
Although Ānanda had heard such a Dharma-sound, his mind was still not yet clear; he bowed his head to the Buddha and said:
"How can it be that my cycle of birth and death and the wondrous, eternal bliss are both identical to these six faculties, and nothing else?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“The faculties and their objects share the same source; bondage and liberation are non-dual; the nature of consciousness is illusory, like flowers in the sky. Ānanda!”
Cognition arises from objects, and appearances exist because of the sense organs; yet both appearance and seeing lack inherent nature, being like the intertwined stalks of a reed.
Therefore, when you now establish cognition within your perception and vision, this is the very root of ignorance;
when perception and vision are free from [the notion of] seeing, this is precisely nirvana—taintless, truly pure.
"How could any other thing possibly exist within this?
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The true nature is empty of conditioned phenomena; Because they arise through conditions, they are like illusions."
The unconditioned has no arising or ceasing; it is unreal, like flowers in the sky.
When delusion speaks, it reveals the various truths; yet delusion and truth are both equally delusive.
Since it is neither true nor untrue, how can there be a seer and that which is seen?
In the interim there is no substantial nature; therefore, they are like intertwined reeds.
Since bondage and liberation share the same cause, there are not two paths for the sage and the ordinary person.
Observe the nature within the interweaving: it is neither emptiness nor existence.
Delusion and obscurity are ignorance; illumination and clarity are liberation.
The untying of knots follows a sequence; when the six are untied, even the one vanishes.
Select the faculty that is most perfectly penetrating; upon entering the stream, you shall achieve true awakening.
The *ādānavijñāna* is a subtle consciousness; its habitual tendencies form a violent torrent.
Fearing that people might mistake the real for the unreal, I have never openly taught it.
When the mind takes hold of its own mind, what is not illusory becomes an illusory phenomenon.
There is nothing that is not illusion; since even non-illusion does not arise, how could illusory phenomena be established?
The precious awakening of the Vajra King is the samādhi of illusion.
"In a single snap of the fingers, one transcends to the stage beyond training.
This Abhidharma is the sole path to Nirvana for the Bhagavāns of the ten directions.

Thereupon, Ānanda and the great assembly, having heard the Buddha-Tathāgata’s unsurpassed compassionate instruction—this *geya* and *gāthā* which were interwoven, refined, exquisite, and crystal clear—felt their minds and eyes opened to clarity, and they marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
Ānanda joined his palms, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said to him:

“Now that I have heard the Buddha’s words of unobstructed great compassion—pure by nature, wondrously eternal, and true—I still do not fully comprehend the sequence for loosening the knots so that the six may be resolved and the one may vanish.”
"May you deign to extend great compassion once more to this assembly and those of the future, bestowing the sound of the Dharma to wash away our deep-seated defilements.

Immediately, from his lion throne, the Tathāgata adjusted his *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* robe, gathered his *saṃghāṭī*, and looked down at a seven-jeweled table. Reaching out his hand over the table, he took the flowered cloth offered by the deva Kāpila and, before the great assembly, tied it into a single knot.
He pointed to it and said to Ānanda, "What is this called?"
Ānanda and the great assembly together addressed the Buddha, saying,
“This is called a knot. Thereupon,
the Tathāgata took the folded flower-scarf and tied another knot, asking Ānanda once more:
“What is this called?
Ānanda and the great assembly again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“This is also called a knot.”

In this manner, he successively folded and twisted the flowered cloth until six knots were formed; as each knot was completed, he took hold of the knot he had just made and asked Ānanda, "What is this called?"
Ānanda and the great assembly were likewise; they responded to the Buddha in succession, and this was called "tying.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"When I first tied the cloth, you called it a 'knot. This folded flower-cloth was originally but a single strip; as for the second and third folds, why do you all again call them 'knots'?"
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This cloth made from woven layers of precious flowers, though originally a single substance, as I contemplate it:”

"Just as a single twist of a cord receives the name 'one knot,' and if one twists it a hundred times, it will ultimately be called 'a hundred knots,' how much more so with this cloth which has only six knots; it will never reach seven, nor will it stop at five."
"How is it that the Tathāgata permits only the first [knot], while the second and third are not called 'knots'?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"Regarding this precious flowered cloth, you know that this cloth originally consists of only a single strand; when I tied six knots, there were six knots. Examine this carefully: the substance of the cloth is the same, but differences arise because of the knots."
"What do you think? The first knot tied was called the first; in this manner, up to the sixth knot being formed—now, do I wish to designate the name of the sixth knot as the first?"
"No, World-Honored One!

As long as the six knots remain, this sixth name will ultimately never become the first. Even if I were to spend my entire life exhausting every power of eloquence, how could I cause these six knots to have their names confused?"
The Buddha said:

"The six knots are different, yet when one traces them back to their original cause, they were all fashioned from a single cloth; if you attempt to make them disordered, they can never be so. Thus it is with your six faculties: within that which is ultimately identical, you produce that which is ultimately distinct."
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"If you find these six knots unsatisfactory and wish instead for them to become one, how can that be achieved?
Ānanda replied:

"If this knot remains, disputes will arise within it of their own accord: 'This knot is not that one; that knot is not this one. If the Tathāgata were to untie them all today, and the knots did not arise, then there would be no 'this' or 'that'; they would not even be called 'one,' so how could 'six' be established?"
The Buddha said:
“The dissolution of the six and the disappearance of the one are likewise thus.

Because from time immemorial your mind-nature has been deranged, false perceptions have arisen; as these false perceptions arise without ceasing, the laboring faculty of sight gives rise to dust, just as when one strains the eyes, there appear floating flowers within the serene and brilliant clarity. Without cause, these arise in confusion as all the mountains, rivers, great earth, birth-and-death, and nirvana of the world—all of which are merely the delusive, inverted appearances of those floating flowers.”
Ānanda said: "This knot is identical to the previous one; how can it be untied?
The Tathāgata took the knotted cloth with his hand, pulled it to the left, and asked Ānanda:
"Do you understand it thus?
"No, World-Honored One!
He then again pulled the right side with his hand and asked Ānanda once more:
"Do you understand it thus?
"No, World-Honored One.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"I have now tried to pull it apart from both the left and right with my hands, but I cannot untie it. You should employ some skillful means; how can it be untied?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One!"
"When the knot at the heart is untied, they immediately disperse.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "So it is, so it is!"
If you wish to eliminate the fetters, you must do so at the very heart of the fetters.

Ānanda! I teach that the Buddha-dharma arises from causes and conditions; it does not grasp at the coarse appearances of worldly conjunctions. The Tathāgata illuminates both mundane and supramundane dharmas, knowing their fundamental causes and how they emerge according to their respective conditions. Thus, even as far as worlds beyond the sands of the Ganges, he knows the number of drops in a single drop of rain; he fully understands the underlying reasons for all the various things before us—the straightness of pines, the curvature of thorns, the whiteness of cranes, and the blackness of crows.
Therefore, Ānanda! Choose whichever of the six sense faculties you prefer from within your mind;
once the knots of the faculties are untied, the appearances of dust will naturally vanish. When all delusions have been extinguished, what need is there for that which is not real?
"Ānanda! I now ask you:
regarding these six knots currently manifest in this karpāsa cloth, can they all be untied and removed simultaneously?
"No, World-Honored One!"

These knots were originally tied in successive order; today they must be untied in that same sequence. Since the six knots share the same substance but are not tied at the same time, how could they all be removed simultaneously when they are being untied?
The Buddha said:
"The liberation of the six sense faculties is likewise.

When this faculty is first liberated, one first attains the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). When the nature of emptiness becomes perfectly luminous, one achieves liberation from phenomena (*dharma-vimokṣa*). Once liberation from phenomena is attained, both [person and phenomenon] are empty and do not arise; this is called a Bodhisattva attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) from within samādhi."
Ānanda and the great assembly, having received the Buddha’s instruction, attained perfect clarity through wisdom and were freed from all doubt.
At that moment, they joined their palms, prostrated at his feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Today our bodies and minds are radiant and clear; we have swiftly attained unimpeded understanding. Although we have realized the meaning of the 'one' and the 'six' being non-existent, we have yet to reach the fundamental root of perfect penetration."
"Bhagavān!

We have been adrift for accumulated kalpas, orphaned and exposed; what heart or what thought could have anticipated joining the celestial kinship of the Buddha? We are like infants who have lost their milk and suddenly encounter a compassionate mother. If, through this meeting, the Way is realized and the secret words obtained are identical to our original awakening, then there will be no difference between having heard them now and not having heard them at all."
"May you deign to bestow your great compassion upon us and grant us this secret adornment, so that we may fulfill the final instruction of the Tathāgata.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground and withdrew to conceal his secret intent, hoping for the Buddha’s silent transmission.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed all the great Bodhisattvas and the great Arhats whose outflows were exhausted within the assembly, saying:
"You Bodhisattvas and Arhats have been born into my Dharma and have attained the state of no-more-learning."
"I now ask you: among those who first resolved their minds and awakened to the eighteen realms, who attained perfect penetration?
By what skillful means did they enter samādhi?
The five bhikṣus, including Kaundinya, immediately rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In the Deer Park and at Kukkutārāma, I beheld the Tathāgata’s initial attainment of the Way; through the Buddha’s voice, I awakened to and clarified the Four Noble Truths.
When the Buddha questioned the bhikṣus, I was the first to declare my understanding, and the Tathāgata certified me with the name Ajñāta."
"The wondrous sounds are subtle and perfect; through these sounds, I have attained Arhatship.
When the Buddha asks about the most perfect penetration, according to my realization, sounds are supreme!
Upānanda then rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I too observed the Buddha at the time of his initial attainment of enlightenment; observing the signs of impurity, I gave rise to great revulsion. I realized that the nature of all forms arises from impurity, and that white bones and subtle dust ultimately return to emptiness. When both emptiness and form are non-existent, one achieves the path of no-more-learning. Thus, the Tathāgata sealed me with the name Niṣadha."
"Once the coarse forms have been exhausted, the wondrous forms become subtle and perfect; I attained Arhatship through these forms.
When the Buddha asks about the most direct path to enlightenment, according to my realization, the sense-base of form is supreme!"
The youth Gandhahastin immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I have heard the Tathāgata instruct me to contemplate thoroughly the characteristics of all conditioned phenomena.”

At that time, having taken leave of the Buddha, I was dwelling in quiet seclusion during a period of purification. I saw various bhikṣus burning aloeswood incense; the fragrance was serene as it entered my nostrils. I observed that this scent was neither wood, nor space, nor smoke, nor fire; it departed without attachment and arrived from nowhere. Through this, my conceptual mind dissolved and I realized the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*). The Tathāgata confirmed me with the title "Aragha" (Incense-Vigorous).
Dust and vapors suddenly vanished, and wondrous fragrances became subtle and pervasive; through these fragrant strictures, I attained arhatship.
When the Buddha asks about the perfect penetration of the faculties, according to my own realization, the strictures of fragrance are supreme!

The two Dharma-Prince sons, Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata, together with five hundred Brahmās present in the assembly, rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Since beginningless kalpas, we have served as skilled physicians for the world. We have tasted the herbs, trees, metals, and stones of this Sahā world; their names and numbers total one hundred and eight thousand. Thus we fully know their tastes—bitter, sour, salty, bland, sweet, and pungent—as well as their combinations, natural properties, and transformations. Whether they are cold or hot, poisonous or non-poisonous, we are able to know them all thoroughly.”

Having served the Tathāgata, we have realized that the nature of taste is neither empty nor existent, neither identical to the body and mind nor separate from the body and mind; through this, we have awakened to the causes of taste and received the seal of the Buddha Tathāgata upon the names of us two brothers, the Bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata.
Now, within this assembly, I am a Dharma Prince; through the awakening to clarity via the sense of taste, I have ascended to the rank of Bodhisattva.
When the Buddha asks about perfect penetration, according to what I have realized, the faculty of taste is supreme!
Bhadrapāla and his sixteen companions, the bodhisattvas, rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“In the past, we heard the Dharma under the Buddha Majestic Sound King and left the household life. Once, while following the custom of entering the bathhouse during the time of the monks’ bathing, we suddenly realized that the cause of water neither washes away dust nor washes the body; in the interval between these two, we attained a state of tranquil non-existence.”

My past habits have not been forgotten until this present time; having followed the Buddha into the homeless life, I have now attained the state of No-More-Learning (aśaikṣa). That Buddha named me Bhadrapāla.
With wondrous touch fully manifest, I dwell as a son of the Buddha.
The Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the faculties. "As I have realized it," [Mahākāśyapa] said, "the faculty of touch is supreme!
Then Mahākāśyapa, the Bhikṣuṇī of Purple Golden Light, and others rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed him, saying:

"In a past kalpa, within this world-system, there appeared a Buddha named Candrasūryapradīpa. I was able to draw near to him, hear the Dharma, and practice its teachings. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, I made offerings to his relics, lit lamps to continue the light, and coated the Buddha’s image with purple-gold. From that time onward, in birth after birth throughout successive lives, my body has always been perfectly complete as a mass of purple-gold light. This bhikṣuṇī Purple-Gold Light is a member of my own retinue; we simultaneously resolved our minds [for enlightenment]. Observing that the six sense-objects in the world are subject to decay and transformation, I cultivated the cessation of all things through emptiness and stillness; thus, my body and mind were able to pass through hundreds of thousands of kalpas as easily as a finger-snap."
"By means of the dharma of emptiness, I attained arhatship.
The World-Honored One declared me the foremost among those who practice dhūta; through the illumination of the sublime dharma, all outflows were extinguished.
When the Buddha asks about perfect penetration, according to what I have realized, the causal factor of dharmas is supreme!"
Aniruddha rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: “When I first left the household life, I was constantly fond of sleep.

The Tathāgata rebuked me as being of the class of beasts; hearing the Buddha’s reproach, I wept and reproached myself. For seven days I did not sleep, and thereby lost both my eyes. The World-Honored One showed me the Vajra Samādhi of Joyful Vision and Illumination. Without relying on my eyes, I perceived the ten directions; their essential truth was transparently clear, as if I were looking at fruit in the palm of my hand. The Tathāgata certified me as having attained Arhatship.”
“The Buddha asks about perfect penetration; according to what I have realized, to revolve the faculty of sight and follow back to its source is the foremost method!
Cūḍapanthaka then rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“I lacked the capacity for recitation and retention, and thus possessed no nature for extensive learning. At first, I encountered the Buddha, heard the Dharma, and left the home life. I attempted to memorize a single verse of the Tathāgata, yet for a hundred days I could only grasp the beginning and lose the end, or grasp the end and lose the beginning. The Buddha took pity on my stupidity and instructed me to dwell in retreat and regulate my inhalation and exhalation.”

At that time, as I contemplated the breath until it became subtle and reached its ultimate limit, I perceived the moments of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). My mind suddenly opened wide and attained great non-obstruction; eventually, with the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), I became an Arhat, sitting beneath the Buddha’s seat and being certified as one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
“The Buddha asks about perfect penetration; according to what I have realized, returning the breath to follow emptiness is the foremost method!
Gāvalgaṇḍī immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: “I had karmic faults of speech;

in past kalpas, I habitually mocked śramaṇas, and thus in life after life I suffered from the disease of a cow’s rumination. The Tathāgata showed me the Dharma-door of the single-flavor pure mind-ground. I attained the cessation of the mind and entered samādhi, observing that the cognition of taste is neither the substance nor the object. In an instant, I transcended all worldly outflows; internally I was liberated from body and mind, and externally I left behind the world. I distanced myself from the three realms of existence as a bird escapes its cage. With defilements wiped away and dust dissolved, my Dharma-eye became pure and I became an arhat, personally certified by the Tathāgata to have ascended the path of no-more-learning.”
“The Buddha asks about perfect penetration; according to what I have realized, returning the taste and revolving the faculty of cognition is the foremost!
Pilingakṣa then rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“When I first resolved to attain enlightenment and entered the Path under the Buddha, I frequently heard the Tathāgata speak of the many things in the world that are not to be relished. While begging for food in the city, my mind was contemplating the Dharma-gate, when I did not notice a poisonous thorn piercing my foot. My entire body was in pain. I thought of the presence of cognition, realizing that this deep pain was known by cognition. Although the cognition perceived the pain, within the pure mind of cognition there was neither pain nor the perception of pain. I further reflected: how could there be two simultaneous cognitions in a single body?”

Not long after he had focused his mindfulness, his body and mind suddenly became empty; within twenty-one days, all outflows were exhausted, and he attained arhatship, receiving the personal seal of approval and manifesting the state of no-more-learning.
The Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the Way. "According to what I have realized," Subhūti said, "the complete awareness that leaves no trace of a body is the foremost!
Subhūti then rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"For kalpas as vast as space, my mind has attained unimpededness. I recall my births, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; from the very moment I was in my mother’s womb, I knew emptiness and stillness. Thus it continued until the ten directions became empty, and I also enabled sentient beings to realize the nature of emptiness. Having been inspired by the Tathāgata to awaken to true emptiness, and having attained the perfect clarity of the nature of emptiness, I achieved Arhatship. Suddenly entering the Tathāgata’s precious, luminous sea of emptiness, I shared in the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, being sealed as one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). In the liberation of the emptiness of nature, I am unsurpassed."

The Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the Way. "As I have realized it," [Ānanda] said, "all phenomena enter into non-existence; when that which is not non-existence is exhausted, one turns back from phenomena to return to the Unconditioned—this is the foremost! Śāriputra then rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
