"Since the distant kalpas of the past, my mind-faculty has been pure. Thus have I undergone births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Whether mundane or supramundane, all manner of transformations were understood by me upon a single glance, such that I attained unimpeded mastery. On the road, I encountered Kāśyapa, who was traveling with his brothers proclaiming the causes and conditions of the Dharma. I awakened to the boundlessness of the mind and left the household life under the Buddha. Seeing that the clarity of my perception was perfect and complete, I attained great fearlessness. I became an Arhat and the eldest son of the Buddha, born from the Buddha’s own mouth and transformed by the Dharma."

The Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the Way. "As I have realized it," [the Bodhisattva] said, "when the mind and vision emit light, and that light reaches its ultimate limit of knowing and seeing—this is the foremost!
Then the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I have already served as a Dharma Prince to Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. When the Tathāgatas of the ten directions instruct their disciples, those Bodhisattvas of keen faculties who cultivate the practices of Samantabhadra receive their names from me."
“World-Honored One!

I employ the mind to hear and discern all the knowledge and views of sentient beings. If, beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in other directions, there is a single sentient being who brings forth within their heart the practice of Samantabhadra, at that time I shall mount my six-tusked elephant and manifest hundreds of thousands of bodies, arriving at that very place. Even if that person’s obstructions are so deep that they are not yet fit to see me, I will secretly stroke their crown with my hand, providing protection and consolation to ensure their accomplishment.”
“The Buddha asks about perfect penetration; I shall explain its fundamental cause. When the mind’s hearing becomes luminous and discernment is sovereign, this is the foremost method!
Sundarananda then rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“When I first left the household life to enter the Path under the Buddha, although I was fully endowed with the precepts, my mind was constantly distracted and agitated regarding *samādhi*, and I had not yet attained the state of outflowlessness (*anāsrava*).”

"The World-Honored One instructed me and Śāriputra to contemplate the white at the tip of the nose. When I first began this earnest contemplation, after twenty-one days had passed, I saw the breath entering and exiting the nostrils like smoke. My body and mind became inwardly luminous, and the world appeared as a perfectly clear and hollow space, universally pure and translucent like lapis lazuli. As the appearance of smoke gradually vanished, the nasal breath became white; my mind opened and the outflows were exhausted. All inhalations and exhalations were transformed into radiance, illuminating the worlds of the ten directions, whereby I attained Arhatship. The World-Honored One then prophesied that I would attain Bodhi."

“The Buddha asks about perfect penetration; by means of the prolonged illumination through the extinction of breath, that illumination became perfect and exhausted all outflows—this is why it is foremost!
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra then rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“For kalpas past, my eloquence has been unimpeded; I have proclaimed suffering and emptiness, deeply penetrating the true mark of reality. Thus, even regarding the secret dharma-gates of Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, I am able to provide subtle and wondrous expositions among the assembly, attaining fearlessness.”

The World-Honored One, knowing that I possess great eloquence, instructed me with the wheel of his voice to proclaim it forth. In the presence of the Buddha, I assisted him in turning the wheel; through this lion's roar, I became an Arhat, and the World-Honored One certified me as supreme in the preaching of the Dharma.
“The Buddha asks about perfect penetration; I shall say that by means of the Dharma-sound I subdue demonic enemies and extinguish all outflows—this is the foremost!

Upāli then rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: “I personally followed the Buddha when he left the city to renounce the world; I personally witnessed the Tathāgata’s six years of diligent austerity;

I personally saw the Tathāgata subdue all demons and restrain all non-Buddhists, liberating the world from the outflows of greed and desire. I received the Buddha’s instruction on the precepts, including the three thousand majestic deportments and eighty thousand subtle rules, such that my nature-based and prohibitive offenses were entirely purified. My body and mind became tranquil and extinct, and I attained the state of an Arhat. I am the leader within the Tathāgata’s assembly; the Buddha himself has certified my heart, and among those who uphold the precepts and cultivate the person, the multitude ranks me as unsurpassed.”

The Buddha asked about the means of perfect penetration; by means of grasping the body, I attained mastery over the body, and by gradually grasping the mind, I attained thorough penetration of the mind. Thereafter, both body and mind were entirely functional and beneficial—this is why it is foremost!
Mahāmaudgalyāyana immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“When I first encountered the three Kāśyapa brothers—Uruvilvā, Gayā, and Nadī—while begging for alms along the road, they proclaimed the profound meaning of the Tathāgata’s causes and conditions. Instantly my mind was awakened and I attained great penetration. The Tathāgata bestowed upon me a *kāṣāya* robe; as it touched my body, my beard and hair fell away naturally. As I traveled through the ten directions, I met with no obstructions. My supernormal powers were so manifest that I was ranked supreme, and I became an Arhat.”
Not only does the World-Honored One praise my spiritual power, but the Tathāgatas of the ten directions also extol it as being perfect, bright, pure, sovereign, and fearless.

When the Buddha asks about the perfect penetration of the Way, I declare that by turning back the turbid flow of the mind and manifesting its luminous essence, it becomes clear and crystalline; this is why I consider my method to be the foremost!
Ucchuṣma joined his palms before the Tathāgata, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: “I recall that in the distant past, many kalpas ago, I was naturally full of lust.

There was a Buddha who appeared in the world named King of Emptiness (*Śūnyarāja*), who taught that those with excessive passion become a mass of fierce fire. He instructed me to contemplate my entire body—my hundred bones and four limbs—and how the various warm and cold breaths and spiritual lights were concentrated within; thus, he transformed my lustful mind into the fire of wisdom. From then on, all Buddhas have called me by the name ‘Fire-Head’ (*Agnimukha*). By the power of the Fire-Light Samādhi (*Jvālana-prabhā-samādhi*), I have attained Arhatship.”
I made a great vow: "When all Buddhas attain the Way, may I become a powerful being to personally subdue their demonic enemies.

When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the faculties, I replied: "By clearly observing that the warmth and tactile sensations within my body and mind flow through unimpeded, all outflows were extinguished; I gave rise to the great jewel-flame and ascended to supreme enlightenment. This is why it is foremost!"

The Bodhisattva Earth-Holder immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: “I recall that in the past, when the Tathāgata Universal Radiance appeared in the world, I was a bhikṣu.

I constantly leveled and filled all major roads, ferry crossings, fields, and narrow passes where there were improper obstructions or damage to carts and horses; I built bridges or carried sand and earth myself. Thus I underwent such diligent hardships through the appearance of immeasurable Buddhas in the world. Furthermore, whenever there were sentient beings in marketplaces who needed someone to carry their goods, I would carry them for them first; once they had reached their destination and set down the goods, I would depart without taking any payment.”

When the Buddha Viśvabhū was in the world, there was widespread famine. I was a porter; regardless of distance, I would accept only one coin. If a cart or ox became mired in the mud, I possessed the spiritual power to push its wheels and relieve their suffering. At that time, the Great King of the country prepared a feast for the Buddha. I leveled the ground to await the Buddha, and the Tathāgata Viśvabhū touched my head and said to me:
"You should level the mind-ground; then all the lands of the world will be level."

My mind was immediately opened, and I saw that the minute particles of my own body and all the minute particles constituting the world were equal and without distinction. These particles, by their very nature, do not touch one another; even weapons cannot touch them. Thus, regarding the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), I realized the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and became an Arhat.

Having now turned their minds to enter the stage of the Bodhisattvas, they hear the Tathāgatas proclaim the ground of the Buddhas' wondrous Lotus wisdom and vision; I shall first bear witness to them as their leader.

The Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the Way; I, by means of clear contemplation, observed that the two objects—the body and the realm—are equal and without distinction. Originally they are the Tathāgata-garbha, yet through delusion these objects arise. When the objects are extinguished and wisdom becomes perfect, one accomplishes the Unsurpassed Way; this is the foremost!
The youth Candraprabha rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“I recall that in the past, as many eons ago as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, a Buddha appeared in the world named Jaleśvara. He taught various bodhisattvas to practice the water-essence and enter samādhi, observing that the water-element within the body cannot be displaced. Beginning with nasal mucus and saliva, he traced it through the fluids, essence, blood, feces, and urine until he reached the end; he saw that the swirling waters within the body were identical to the water-element everywhere. Thus, he perceived the water within his own body as no different from the fragrant oceans of the Floating Banner King Land outside the world.”

At that time, when I first achieved this contemplation, I saw only water and had not yet attained the state of bodilessness. While I was practicing dhyāna in my room as a bhikṣu, a disciple of mine peered through the window to observe the room; he saw only clear water filling the entire chamber with nothing else visible. Being ignorant, the boy picked up a piece of tile and threw it into the water; it struck the water with a splash, and he looked back at me before departing. After I emerged from samādhi, I suddenly felt pain in my heart, like Śāriputra when he encountered the malevolent ghost.

I thought to myself: "I have now attained the path of Arhatship and have long been free from the conditions of illness; why does heart-pain suddenly arise today? Could it be that I am regressing and losing my realization?"
"At that time, the youth came quickly before me and reported the matter as described above. I then told him:
'If you see water again, you may immediately open the door and enter this water to remove the tiles and debris.'"

The youth followed these instructions; later, when he entered meditative concentration, he again saw the water and the rubble exactly as they were. He opened the door and cleared them out. When I later emerged from concentration, my physical body was restored to its original state. Thus I encountered immeasurable Buddhas, continuing in this manner until I reached the Tathāgata King of Sovereign Penetrations of Mountains and Seas, where I finally attained the dissolution of the self. My nature became one with the empty truth of all the fragrant water-seas throughout the ten directions, without duality or distinction. Now, before the Tathāgata, I have received the name "Childlike Innocence" and am enrolled in the assembly of Bodhisattvas.

“The Buddha asks about perfect penetration; because I have attained the single flavor of universal flow within the nature of water, I have realized the patience of non-arising and perfected Bodhi—this is why I consider myself foremost!
The Dharma Prince Vaidūryaprabha then rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“I recall that in the past, through kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Amitaghoṣa (Immeasurable Sound). He revealed to the bodhisattvas the wondrous clarity of fundamental enlightenment, teaching them to observe this world and the bodies of sentient beings as all being driven by the power of the wind of delusive conditions.”

At that time, I observed the establishment of the realms, the movement of the world, the motion and stillness of the body, and the stirring thoughts of the mind; all these movements were non-dual and without distinction. I then fully realized the nature of this multitude of movements: they come from nowhere and go nowhere. The deluded beings throughout the micro-dust motes of the ten directions are one in their shared unreality. Thus it extends even to all sentient beings within a single world-system of three thousand great thousandfold worlds, like a hundred mosquitoes and gnats contained within a single vessel, chirping and clamoring together in a frantic noise within a mere fraction of space.

Not long after meeting the Buddha, he attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*). At that moment, his mind opened and he beheld the land of Akṣobhya Buddha in the eastern direction; as a Dharma Prince, he served the Buddhas of the ten directions, and his body and mind emitted light, penetrating through all things without obstruction.

The Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of dhyāna; through my observation that the power of wind has no basis, I awakened to the Bodhicitta and entered samādhi. This merging of the minds of the Buddhas of the ten directions into one wondrous mind is, for me, the foremost!
The Bodhisattva Gaganagañja immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I and the Tathāgata attained the body of boundless extent from the Buddha Dīpaṃkara. At that time, holding four great precious jewels in my hands, I illuminated the Buddha-lands as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions, transforming them into empty space. Furthermore, I manifested a great round mirror within my own mind; from within it, ten kinds of subtle and wondrous jewel-lights were emitted, flowing and pouring through the ten directions until all the *dhvajarāja* (banner-king) lands reaching the limits of empty space entered into the mirror and merged with my body. My body became identical to empty space, without mutual obstruction; my body was able to skillfully enter lands as numerous as motes of dust, extensively performing Buddha-deeds and attaining great accordance. This great supernormal power arose from my contemplation that the four elements have no basis and are born and perish through delusive thought; that empty space is non-dual and the Buddha-lands are fundamentally the same. By realizing this sameness, I attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)."
"The Buddha asks about perfect penetration; by contemplating the boundlessness of space, I entered samādhi, and through this wondrous power of perfect clarity, I am foremost!
Maitreya Bodhisattva then rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I recall that in the past, after the passing of atoms of kalpas, a Buddha appeared in the world named Candrasūryapradīpa. I left the household life under that Buddha, yet my mind was preoccupied with worldly reputation and I delighted in visiting noble families."

At that time, the World-Honored One instructed me to practice the samādhi of mind-only consciousness to enter into samādhi. Throughout kalpas past, I have served Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges through this samādhi; my pursuit for worldly fame and mind has ceased and been extinguished. When Dīpaṃkara Buddha appeared in the world, I then attained the unsurpassed, wondrously perfect samādhi of the conscious mind; even all the lands of the Tathāgatas throughout the entirety of space—whether pure or defiled, existent or non-existent—are all manifestations produced by the transformations of my own mind.
World-Honored One!

Because I have thoroughly understood that all is but mind and consciousness, from the nature of consciousness there flow forth immeasurable Tathāgatas; I have now received the prediction that I shall next succeed to the seat of Buddhahood.

The Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the Way; I replied that by clearly observing that the ten directions are but consciousness, my conscious mind became perfectly luminous and entered the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Thereby I distanced myself from the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), attaining the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); this is why it is foremost!
The Dharma Prince Mahāsthāmaprāpta, together with fifty-two bodhisattvas of his same rank, rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“I recall that in the past, during kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, a Buddha appeared in the world named Amitābha. Twelve Tathāgatas succeeded one another for the duration of that kalpa, the last of whom was named Sūryacandraprabhābhibhū. Under that Buddha, he taught me the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha.”

It is like two people: one who is single-mindedly intent on remembering another, and one who is single-mindedly intent on forgetting them. Such two people may meet or not meet, or see each other or not; yet because they remember one another and their mutual remembrance is deep, this continues from birth to birth, like a form and its shadow, never diverging. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions cherish and pity sentient beings as a mother remembers her child; yet if the child runs away, what can that remembrance accomplish?

If you, my son, remember your mother as much as your mother remembers you, then throughout successive lives, mother and child shall never be far apart. If sentient beings with sincere hearts remember the Buddha and recite his name, they will certainly see the Buddha in the present and the future; they will not be far from the Buddha, and without relying on expedient means, their minds will naturally open. It is like a person who has been perfumed with incense: their body carries a fragrance. This is what is called "Adornment of Fragrant Light."

"In my original stage of practice, I entered the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) by means of the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha; now, within this world-system, I gather those who mindfully recite the Buddha's name and lead them back to the Pure Land.

When the Buddha asks about perfect penetration, I have no preference for any other method: to gather all six sense faculties under control, to maintain the continuity of pure mindfulness, and thereby attain *samādhi*—this is the foremost!"
The Great Buddha-Usnīṣa Sūtra on the Myriad Practices of Śūraṅgama, Fascicle Five.

The Great Buddha-Usnīṣa Tathāgata’s Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization, the Definitive Meaning of the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas’ Śūraṅgama, Fascicle Six. Also known as: [Translated at] Nālandā in Central India.
The Sūtra of the Great Place of Practice, extracted from the Abhiṣeka Section and circulated separately;
translated by the Tang Dynasty Indian Śramaṇa Prajñāmitra. At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

I recall that in the past, incalculable kalpas ago as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Avalokiteśvara. Under that Buddha, I gave rise to the bodhicitta; he taught me to enter samādhi through hearing, contemplation, and cultivation.

At first, within the faculty of hearing, one enters the stream and loses the object; once that which is entered has become still, the two aspects of movement and stillness clearly cease to arise. As this gradually increases, both the hearing and the object of hearing are exhausted. When the exhaustion of hearing does not persist, the awareness and the object of awareness are empty. When the emptiness of awareness is perfectly fulfilled, both emptiness and the object of emptiness are extinguished. With the cessation of arising and ceasing, quiescent extinction manifests before one. Suddenly transcending the mundane and supramundane worlds, one attains two kinds of sublime excellence:
first, above, one harmonizes with the fundamental, wondrously enlightened mind of all Buddhas of the ten directions, sharing the same compassionate power as the Buddha-Tathāgatas;
second, below, one harmonizes with all sentient beings of the six realms throughout the ten directions, sharing the same sorrowful longing as all those beings.
“World-Honored One!

Because I made offerings to the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvara, I received from that Tathāgata the Vajra Samādhi of Hearing-Perfuming and Hearing-Cultivation, which is like an illusion; and because I share the same power of compassion as the Buddha-Tathāgatas, my body has become capable of thirty-two manifestations to enter all lands.”
“World-Honored One!

If there are bodhisattvas who have entered samādhi and are progressing in their cultivation so that their untainted resolute understanding becomes fully manifest, I will manifest in the body of a Buddha to preach the Dharma for them, causing them to attain liberation.

If there are those in training (śaikṣa) whose tranquil, wondrously luminous, and most sublime realization has become fully manifest, I will appear before them in the body of a Pratyekabuddha to preach the Dharma for them, causing them to attain liberation.”

If there are those in training who sever the twelve links of dependent origination, and through the severing of these conditions their superior nature becomes preeminent and perfectly manifest, I appear before them in the body of a Pratyekabuddha and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to attain liberation;

if there are those in training who realize the emptiness of the Four Noble Truths, and through the path of cultivation enter cessation so that their superior nature becomes preeminent and perfectly manifest, I appear before them in the body of a Śrāvaka and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to attain liberation;

if there are sentient beings who desire to clarify their minds and awaken, who do not transgress the dust of desire and whose bodies are pure, I appear before them in the body of a Brahmā King and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to attain liberation.

If there are sentient beings who wish to become lords of devas to rule over the celestial realms, I appear before them in the form of Śakra and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve their goal;

if there are sentient beings who wish to have physical mastery as they travel throughout the ten directions, I appear before them in the form of Īśvara and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve their goal;

if there are sentient beings who wish to have physical mastery as they fly through space, I appear before them in the form of Maheśvara and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve their goal.

If there are sentient beings who love to preside over spirits and deities to protect their lands, I appear before them in the form of a Great Heavenly General and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve their goal;

if there are sentient beings who love to govern the world and protect its inhabitants, I appear before them in the form of one of the Four Heavenly Kings and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve their goal;

if there are sentient beings who love to be born in celestial palaces and command spirits and deities, I appear before them in the form of a prince of the realm of the Four Heavenly Kings and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve their goal.
If there are sentient beings who delight in being rulers of men, I manifest before them in the body of a human king and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve their goal;

if there are sentient beings who love to be heads of clans and are honored by the world, I manifest before them in the body of an elder and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve their goal;

if there are sentient beings who delight in discussing refined terminology and purifying their dwellings, I manifest before them in the body of a lay devotee (*gṛhapati*) and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve their goal.

If there are sentient beings who love to govern territories and adjudicate the affairs of states and districts, I appear before them in the body of a high official and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve their goal;

if there are sentient beings who love various arts and calculations to protect themselves and maintain their livelihood, I appear before them in the body of a Brahmin and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve their goal;

if there are men who delight in learning, leave the household life, and uphold the various precepts, I appear before them in the body of a bhikṣu and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve their goal.

If there is a woman who delights in study, leaves the household life, and upholds the various prohibitive precepts, I will manifest before her in the body of a bhikṣuṇī and preach the Dharma for her, enabling her to achieve fulfillment.
If there is a man who delights in upholding the five precepts, I will manifest before him in the body of an upāsaka and preach the Dharma for him, enabling him to achieve fulfillment.
Furthermore, if there is a woman who abides by the five precepts, I will manifest before her in the body of an upāsikā and preach the Dharma for her, enabling her to achieve fulfillment.

If there are women who manage internal affairs and establish themselves to cultivate their households and states, I appear before them in the form of a queen, a state lady, a titled consort, or a great matron to preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve fulfillment.
If there are sentient beings who do not damage their male organs, I appear before them in the form of a young boy to preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve fulfillment.

If there are virgins who cherish their status and do not seek violation or assault, I appear before them in the form of a young girl to preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve fulfillment.
If there are devas who wish to leave their celestial status, I manifest in a deva body and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve success;
if there are nāgas who wish to leave their nāga status, I manifest in a nāga body and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve success;
if there are yakṣas who wish to transcend their own kind, I appear before them in the form of a yakṣa and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve success.
If there are gandharvas who wish to be liberated from their kind, I manifest before them in the body of a gandharva and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve success;
if there are asuras who wish to be liberated from their kind, I manifest before them in the body of an asura and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve success;
if there are kinnaras who wish to be liberated from their kind, I manifest before them in the body of a kinnara and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve success.
If mahoragas desire liberation from their kind, I manifest before them in the body of a mahoraga and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve it;
if sentient beings desire to become humans or cultivate the human path, I manifest in a human body and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve it;

if there are non-human beings—whether with form or without form, with perception or without perception—who desire to transcend their kind, I manifest my own body before each of them and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve it.

This is called the thirty-two kinds of wondrously pure bodies that enter various lands; all are accomplished through the sovereign power of effortless wondrous efficacy, achieved by perfuming the hearing with samādhi and cultivating the hearing.
“World-Honored One!

Furthermore, by means of this power of the unconditioned wondrous samādhi of hearing-perfuming and hearing-cultivation, and because I share in the same compassion and yearning as all sentient beings of the six realms throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, I cause all sentient beings to obtain fourteen kinds of fearlessness within my body and mind:
First, because I do not observe myself but observe the observer, I cause those suffering and distressed sentient beings of the ten directions to attain liberation simply by observing my voice.”
Second, by the revolving and restoration of knowledge and vision, one causes all sentient beings such that even if they enter a great fire, the fire cannot burn them;
third, by the revolving and restoration of observation and hearing, one causes all sentient beings such that even if they are swept away by a great flood, the water cannot drown them;

fourth, by the cessation and extinction of deluded thoughts so that the mind is free from killing and harm, one causes all sentient beings such that even if they enter the realms of ghosts, the ghosts cannot harm them.

Fifth, the cultivation of hearing perfects the faculty of hearing; the six sense organs are dissolved and restored so that they function identically to the auditory faculty, such that it can cause sentient beings who are about to be harmed by weapons—having their bodies severed piece by piece—to perceive those weapons as if cutting through water or blowing upon light, their nature remaining unshaken.

Sixth, when the cultivation of hearing becomes pure and brilliant, pervading the entire Dharma-realm, then the nature of all dark obscurations cannot prevail; it can cause yakṣas, rākṣasas, kumbhāṇḍa ghosts, piśācas, pūtanas, and the like, such that even though they draw near, their eyes cannot see.

Seventh, when the nature of sound is completely dissolved and the faculties of seeing and hearing turn back into themselves, leaving behind all sensory dust and delusions, it can cause sentient beings to be unable to be bound by shackles or fetters.
Eighth, by extinguishing sound, hearing becomes perfect and universally generates the power of compassion, enabling sentient beings to pass through perilous paths unrobbed by thieves;
ninth, by perfuming the hearing and departing from sensory dust, one is not robbed by forms, enabling all sentient beings with excessive lust to distance themselves from greed and desire;

tenth, when pure sound is free from dust, the faculties and objects are perfectly fused so that there is neither subject nor object, enabling all sentient beings harboring anger and resentment to leave behind all hatred.

Eleventh is "Dissolving Dust and Revolving Clarity": the body and mind of the dharma-realm become as transparent and unobstructed as lapis lazuli, enabling all those with dull natures and karmic obstructions, including the icchantikas, to forever leave behind the darkness of ignorance.

Twelfth is "Merging Form and Restoring Hearing": without leaving the site of enlightenment, one enters the mundane world; without destroying the world-systems, one pervades the ten directions, making offerings to Buddhas as numerous as motes of dust, becoming a Dharma Prince at the side of each Buddha, and enabling childless beings in the dharma-realm who seek a son to give birth to a son endowed with merit and wisdom.

Thirteenth: The six sense organs are perfectly penetrating; their luminous clarity is non-dual and encompasses the worlds of the ten directions. This establishes the Great Perfect Mirror, the Empty Tathāgata-garbha, which receives and upholds the secret Dharma gates of the Buddhas as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions without loss. It can cause those beings within the Dharma-realm who have no children, and those who desire daughters, to give birth to daughters who are upright, endowed with merit and virtue, gentle and compliant, beloved and respected by all, and possessed of auspicious marks.

Fourteenth: Within this trichiliocosm of ten billion suns and moons, there are currently dwelling in the world dharma-princes whose number equals sixty-two Ganges-sands. They cultivate practices and establish models to teach and transform sentient beings, following their inclinations; yet their skillful means and wisdom differ from one another. By means of the fundamental root of perfect penetration that I have attained—the wondrous gate of the ear—my body and mind have become subtle and wondrous, encompassing and pervading the entire Dharma-realm. If sentient beings were to hold my name, their merit would be exactly equal to that of those who hold the names of all sixty-two Ganges-sands of dharma-princes; there would be no difference between the two.
“World-Honored One!
My single name is no different from those many names; it is because I have cultivated this that I have attained true and perfect penetration.
This is called the fourteenth power of bestowing fearlessness, through which blessings are fully provided for all sentient beings.”
“World-Honored One!
Because I have also attained this perfect penetration and realized the unsurpassed Way, I have further been able to skillfully attain four inconceivable, unconditioned, and wondrous virtues:

First, because from my initial attainment of the wondrously wondrous faculty of hearing, the essence of mind has left behind all hearing; seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing can no longer be separated, forming a single, perfectly integrated, pure, and precious awakening. Therefore, I am able to manifest many wondrous forms and speak boundless secret divine mantras. Within these, I may appear with one head, three heads, five heads, seven heads, nine heads, eleven heads, and so on, up to one hundred and eight heads, a thousand heads, ten thousand heads, or eighty-four thousand *śakara* heads.”

With two arms, four arms, six arms, eight arms, ten arms, twelve arms, fourteen, sixteen, eighteen, twenty, up to twenty-four; and thus even up to one hundred and eight arms, a thousand arms, ten thousand arms, or eighty-four thousand *mudrā*-arms;

with two eyes, three eyes, four eyes, nine eyes, and thus even up to one hundred and eight eyes, a thousand eyes, ten thousand eyes, or eighty-four thousand pure jewel-eyes—whether manifesting kindness, majesty, meditative concentration, or wisdom—they rescue and protect sentient beings, attaining great sovereignty.

Second, because I have been liberated from the six sense objects through hearing and reflection, just as sound passes over a wall without being obstructed, I am able to manifest every single form and recite every single mantra with marvelous skill. These forms and mantras can bestow fearlessness upon all sentient beings; therefore, throughout the lands of the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, I am known as the One Who Bestows Fearlessness.

Third, because I have cultivated the fundamentally wondrous, perfect, and penetrating root of purity, all the worlds I visit cause sentient beings to relinquish their bodies and precious treasures to seek my compassion.

Fourth, having attained the Buddha-mind and realized the ultimate, I am able to offer various precious treasures as offerings to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, extending also to all sentient beings within the six realms of the Dharma-realm: those who seek a wife obtain a wife; those who seek a son obtain a son; those who seek samādhi obtain samādhi; those who seek long life obtain long life; and so on, even to those who seek Great Nirvana and obtain Great Nirvana.

The Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the Way; I attained it through the gate of the ear, via the Samādhi of Universal Illumination. By means of the mind’s freedom from conditions and its entry into the phase of the returning flow, I achieved Samāpatti and perfected Bodhi—this is the foremost!
“World-Honored One!

That Buddha-Tathāgata praised me for having well attained the Dharma-door of Perfect Penetration. In the midst of that great assembly, he conferred upon me the title of Avalokiteśvara. Because I contemplate and listen to the perfect luminosity of the ten directions, the name ‘Avalokiteśvara’ pervades the worlds of the ten directions.”

At that time, from his five limbs upon the lion throne, the World-Honored One emitted precious light that reached far to drench the crowns of the heads of the Tathāgatas as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions, as well as the Bodhisattvas who are Dharma Princes.

Those Tathāgatas likewise emitted precious light from their five limbs, which came from the motes-of-dust directions to drench the crown of the Buddha’s head, as well as the great Bodhisattvas and Arhats within the assembly. The trees, forests, ponds, and marshes all resonated with the sounds of the Dharma; the interlacing lights meshed together like a net of precious threads. This great assembly attained what they had never experienced before, and all universally obtained the Vajra Samādhi.

At that moment, a rain of hundred-jeweled lotuses fell from the sky—blue, yellow, red, and white, intermingling and blending together. The voids of the ten directions turned the color of the seven treasures. The great earth, mountains, and rivers of this Sahā world simultaneously vanished; there was seen only a single realm formed by the combination of lands as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions, while the sounds of Brahma-songs and hymns were spontaneously performed.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata addressed Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince:

“Observe now these twenty-five great Bodhisattvas beyond training and Arhats, each of whom has spoken of the skillful means by which they first attained the Way, all claiming to have cultivated true and perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*). In their respective practices, there is truly no distinction of superior or inferior, nor of priority or sequence;
yet I now wish to cause Ānanda to attain awakening—among these twenty-five modes of practice, which one corresponds to his faculties?”

"Furthermore, after my parinirvāṇa, for those sentient beings in this world who enter the Bodhisattva Vehicle to seek the Unsurpassed Way, by what gate of skillful means can they easily achieve success?

Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, having received the Buddha’s compassionate command, immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, spoke these verses in response to the Buddha:
"The nature of the ocean of awakening is clear and perfect; The perfect clarity of awakening is fundamentally subtle and wondrous."
The original illumination gives rise to the locus; once the locus is established, the nature of illumination perishes.
Through delusion and confusion there is empty space; based on space, the world is established.
When thought becomes clear and settled, it forms the land; when cognition arises, it becomes sentient beings.
Emptiness arises within the Great Enlightenment, like a single bubble emerging from the sea;
the lands of conditioned dust and atoms are all born from emptiness.
When the bubble vanishes, emptiness is fundamentally non-existent—how much more so, then, the various realms of the three worlds?
The nature of returning to the source is non-dual, yet there are many gates of expedient means.
The sagely nature is all-pervasive; both following and reversing are expedient means.
For those of initial resolve entering samādhi, their progress—whether slow or swift—is not of the same order.
Visual forms and perceptions congeal into dust; though refined, they cannot be penetrated.
How can one attain perfect penetration without such clear penetration?
Sounds and voices are mixed with language; they are merely names, phrases, and flavors.
One does not contain all things; how, then, can one attain perfect penetration?
Fragrance is known through contact; when separated, it fundamentally does not exist.
Since that which is perceived is not constant, how can one attain perfect penetration?
The nature of taste is not original; it exists only when there is tasting.
Since its perception is not constant or uniform, how can it attain perfect penetration?
Touch is clarified by that which is touched; there is nothing it does not clearly touch.
The nature of union and separation is not fixed; how can one attain perfect penetration?
Designating phenomena as "internal objects" implies that by relying on these objects there must be a subject;
since subject and object do not pervade all things, how can one attain perfect penetration?
Although the seeing-nature is clear and penetrating, it illuminates what is before but not what is behind;
since half is missing in the four directions, how can it be called perfect penetration?
The breath of the nose flows in and out, yet there is no mingling of these two currents as they pass before one.
Fragmented and disjointed, it cannot be entered; how then can one attain perfect penetration?
The tongue is not an entrance without cause; it gives rise to cognition because of flavors.
When flavor ceases, cognition has no existence; how then can one attain perfect penetration?
The body and its objects of touch are alike; each is not the contemplation of Perfect Enlightenment.
Since their boundaries do not merge in harmony, how can one attain perfect penetration?
To know that the faculties involve confused thoughts, yet to seek a clear realization through them, is ultimately to see nothing at all.
Thoughts and perceptions cannot be escaped; how, then, can one attain perfect penetration?
Consciousness and vision are a mixture of the three harmonies; when their root is examined, they are called "without marks.
Since their own substance has no fixed nature from the start, how can one attain perfect penetration?
The mind-hearing penetrates the ten directions, born from the power of great causes;
if the initial mind cannot enter it, how can one attain perfect penetration?
The contemplation of the nose is fundamentally a provisional device, intended merely to cause the mind to settle and abide.
Abiding in the mental factors of abiding, how can one attain perfect penetration?
By expounding the Dharma through sounds and texts, you first achieved awakening;
yet names and phrases are not themselves untainted—how then can one attain perfect penetration?
Observing precepts and violating them merely restrain the body; if there were no body, there would be nothing to restrain.
Since [the body] is fundamentally not omnipresent, how could one attain perfect penetration?
Spiritual powers are rooted in past causes; what connection have they with the discrimination of dharmas?
If mindfulness takes objects as its condition and does not transcend them, how can one attain perfect penetration?
If you contemplate the nature of earth, it is solid and obstructive, not pervasive;
as a conditioned phenomenon, it is not the nature of the sages—how then can one attain perfect penetration?
If one contemplates through the nature of water, thoughts and perceptions are not real;
if it is suchness beyond conceptualization and observation, how can one attain perfect penetration?
If one contemplates through the nature of fire, to loathe existence is not true transcendence.
This is not the expedient means of the initial mind; how could one thereby attain perfect penetration?
If one contemplates the nature of wind, motion and stillness are not without opposition;
since opposition is not the supreme awakening, how could one thereby attain perfect penetration?
If you observe through the nature of emptiness, the dull and darkened mind was not originally awakened;
since non-awakening differs from Bodhi, how could you attain perfect penetration?
If you observe through the nature of consciousness, observing that consciousness is not permanent;
If the mind is focused on the illusory, how can one attain perfect penetration?
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; the nature of thought is fundamentally subject to arising and ceasing.
Since cause and effect now yield such disparate results, how can one attain perfect penetration?
I now address the World-Honored One:
Since the Buddha has appeared in this Sahā world, the true essence of the teaching in this direction is that purity resides in hearing sounds;
if one wishes to attain samādhi, it must truly be entered through hearing.
Freed from suffering and attaining liberation—how excellent is Avalokiteśvara!
Throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he enters buddha-lands as many as motes of dust;
having attained the power of great mastery, he bestows fearlessness upon sentient beings.
Sublime Sound, Avalokiteśvara, Brahmic Sound, Tide-like Sound,
Bringing peace and security to all in the world, Transcending the world to attain eternal abiding.
I now address the Tathāgata As Avalokiteśvara has taught:
For example, when a person sits in quietude, if drums are struck simultaneously in the ten directions, they hear them all at once in those ten places; this is the reality of perfection.
The eyes do not see beyond obstructions, and the same is true for the mouth and nose.
The body knows through contact; the mind’s thoughts are chaotic and without order.
Hearing sounds across a wall, both near and far can be perceived;
since the five sense organs are not equal in this regard, this is what penetrates the ultimate reality.
The nature of sound is movement and stillness; within hearing, it is either present or absent.
When there is no sound, it is called "no-hearing," yet this is not truly the absence of the nature of hearing.
Since sound is absent, there is no cessation; since sound is present, there is no arising.
When both arising and ceasing are perfectly transcended, this is the eternal reality.
Even if one is in a dream, it is not absent when not being thought of;
it transcends discursive observation and deliberation, such that body and mind cannot reach it.
Now, in this Sahā world, the science of phonetics may be proclaimed and clarified;
yet sentient beings are deluded regarding their fundamental hearing and, by following after sounds, they wander through the cycle of rebirth.
Even if Ānanda possessed powerful memory, he could not avoid falling into deviant thoughts.
Is it not that by following wherever one sinks, one may reverse the flow and attain non-delusion?
Ānanda, listen attentively! Upholding the Buddha’s majestic power, I shall proclaim the Vajra King, which is like an illusion and inconceivable.
The True Samādhi of the Buddha-Mother:
All Secret Gateways. If one does not first eliminate the outflows of desire, the accumulation of learning will result in error.
If you are about to hear and maintain the Buddhas and Buddhas, why do you not hear your own hearing?
Hearing does not arise spontaneously; it exists as a name because of sound.
When hearing turns back and detaches from sound, who is there to be named as that which can detach?
When one faculty returns to its source, all six faculties achieve liberation.
If the three realms are like flowers in the sky, then as hearing is restored, the cataracts of the sense organs are removed;
when sensory objects dissolve, awareness becomes perfectly pure.
The pure, ultimate radiance penetrates all; its tranquil illumination encompasses the void.
It is like a matter within a dream: Mātaṅgī is but a dream—whence could she retain your form?
Illusions manifest as various men and women; though their faculties are seen to move, they are all drawn by a single mechanism.
When the mechanism ceases and returns to stillness, all illusions become devoid of inherent nature.
The six sense organs are likewise so: originally they depend on a single luminous intelligence, yet they are divided into six harmonious combinations.
When one locus attains rest and restoration, the functions of all six cease to exist.
Dust and defilements dissolve at the mere thought [of this], achieving perfect, luminous, pure, and wondrous clarity;
yet with residual dust remaining, one is still among those in training. When clarity reaches its ultimate limit, one is a Tathāgata.
Great Assembly and Ānanda: turn back your inverted faculty of hearing.
Turning the hearing back to hear its own nature, That nature achieves the Unsurpassed Way;
Such indeed is perfect penetration.
This is the single path to the gate of Nirvana; All Tathāgatas of the past,
This gateway has already been accomplished;
now each enters perfect clarity. Future practitioners of the Way should rely upon this Dharma.
I, too, have realized this from within it; it is not only Avalokiteśvara.
Consult me regarding all skillful means to rescue those of the final age, for seekers of the supramundane who wish to perfect the mind of nirvāṇa.
Avalokiteśvara is supreme;
all this is through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power. By engaging with phenomena, one abandons worldly toil;
it is not a matter of long-term cultivation or study, for the teachings on the shallow and the deep are proclaimed as one.
I prostrate to the Tathāgatagarbha, Untainted and inconceivable;
May you grant your empowerment so that those in the future May have no doubts regarding this gateway And easily achieve its skillful means.
"And even during the final kalpa of sinking and delusion, if one cultivates only this faculty, its perfect penetration will surpass all others; such is the true mind.

Thereupon, Ānanda and the great assembly, with body and mind clearly illuminated, received this great instruction. They contemplated the Buddha’s Bodhi and Great Nirvāṇa as being like a person who has traveled far away on business and has not yet returned, yet clearly understands the path by which they must return home.

The entire assembly—the eight classes of devas and nāgas, those of the two vehicles still in training, and all the newly resolved bodhisattvas, numbering as many as ten Ganges-sands—each attained their original mind, became free from dust and defilement, and obtained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
Upon hearing the verses, the bhikṣuṇī Śrī attained arhatship;
and immeasurable sentient beings all gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, which is peerless.

Ānanda adjusted his robes, joined his palms in homage toward the great assembly, and with a mind and traces of conduct perfectly luminous, filled with a mixture of sorrow and joy, he bowed his head to the Buddha and said:
"O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One! For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings of the future, I pray you speak."
I have now awakened to the Dharma-gate of attaining Buddhahood; practicing within it, I have attained freedom from doubt and confusion. I have constantly heard the Tathāgata speak these words:
"To first seek to deliver others before one has delivered oneself is the aspiration of a Bodhisattva;
to awaken others once one's own awakening is perfected is the manifestation of a Tathāgata in the world."
"Although I have not yet attained liberation myself, I vow to deliver all sentient beings of the final age.
World-Honored One!

These sentient beings are gradually moving further away from the Buddha, and false teachers preach the Dharma as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. How may I cause their minds to be gathered and enter samādhi; how may I cause them to establish themselves at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), remain far removed from demonic activities, and attain no retreat or discouragement regarding the mind of Bodhi?"
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Ānanda amidst the great assembly:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"As you have asked regarding the establishment of a site of enlightenment to rescue and protect sentient beings drowning in the final age, listen attentively now; I shall speak for you.
Ānanda and the great assembly responded, "So be it," and respectfully received the instruction.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"You have often heard me, within the Vinaya, proclaim the three principles of definitive practice: namely, that gathering the mind constitutes the precepts; from the precepts arises concentration; and from concentration issues forth wisdom."
This is what is called the three trainings in the outflow-free (anāsrava). Ānanda!
Why do I say that the gathering of the mind is called precept (śīla)?
If the sentient beings of the six realms in all worlds do not harbor lustful hearts, they will not follow along with the continuity of birth and death.

You practice samādhi in order to emerge from worldly toil; if the lustful heart is not eliminated, you cannot escape the dust of the world. Even if you possess great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before you, if you do not sever lust, you will inevitably fall into the paths of demons—either as high-ranking demon-kings, mid-level demon-subjects, or low-grade demonesses. These various demons also have their own followers, each claiming for themselves that they have attained the Unsurpassed Way.

After my parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Final Dharma, many such followers of Māra will flourish in the world. They will widely practice greed and lust while posing as spiritual teachers (kalyāṇamitra), causing sentient beings to fall into the pit of craving and false views and lose the path to Bodhi.

When you teach the people of the world to cultivate samādhi, they must first sever sexual desire in the mind; this is called the Tathāgata’s foremost, definitive, pure, and clear instruction from the Buddhas of the past.
"Therefore, Ānanda!

If one does not sever lust yet cultivates meditative concentration, it is like steaming sand and stones hoping they will become rice; even after hundreds of thousands of kalpas, they will merely be called hot sand."
Why is this? Because this is not rice, but is composed of stones and sand.

If you seek the wondrous fruit of Buddhahood with a lustful body, even if you should attain wondrous enlightenment, it will all be rooted in lust. With lust as its fundamental basis, you will revolve through the three miserable realms and certainly be unable to escape; by what path, then, could you cultivate and realize the Nirvana of the Tathāgata?
One must ensure that the mechanism of lust is severed in both body and mind, and even the nature of this severance is non-existent; only then can one hope for the Bodhi of the Buddha.
What I have spoken thus is called the teaching of the Buddha;
what is not spoken thus is the teaching of Pāpīyān.
“Ānanda! Furthermore, if the beings of the six realms in all worlds do not harbor the intent to kill, they will not follow along with the continuity of birth and death.

You cultivate samādhi to fundamentally escape the toil of the mundane world; if the murderous mind is not eliminated, you cannot transcend the dust. Even if you possess great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before you, if you do not sever killing, you will inevitably fall into the realm of spirits. Those of the highest grade become powerful ghosts; those of the middle grade become flying yakṣas, various ghost generals, and the like; those of the lowest grade become earth-walking rākṣasas. These ghosts and spirits also have their own followers, each claiming for themselves that they have attained the Unsurpassed Way.”
"After my parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Final Dharma, many such spirits and ghosts will flourish in the world, claiming that by eating meat one attains the path to Bodhi.
Ānanda!"

"I have permitted the bhikṣus to eat the five kinds of pure meat; these meats were all produced through my supernatural power and originally possessed no life-force. You, O Brahmin, live in a land where the soil is mostly damp and humid, and because it is further burdened by sand and stones, grasses and vegetables do not grow. It was through the application of my great compassionate supernatural power that I provisionally named this 'meat' out of great kindness so that you might obtain its flavor. How can it be, after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, that those who eat the flesh of sentient beings call themselves disciples of the Śākya?"

You should know this: even if those who eat meat should attain an opening of the mind that resembles *samādhi*, they are all great *rākṣasas*. When their retribution ends, they will inevitably sink into the bitter sea of birth and death; they are not disciples of the Buddha. Since such people continue to kill, devour, and consume one another without end, how could they ever escape the three realms?

"You should teach the people of the world to cultivate samādhi and next to cease killing; this is called the Tathāgata’s second definitive, pure, and clear instruction following the World-Honored Buddhas of the past."
"Therefore, Ānanda!

If one does not cease killing while practicing meditative concentration, it is like a person who blocks their own ears and shouts at the top of their voice, seeking for others not to hear them; such people are said to 'conceal what they wish to hide, yet make it even more manifest.'"
Pure bhikṣus and bodhisattvas do not even tread upon living grass when walking along a forked path, much less pluck it with their hands;
how then could those of great compassion take the flesh and blood of sentient beings to serve as food?

If bhikṣus do not wear silks, cotton, or fine fabrics from the East, nor the boots, furs, or woolens of this land, nor consume milk, curd, or clarified butter, such bhikṣus are truly liberated from the world; they have repaid their karmic debts and no longer wander within the three realms.
Why is this? Because serving any part of their bodies constitutes a causal condition for them; it is like a person who eats the hundred grains from the earth—their feet never leave the ground.

If one ensures that, regarding all sentient beings, whether in their entirety or in parts of their bodies, one neither serves nor consumes them through either body or mind—these two paths—I declare such a person to be truly liberated.
"What I have spoken in this way is called the Buddha's teaching;
what is not spoken in this way is the teaching of Pāpīyān. Ānanda!
Furthermore, if the beings of the six realms within the world do not harbor a mind of theft, they will not follow the continuous succession of birth and death.

You cultivate samādhi fundamentally to emerge from worldly toil; if the thieving mind is not eliminated, you cannot escape the dust of the world. Even if you possess great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before you, if you do not sever the thieving mind, you will inevitably fall into deviant paths. There you will be possessed by superior spirits, middling ghosts and demons, or inferior wicked persons and various malevolent spirits. These various deviant hordes also have their own followers, each claiming for themselves that they have attained the Unsurpassed Way.

After my parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Final Dharma, many such demonic and heterodox beings will flourish in the world; they will secretly harbor deceit and fraud while claiming to be "good spiritual friends" (kalyāṇamitra), each asserting for themselves that they have attained the dharmas of a superior person (uttarapudgala). They will delude and mislead the ignorant, terrifying them into losing their minds, and wherever they go, the households they visit will suffer depletion and ruin.

I have taught the bhikṣus to wander for alms according to their direction, so that they may abandon greed and accomplish the path of a bodhisattva. These bhikṣus do not cook food for themselves; they entrust their remaining lives to a transient sojourn within the three realms, demonstrating that after this single journey back and forth, there shall be no returning.

How is it that these thieves, wearing my robes, peddle themselves as Tathāgatas and create all manner of karmic deeds? They all claim that the Buddha-dharma is contrary to leaving the home life, and they assert that the fully ordained bhikṣu follows the path of the Hīnayāna.
Because of these doubts and errors, immeasurable sentient beings fall into the Avīci Hell.

After my parinirvāṇa, if there are bhikṣus who resolve their minds to cultivate samādhi, and who, before an image of the Tathāgata, burn a single lamp, sacrifice a finger-joint, or burn a single incense stick upon their bodies—I declare that such persons shall at once repay all their karmic debts from beginningless time. They shall forever distance themselves from the world and eternally escape all outflows (āsravas). Although they may not yet clearly perceive the path to supreme enlightenment, such persons have already attained a resolute mind regarding the Dharma. If they do not perform this minor cause of sacrificing the body, even if they were to attain the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), they would necessarily return to the human realm to repay their karmic debts, no different from my own experience with the horse-barley.

"You shall teach the people of the world to cultivate samādhi first, and only thereafter sever the habit of stealing; this is called the third definitive, pure, and clear instruction of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One of former Buddhas."
"Therefore, Ānanda!

If one does not cease stealing while practicing meditative concentration, it is like a person pouring water into a leaking cup hoping to fill it; even if they pass through kalpas as numerous as dust motes, it will never be restored."

If bhikṣus do not store even a fraction of what remains from their robes and alms bowls; if they give the remnants of their begged food to hungry sentient beings; if they join their palms and pay homage to the assembly at great gatherings; if they regard being struck or reviled by others as being praised; if they ensure that both body and mind are completely relinquished, such that their flesh, marrow, and blood are shared with all beings; and if they do not take the Buddha’s teachings of provisional meaning and twist them into their own interpretations to mislead beginners—the Buddha certifies that such a person has attained true samādhi.
"What I have spoken is what is called the Buddha's teaching;
that which is not spoken thus is the teaching of Pāpīyān. Ānanda!"

Thus, among the sentient beings of the six realms in this world, even if their bodies and minds are free from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—such that these three practices are already perfected—if they engage in great falsehoods, their *samādhi* will not attain purity;
they will become demons of craving and views, losing the seed of the Tathāgata.

This refers to those who claim what they have not attained as attained, and say they have realized what they have not realized; or those who seek worldly preeminence and superiority, saying to others:

"I have now attained the fruit of a *srotāpanna*, the fruit of a *sakṛdāgāmin*, the fruit of an *anāgāmin*, the path of an *arhat*, the vehicle of a *pratyekabuddha*, the ten stages (*bhūmi*), and the various bodhisattva stages prior to the stages."

To seek offerings by performing prostrations and repentances for such ends is to commit an *icchantika* offense that extinguishes the seeds of Buddhahood. It is like a person cutting down a *tāla* tree with a sword; the Buddha has declared that such a person will forever sever their roots of goodness and no longer possess wisdom or insight, sinking into the ocean of the three sufferings and failing to achieve samādhi.

After my parinirvāṇa, I shall command various bodhisattvas and arhats to manifest their response-bodies within that age of the final dharma, assuming diverse forms to deliver those wandering in saṃsāra. Whether appearing as śramaṇas, lay devotees, kings, ministers, youths, or maidens—and even as courtesans, widows, thieves, or butchers—they shall engage in the same activities as others while praising the Buddha Vehicle, causing their bodies and minds to enter samādhi. Yet they shall never say of themselves, "I am a true bodhisattva" or "I am a true arhat."

To divulge the Buddha’s secret causes and speak lightly of those who have not yet studied—except when, at the end of life, there is a hidden entrustment—how can such a person delude the masses and commit a great falsehood?

"You shall teach the people of the world to practice samādhi and thereafter eliminate all great false claims; this is called the fourth definitive, pure, and clear instruction of the Tathāgata and the World-Honored Buddhas of the past."
"Therefore, Ānanda!
If one does not sever this great falsehood, it is like carving human excrement into the shape of sandalwood; to seek a fragrant scent from it is impossible."

I teach that bhikṣus take the straightforward mind as their place of practice; even within the four modes of deportment and all their actions, they must be free from hypocrisy. How then can you claim to have attained the dharmas of a superior person?
For example, it would be like a destitute person falsely claiming to be an emperor, only to bring about his own execution; how much more so for one who would falsely usurp the title of Dharma King?
If the ground is not upright, the fruit will be crooked; seeking the Bodhi of the Buddha like a man trying to bite his own navel—who could possibly achieve success?

If bhikṣus have minds as straight as a bowstring and are entirely true to reality, entering samādhi without ever encountering demonic interference, I certify that such persons shall achieve the unsurpassed awakening of a bodhisattva.
What I have thus spoken is called the teaching of the Buddha;
what is not spoken in this way is the teaching of Pāpīyān.
*The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ten Thousand Practices*, Fascicle Six.

The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Cultivation and Realization of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata’s Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa, Being the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas; Fascicle Seven.
Also known as the Mahāmaṇḍala Sūtra of Nālandā in Central India, excerpted from the Abhiṣeka Section and circulated separately.
Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Prajñāmitra of the Tang Dynasty: “Ānanda!
Regarding your question on gathering the mind, I shall first explain the wondrous gateway for training in entering samādhi.”

In seeking the Bodhisattva path, one must first maintain these four types of discipline as pure as ice and frost; otherwise, one cannot produce any branches or leaves, and the three actions of the mind and four of the body will have no cause for arising.
Ānanda! If these four matters are not lost or neglected, the mind will not even take as its object form, sound, smell, taste, or touch; how then could any demonic activities arise?

If there are those whose past habitual tendencies cannot be extinguished or eliminated, you should instruct them to single-mindedly recite this unsurpassed divine mantra of my *Buddhōṣṇīṣavijaya-mahāsātranta-praṇidhāra*. This is the Tathāgata’s mark of the invisible crown; it is the heart-mantra issued from the radiance of the Unconditioned Mind-Buddha as he sat upon a precious lotus flower. Furthermore, your karmic affinity with Mātangi over successive kalpas and your habituated tendencies of affectionate attachment are not merely the result of one lifetime or a single kalpa;
yet, by my single proclamation, your love-attachment was forever severed and you became an Arhat.
That courtesan had no intention to practice, yet she was secretly aided by spiritual power and swiftly realized the stage of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa*);
how much more so for you, the śrāvakas in this assembly, who seek the Supreme Vehicle and are determined to attain Buddhahood?
It is like throwing dust against the wind; what difficulty or danger could there be?

If anyone in the final age wishes to sit at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), they must first uphold the pure prohibitions of a bhikṣu. They must choose as their teacher a foremost śramaṇa whose precepts are pure. If they do not encounter a truly pure monk, their observance of the precepts will certainly not be perfected. Once the precepts are perfected, they should don new, clean robes, burn incense, and dwell in seclusion, reciting this divine mantra spoken by the Mind-Buddha one hundred and eight times. Thereafter, they shall demarcate the boundary and establish the site of enlightenment, beseeching the Unsurpassed Tathāgatas currently dwelling in the lands of the ten directions to emit rays of great compassionate light and pour them over their crowns.

Ānanda! Thus, in the final age, if pure bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, or lay donors extinguish lust in their hearts and uphold the Buddha’s pure precepts, making bodhisattva vows within the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), entering and leaving for ablutions, and practicing the Way throughout the six periods of the day and night—remaining thus without sleep for twenty-one days—I shall manifest my own body before that person, stroke their head to comfort them, and cause them to attain awakening.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Having received the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed compassionate instruction, my mind has already attained awakening; I know for myself that I have cultivated and realized the path of no-more-learning.”
"In the age of the Final Dharma, when one establishes a site for practice, how should one demarcate the boundaries in accordance with the pure regulations of the Buddha, the World-Honored One?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"If those in the world during the final age wish to establish a site for practice, they should first take a powerful white ox from the Snowy Mountains that feeds on the lush, fatty fragrant herbs of those mountains. This ox drinks only the clear water of the Snowy Mountains, so its dung is fine and subtle; one may take this dung and mix it with sandalwood to plaster the ground."

If it were not for the Snowy Mountains, the cattle there would be so foul-smelling that their dung could not even be used to smear the ground. Therefore, apart from the plains, one must dig five feet beneath the surface of the earth to take the yellow soil. This is then mixed with the ten kinds of incense—sandalwood, aloeswood, *suhaka*, *kunduruka*, saffron, *guggulu*, *śrīveṣṭaka*, *kāśmīra*, *kālānusāri*, and clove—and finely ground into powder. This powder is combined with the soil to form a paste, which is then used to smear the ritual site.
Construct an octagonal altar measuring sixteen feet in circumference. At the center of the altar, place a lotus flower made of gold, silver, copper, or wood;
upon the flower, set a bowl. Within the bowl, first fill it with dew collected during the eighth month, and place whatever lotus petals are available within the water.
Take eight round mirrors and position them one at each of the cardinal and intermediate directions surrounding the flower and bowl. Outside the mirrors...
Establish sixteen lotus flowers, interspersed with sixteen incense burners arranged in a floral pattern;
adorn the incense burners by burning pure aloeswood so that the flames are not visible. Take white cow’s milk and place it in sixteen vessels;
from the milk, prepare fried cakes, along with various granulated sugars, oil cakes, milk porridge, butter confections, honey, and ginger.
Pure ghee, pure honey, various fruits, food and drink, grapes, rock sugar,
and all kinds of exquisite delicacies— each of these sixteen types of offerings surrounding the outer perimeter of the lotus flower—
are presented to the Buddhas and the great Bodhisattvas at every mealtime.

If it is at midnight, take half a *śu* of honey and three *hē* of clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Before the altar, separately set up a small fire hearth; boil *turuṣka* incense to produce scented water, bathe the charcoal, and kindle it until it blazes fiercely. Cast this honey and clarified butter into the flaming hearth and burn them until the smoke has vanished, thereby making an offering to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

Have banners and flowers suspended all around the four outer sides, and within the chamber of the maṇḍala, arrange images of all the Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions upon the four walls.
One should display Vairocana, Śākyamuni, Maitreya, Akṣobhya, and Amitābha facing the front;
and as for the various great transformational forms of Avalokiteśvara, together with Vajragarbha, place them to his left and right.
Śakra, the Brahma King, Ucchuṣma, along with the Lambakas, the various Cāmuṇḍīs, Piṅgala, the Four Heavenly Kings, and the Vināyakas, were stationed on the left and right sides at the entrance.

Furthermore, take eight mirrors and suspend them in the void, facing the mirrors installed within the ritual mandala, so that their forms and reflections interpenetrate one another in successive layers.

“During the first seven days, one should with utmost sincerity prostrate to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, the great Bodhisattvas, and the Arhats; constantly reciting mantras and circumambulating the altar throughout the six periods of the day and night, performing the practice with a sincere heart, always completing one hundred and eight repetitions during each period.
During the second seven days, one should single-mindedly and exclusively resolve upon the Bodhisattva vow without interruption; this is the instruction on vows previously established in my Vinaya.
During the third seven days, throughout the twelve periods, one should single-mindedly maintain the Buddha’s Pañcarakṣā mantra.”

Upon reaching the fourth seven-day period, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions simultaneously appeared at the place where the mirrors reflect one another’s light; receiving the Buddhas’ touch upon their crowns, they immediately cultivated *samādhi* within the site of enlightenment, enabling those practicing in this degenerate age to make their bodies and minds as clear and pure as lapis lazuli.
Ānanda! If among this bhikṣu’s original preceptor and the ten bhikṣus of the assembly, even one is impure, such a site of practice will for the most part not be accomplished.

After three weeks, he sat upright in meditative seclusion for one hundred days; those of sharp faculties attained the stage of *srotāpanna* without rising from their seats, and even if their physical and mental bodies had not yet fully realized the holy fruit, they were certain to know for themselves that their attainment of Buddhahood was unerring.
"You have asked about the site of enlightenment; it is established in this way.
Ānanda prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and said to the Buddha:
"Since I left the household life, I have relied upon the Buddha’s affectionate love; because I sought extensive learning, I have not yet realized the unconditioned."
Having been constrained by the malevolent arts of that Brahmā-deva, although my mind was clear and lucid, my power was not free; it was only by relying on meeting Mañjuśrī that I was liberated.
Although I have received the Buddha-ūṣṇīṣa divine mantra of the Tathāgata and have secretly obtained its power, I have not yet heard it directly.

We only pray that the Great Compassionate One will again proclaim this teaching, out of pity to rescue all practitioners in this assembly, as well as those in saṃsāra of the future; may they receive the Buddha’s secret voice and attain liberation of body and mind.
At that time, the entire assembly in the gathering prostrated themselves, waiting expectantly to hear the secret verses of the Tathāgata.

Then, from within his *uṣṇīṣa*, the World-Honored One emitted a hundred-jeweled light; from within this light emerged thousand-petaled jeweled lotuses, upon which emanated Tathāgatas sat amidst the precious flowers. From their crowns issued ten streams of hundred-jeweled radiance, and within each stream of light were manifested ten *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (Ganges-sand) numbers of Vajrapāṇis, who, bearing mountains and wielding maces, filled the entirety of space. The great assembly gazed upward, feeling a mixture of awe and affection, seeking the Buddha as their protector, and with single-minded devotion listened as the Tathāgata of the Unseen Crown (*anavalokitamūrdha*) emitted light and proclaimed the divine mantra.
