The above mantra phrases consist of four hundred and thirty-nine sentences in total. "Ānanda!
These subtle and wondrous verses of the secret *gāthā* of the Buddha-Usnīṣa-Raśmi-Sañcaya-Sitātapatra give birth to all Buddhas throughout the ten directions."
By means of this mantra-heart, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions have attained unexcelled, right, and universal enlightenment;
by upholding this mantra-heart, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions subdue all māras and restrain all heterodox teachers;
by riding upon this mantra-heart, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions sit upon precious lotus flowers and respond to lands as numerous as motes of dust.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions contain this mantra-heart within themselves, and by it they turn the Great Dharma Wheel in lands as numerous as motes of dust.

The Tathāgatas of the ten directions uphold this mantra-heart, and by it they can bestow the prediction of enlightenment by touching their crowns in the ten directions; even those whose own fruits are not yet mature receive the Buddha’s prediction in the ten directions through it.

Relying on this mantra-heart, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions are able to rescue and deliver beings from all sufferings in the ten directions—namely, the sufferings of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals; the suffering of being joined with what one hates; the suffering of being separated from what one loves; the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks; and the burning intensity of the five aggregates. All great and small calamities are simultaneously liberated: the perils of bandits, armies, kings, prisons, wind, water, and fire, as well as hunger, thirst, and poverty—all are dissolved away at the mere thought of it.

The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, following this mantra-heart, are able to serve spiritual friends throughout the ten directions, making offerings as they wish during the four modes of conduct, and are promoted by the Tathāgatas in assemblies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges as Great Dharma Princes;

the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, practicing this mantra-heart, are able to gather and sustain their kinsmen and causes throughout the ten directions, causing those of the Lesser Vehicle to hear the Secret Treasury without giving rise to alarm or fear;
the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, reciting this mantra-heart, achieve unexcelled enlightenment, sit beneath the Bodhi tree, and enter Great Nirvāṇa.

The Tathāgatas of the ten directions transmit this mantra-heart; after their parinirvāṇa, they entrust it with the affairs of the Buddha-dharma so that it may be ultimately maintained, ensuring that the solemn and pure precepts are entirely kept clear and pure.

"If I were to recite this Buddha-Usnīṣa-Raśmi-Sañcaya Pañcarakṣā Dhāraṇī from dawn until dusk, with the sounds continuous and the syllables and phrases never overlapping, I could not finish it even after kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."

Furthermore, this mantra is called the "Crown of the Tathāgata. For you who are still in training and have not yet exhausted the cycle of saṃsāra, if you resolve with utmost sincerity to attain arhatship, it is impossible that you could sit in the place of practice without upholding this mantra and thereby keep your body and mind far removed from all demonic activities.

“Ānanda! In whatever world, in whatever land, if all sentient beings born in that land take birch bark, palm leaves, paper, or white cotton cloth to write down this dhāraṇī and store it in a fragrant pouch—if such a person’s mind is dull and they are unable to recite or memorize it, yet they either wear it upon their body or keep it written within their home—you should know that for the entirety of that person’s life, no poisons whatsoever shall be able to harm them.”
“Ānanda! I shall now further explain this mantra for you, which protects and delivers the world, grants great fearlessness, and brings about the supramundane wisdom of all beings.”

If, after my parinirvāṇa, there are sentient beings in the final age who can recite this themselves or teach others to recite it, you should know that such sentient beings who maintain it through recitation cannot be burned by fire nor drowned by water; they cannot be harmed by great or small poisons. Furthermore, all evil spells—including those of dragons, devas, ghosts, spirits, *piśācas*, and *mārās*—cannot take hold of them, and their minds will attain right concentration (*samādhi*).

All curses, spells, bewitchments, poisons—whether from gold, silver, plants, trees, insects, snakes, or the poisonous vapors of myriad things—shall turn into the flavor of ambrosia once they enter this person’s mouth. Furthermore, all malevolent stars and various ghosts and spirits who harbor cruel hearts and seek to harm others will be unable to give rise to evil thoughts toward such a person.
The Vināyakas, the various evil ghost-kings, and their retinues shall all acknowledge this profound kindness and constantly provide protection. "Ānanda!

You should know that there are always eighty-four thousand nayutas of Ganges-sands of koṭis of Bodhisattvas of the lineage of Vajragarbha Kings, each with hosts of vajra-beings as their retinue. If there are sentient beings who, even with a distracted mind or a mind not in samādhi, remember and recite this mantra, these Vajra Kings will constantly follow those good sons; how much more so for those who possess the resolute bodhicitta!"

These Vajra-Bodhisattvas, Kings of the Treasury, with their refined minds, secretly and swiftly activate that divine consciousness. At such a time, this person’s mind will be able to remember eighty-four thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* eons; they will know them thoroughly and without doubt, from the first eon until their final body. In every birth, they shall not be born among yakṣas, rākṣasas, pūtanas, kaṭapūtanas, kumbhāṇḍas, piśācas, or other hungry ghosts;

nor in any such evil places, whether possessing form or lacking form, having thought or lacking thought. If this son of good family reads, recites, copies, transcribes, wears, or conceals [this treasury], and makes various offerings, then eon after eon he shall not be born in states of poverty, lowliness, or unpleasantness.

Even if these sentient beings themselves do not perform meritorious deeds, all the merits of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions shall be bestowed upon them. By this means, for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—incalculable, unspeakably unspeakable—they shall always be born in the same place as the Buddhas. Their immeasurable merits, like a cluster of akṣa fruits, shall be cultivated together in that same location, never to be dispersed.
Therefore, it can cause those who have broken the precepts to purify their roots of discipline;
it causes those who have not yet attained the precepts to attain them;
and it causes those who are not yet diligent to attain diligence.
It causes those without wisdom to attain wisdom;
it enables those who are not pure to quickly attain purity;
and it allows those who do not observe the precepts of fasting to spontaneously fulfill them.

"Ānanda! When these good men uphold this mantra, even if they have violated the prohibitive precepts prior to receiving them, all transgressions of the precepts committed after upholding the mantra—regardless of whether they are light or heavy—are extinguished at once.

Even if they should drink alcohol or consume the five pungent roots and various kinds of impurities, all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, celestial immortals, and spirits will not regard it as a fault. Even if they wear impure, tattered, and worn-out clothing, every action and every dwelling place shall be identical to purity."

Even if one does not construct an altar, does not enter a *dharma* hall, and does not practice the Way, yet recites and upholds this mantra, it is equivalent in merit to entering the altar and practicing the Way.

Should one commit the five heinous crimes of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*), or if *bhikṣus* and *bhikṣuṇīs* commit the four grave offenses or the eight grave offenses, once they have recited this mantra, such heavy karmic burdens will be completely eradicated—just as a fierce wind scatters a heap of sand—leaving behind not even a hair’s breadth.

“Ānanda! If there are sentient beings who, throughout immeasurable and incalculable kalpas, have accumulated all manner of light and heavy karmic obstacles from previous lives that they have not yet had the opportunity to repent—if they can read, recite, copy, or carry this mantra upon their person; or if it is placed within their dwelling, house, garden, or villa—then such accumulated karma will vanish like snow melting in boiling water, and before long they shall all attain the realization of the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).”
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

If there are women who have not yet borne children and desire to give birth, if they can recollect this mantra with a sincere heart, or wear this *Sitatapatra* (White Umbrella) upon their bodies, they will give birth to sons or daughters endowed with merit and wisdom;
those who seek long life will quickly obtain long life."
Those who seek the swift fulfillment of karmic rewards shall attain such fulfillment;
their physical life, complexion, and strength shall likewise be so.

After the end of this life, they will be reborn in the lands of the ten directions according to their vows; they will certainly not be born in frontier regions or among the lowly, much less in mixed or inferior forms.

“Ānanda! If there are kingdoms, prefectures, counties, or villages suffering from famine and pestilence, or further threatened by the calamities of war, bandits, and strife, as well as all other lands of misfortune—by transcribing this divine mantra and placing it at the four gates of the city, or upon various *caityas* and *stūpas*, and causing all sentient beings within that land to welcome this mantra, prostrating with reverence and making offerings with single-minded devotion; and if the people each wear it upon their persons or place it in their respective dwellings—all calamities and afflictions shall be entirely extinguished.”

“Ānanda! In whatever lands and regions these mantras exist among sentient beings, the devas and nāgas will rejoice, and wind and rain will follow their proper seasons. The five grains will be abundant, and the myriad people will be at peace and happy. Furthermore, they can subdue all malevolent stars; according to the directions, no strange portents or calamitous obstacles shall arise. People will suffer no untimely deaths, and their bodies shall not be touched by cangues, fetters, stocks, or shackles. Day and night they shall sleep in peace, and they shall never have evil dreams.”

“Ānanda! In this Sahā world-system there are eighty-four thousand calamitous and malevolent stars, with twenty-eight great malevolent stars as their leaders, and furthermore, eight great malevolent stars that act as their sovereigns. When they manifest in various forms appearing in the world, they can produce all manner of calamities and anomalies for sentient beings; however, in lands where this dhāraṇī exists, these are entirely extinguished. Within a boundary of twelve yojanas, no evil portents or disasters can ever enter.”

"Therefore, the Tathāgata proclaims this mantra to protect beginners in future ages. When practitioners enter samādhi, their bodies and minds will be tranquil and they shall attain great peace and security; furthermore, no demons, ghosts, or spirits, nor any karmic debts or calamities from beginningless time, shall come to harass or harm them."

If you, as well as all those among the assembly who are still in training, and all practitioners of future ages, rely upon my ritual arena and maintain the precepts according to the Dharma; if the precept masters you receive are pure monks, and you uphold this mantra-heart without giving rise to doubt or regret—then if such a son of good family does not attain mental penetration within this very body born of his parents, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions would be speaking falsely.

Having spoken these words, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Vajrapāṇis in the assembly simultaneously joined their palms before the Buddha, prostrated with their heads at his feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“In accordance with what the Buddha has taught, we shall protect with sincere hearts those who thus cultivate bodhi.”
At that time, the Brahma King, together with Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and the Four Great Kings, also simultaneously prostrated before the Buddha and addressed him, saying:

"If there are indeed such virtuous persons who practice and study in this way, we shall protect them with our whole hearts and utmost sincerity, ensuring that everything they do throughout their lives shall be fulfilled according to their wishes."

Furthermore, immeasurable yakṣa generals, rākṣasa kings, pūtana kings, kumbhāṇḍa kings, piśāca kings, vināyaka great ghost kings, and various ghost commanders also joined their palms before the Buddha and prostrated themselves, saying:
“We too vow to protect and sustain this person, so that their bodhicitta may swiftly reach full perfection.”

Furthermore, immeasurable Sun and Moon Devas, the Master of Wind, the Master of Rain, the Master of Clouds, the Master of Thunder, along with the Lord of Lightning and others—the various stellar deities who oversee the cycles of the years—also prostrated at the Buddha’s feet within the assembly and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“We, too, shall protect these practitioners of the Way, establishing them in the site of enlightenment so that they may attain fearlessness.”

Furthermore, immeasurable mountain deities and ocean deities, as well as all the spirits and essences of the myriad things dwelling on land, in water, on earth, or in the air, together with the Wind Deity Kings and the gods of the Formless Realm, simultaneously prostrated themselves before the Tathāgata and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“We, too, shall protect these practitioners so that they may attain Bodhi and be forever free from demonic obstacles.”

At that time, eighty-four thousand nayutas of koṭis of Bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, who were all Vajragarbha Kings, rose from their seats within the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

By the merit and accomplishments we have cultivated, may we long attain Bodhi without entering Nirvana, and may we constantly follow this mantra to protect and deliver those who practice Samādhi and cultivate right conduct in the final age.
World-Honored One!

If those who thus cultivate the mind and seek right concentration—whether they are at a place of practice (*maṇḍala*), on their walking paths, or even when their minds are distracted as they roam through villages—we and our followers shall always follow and attend to such persons. Even if Māra or Maheśvara should seek an opportunity against them, they shall ultimately find none;
and all minor ghosts and spirits shall remain ten *yojanas* away from these virtuous people, except for those who have resolved their minds to joyfully cultivate meditation.
"Bhagavān!

If such an evil Māra or his retinue should come to harass this virtuous person, I shall shatter their heads with my precious mallet until they are like fine dust, and I shall ensure that this person’s undertakings always accord with their wishes."
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“We of dull wit were fond of mere erudition, yet our minds remained amidst the outflows (*āsrava*) without seeking liberation. Having received the Buddha’s compassionate instruction, we have attained correct cultivation; our bodies and minds are refreshed, and we have gained great benefit.”
World-Honored One!
When one thus cultivates and realizes the Buddha’s samādhi but has not yet reached nirvāṇa, why is this called the stage of dry wisdom?
And what are the forty-four minds?
To what gradual sequence does one attain the eye of cultivation?
To which place must one go to be said to have entered the stages (*bhūmi*)?
And what is meant by the name "Equal Enlightenment Bodhisattva" (*Samyak-saṃbuddha-bodhisattva*)?

Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground. The great assembly, with one mind, waited expectantly for the Buddha’s compassionate voice, gazing up at him with fixed and wide-eyed devotion.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Ānanda, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!”

You have been able to universally provide for the great assembly and all sentient beings of the final age who cultivate samādhi and seek the Mahāyāna, showing from the stage of an ordinary person up to the ultimate Great Nirvāṇa the unsurpassed path of correct practice.
"Listen attentively now, and I shall speak for you.
Ānanda and the great assembly joined their palms, hollowed their hearts, and silently received the instruction.
The Buddha said:

“Ānanda! You should know that the wondrous nature is perfectly luminous and free from all names and marks; fundamentally, there have been no worlds or sentient beings. Because of delusion, there is birth; because of birth, there is extinction. Birth and extinction are called delusion; the cessation of delusion is called the Real. This is termed the Tathāgata’s unexcelled Bodhi and Great Nirvāṇa—the two designations for the transformation of the basis.”

Ānanda! If you now wish to cultivate the true samādhi and proceed directly to the Great Nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, you must first recognize these two causes of inversion regarding sentient beings and the world. When inversion does not arise, this is the true samādhi of the Tathāgata.
“Ānanda! What is meant by the inversion of sentient beings? Ānanda!”
Because the mind of intrinsic luminosity is perfectly complete in its nature;
from this luminosity, the nature is activated, and from this nature, deluded vision arises.

From ultimate non-existence, there is established ultimate existence; yet this existence and that which exists have no causal source. The state of abiding and the characteristics of what is abided in are utterly devoid of a root. Taking this non-abiding as the basis, the worlds and all sentient beings are established. Being deluded regarding the fundamentally perfect luminosity gives rise to the false; this false nature has no substance and has nothing upon which it relies.

When one seeks to return to the Real, that which is sought as "Real" is already not the true nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Seeking to restore what is unreal merely results in the manifestation of unreal characteristics. It is neither arising nor abiding; it is neither mind nor phenomena. Through successive production, the power of birth is revealed; these are perfumed to form karma, and through the mutual resonance of shared karma, there arise karmic conditions of mutual extinction and mutual generation. It is for this reason that sentient beings undergo perversion.
“Ānanda! What is meant by the inversion of the world?
It is the false arising of segmented existence within what exists; it is because of this that the realms are established.”
That which is not caused by causes, that which has no abiding place yet abides, and that which flows on without ceasing—by this, the world is formed.

The three periods of time and the four directions intermingle and harmonize, transforming sentient beings into twelve categories. Therefore, the world arises from movement producing sound; from sound, form; from form, fragrance; from fragrance, touch; from touch, flavor; and from flavor, the cognition of phenomena (*dharma*). Because these six disordered delusions constitute the nature of karma, the twelve divisions revolve through this cycle. Thus, the sounds, fragrances, tastes, and touches of the world undergo twelve transformations and return as a single rotation.

Because they ride upon this wheel of inverted characteristics, there are in this world beings born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, and born by transformation; those with form and those without form; those with perception and those without perception; those who are neither with nor without form, and those who are neither with nor without perception.

“Ānanda! Due to the causes of the world’s false transmigration and its restless, inverted nature, the combination of vital energies (*vāyu*) gives rise to eighty-four thousand disordered thoughts of flying and sinking.”
Thus, there are those who transmigrate through lands as eggs or *kalala* embryos; fish, birds, turtles, and snakes fill these realms.
"Due to the causes of the world’s defiled saṃsāra and the inversion of desire, eighty-four thousand transverse and vertical disordered thoughts are formed through their conjunction and growth."
Thus, there are the *kalala* and *arbuda* stages of the embryo that circulate through various lands, where humans, animals, dragons, and seers abound.
"Because of attachment to the world and the inversion of the realms of existence, the combination of subtle elements forms eighty-four thousand types of inverted and chaotic thoughts."
Thus, there are moist-phase *bīja* (seeds) that transmigrate through various lands, teeming with crawling and wriggling creatures of every kind.
Due to the false inversion caused by the cycle of transformation within the world, the conjunction of sensory contact gives rise to eighty-four thousand chaotic thoughts of new and old.
Thus, there are transformed beings (*nirmāṇa-lakṣaṇa*) and *kalala* that circulate through lands; those that undergo metamorphosis and fly fill the world.
"Due to the causes of worldly obstruction, cyclic existence, hindrances, and inversion, they combine and become attached, forming eighty-four thousand deluded thoughts of radiant brilliance."
Thus, there are forms characterized by physical marks (*kalala*) that circulate through the lands; those of refined spirits who perceive omens and portents fill these realms.
Because the world dissolves and revolves due to delusion and inversion, the union with darkness gives rise to eighty-four thousand types of obscured and chaotic conceptions.
Thus, there are formless *kalala* beings who transmigrate through the lands; they are as numerous as those who vanish into emptiness or sink away.
"Because the world is subject to the delusive cycle of shadows and inversions, their combined recollections form eighty-four thousand latent knots of chaotic thoughts."
Thus, there are gandharvas possessing the characteristics of perception who circulate through the lands; spirits, ghosts, and numinous beings fill these realms.
Due to the causes of the world’s dullness, the cycle of rebirth, and deluded inversion, they combine with stubborn matter to form eighty-four thousand parched and disordered thoughts.

Thus, there exist the *asaṃjñika-kaḷala* (unconscious embryo) beings who transmigrate through the lands; their spirits are transformed into earth, wood, metal, and stone, and such kinds fill the world.

"Due to the false perversions of the world’s mutual dependence and cyclic existence, they combine with defilement to form eighty-four thousand types of disordered thoughts based on causal conditions."

Thus, there are those who, lacking the physical form of a sentient being, yet possess the characteristics of matter and undergo transformation as *kalala* (embryonic matter) within the realms of existence; such as the various *siphonophores*, which take shrimp for their eyes, and whose like fill the world.
"Because the nature of cyclic existence is inverted by the mutual attraction of worldly phenomena, these combine with mantras to form eighty-four thousand deluded thoughts of summoning.
Consequently, there exist lands where beings flow through as *kalala* (embryonic stages) that are neither material nor immaterial; those born through curses and incantations fill these realms."

"Because the world arises from the conjunction of causes with delusion and the cycle of transmigration through inversion, the blending of differences produces eighty-four thousand types of reciprocal and chaotic thoughts.

Thus, there exist the *kalala* and *arbuda* stages, which are formed from the characteristics of non-existent perceptions becoming perceptions; these, such as the *pulu* and others, are formed from the mutual interaction of different substances, and their kinds fill the lands."
"Due to the causes of the world’s cycle of enmity and killing, which are inverted, there arise eighty-four thousand strange combinations that give rise to the notion of eating one's own parents.

Thus, there exist lands where beings with non-non-perceptual characteristics and non-perceptual *kalala* (embryonic stages) circulate; such as the earth-owl, which fashions its young from clods of earth, and the 'broken-mirror' bird, which nurtures its offspring by clutching the fruits of poisonous trees. Once the offspring are formed, both parents are devoured by them, and such species fill the land."
"These are called the twelve kinds of sentient beings.

The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ten Thousand Practices of the Bodhisattvas, Scroll Eight. Also known as the Great Maṇḍala Sūtra of Nālandā in Central India;
excerpted from the Abhiṣeka Section and circulated separately.
Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Prajñāmitra of the Tang Dynasty. "Ānanda!
Thus, within each and every class of sentient beings, there likewise exists twelve types of inversion;

just as flowers appear when one presses upon the eyes, these inversions arise from the wondrous, perfect, truly pure, and luminous mind, which is thus fully possessed of such false and deluded conceptions.
As you now cultivate and realize the Buddha’s samādhi, you must establish three gradual stages to eliminate the fundamental deluded thoughts that originally caused this state;
it is like removing poisonous honey from a clean vessel, washing and rinsing that vessel with various hot waters mixed with ashes and incense, so that it may later hold ambrosia.
What are called the three gradual stages?
First is cultivation, which eliminates their auxiliary causes;
second is true cultivation, which excises their fundamental nature.
Third is "progression," which contradicts its present karma.
"What is the auxiliary cause? Ānanda!

Thus, the twelve classes of beings in this world cannot sustain themselves independently but rely on the four kinds of nutriment—namely, edible food, contact-food, volition-food, and consciousness-food; for this reason, the Buddha taught that all sentient beings abide by means of nutriment.
Ānanda! All sentient beings live because they consume what is sweet and die because they consume what is poisonous.

Those sentient beings who seek *samādhi* must sever their consumption of the five kinds of pungent vegetables. These five pungent vegetables, when eaten cooked, arouse lust; when eaten raw, they increase anger. Thus, in this world, those who eat pungent things—even if they can expound the twelve divisions of the scriptures—will be shunned by the celestial beings of the ten directions who loathe their foul stench. Various hungry ghosts, upon seeing them eating, will lick their lips and mouths, causing them to dwell constantly with ghosts. Their merit and virtue will diminish daily, and they will find no lasting benefit.

When those who eat pungent roots practice samādhi, Bodhisattvas, celestial immortals, and the virtuous deities of the ten directions will not come to protect them. A powerful Mara seizes this opportunity to manifest in the form of a Buddha and preach the Dharma to them, reviling the prohibitions and precepts while praising lust, anger, and ignorance. At the end of their lives, they become members of the Mara’s retinue; once their demonic blessings are exhausted, they fall into the Avīci Hell.
Ānanda! One who cultivates bodhi must forever sever the five pungent roots; this is called the first stage of progressive cultivation.
What is right nature?

Ānanda! When sentient beings enter samādhi in this manner, they must first strictly maintain pure precepts, forever severing lustful thoughts, abstaining from wine and meat, consuming food purified by fire, and never eating anything that still possesses life-force.

Ānanda! For a practitioner of the path, if they do not sever lust and killing, it is impossible for them to transcend the three realms. You should contemplate sensual desire as being like a venomous snake or as encountering a hostile thief.

First, uphold the four parājikas and eight śaikṣas of the Śrāvaka to keep the body from wavering; later, practice the pure discipline of the Bodhisattva to prevent the mind from arising. When the prohibitions and precepts are perfected, one will forever be free from the karma of mutual birth and mutual killing within the world; theft and robbery will not occur, there will be no mutual burdens or debts, and one will likewise have no further karmic debts to repay in the world.

These pure persons cultivate samādhi; without needing the divine eye, their physical bodies naturally perceive the worlds of the ten directions. They behold the Buddhas, hear the Dharma, and personally receive the holy instructions. Attaining great supernormal powers, they travel through the worlds of the ten directions; with their past lives purified, they encounter no hardships or perils.
This is called the second stage of progressive cultivation.
What is present karma? Ānanda!

Thus, when one who maintains the pure precepts has no mind of greedy lust and does not allow the senses to flow excessively toward the six external objects, because they do not flow outward, they revolve back to their source and return to themselves. When the objects are no longer conditioned, the sense organs have nothing to pair with; as they flow back to become entirely one, the six functions cease to operate. The lands of the ten directions are then brilliantly pure, like a bright moon suspended within lapis lazuli.

Body and mind are blissful, wondrously perfect, and equanimous, attaining great peace and stability; all the secret, perfect, pure, and subtle [realms] of all Tathāgatas manifest within it, and this person immediately attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
From this point, one gradually cultivates, establishing the stages of sagehood according to the practices undertaken; this is called the third stage of progressive cultivation. "Ānanda!

This good man’s craving for existence has been dried up; as his faculties and objects no longer meet, his remaining physical form will not continue to be reborn. His grasping mind is empty and luminous, consisting purely of wisdom; the nature of this wisdom is bright and perfect, illuminating the ten directions. Because he possesses this wisdom while still in a state of dryness, it is called the Ground of Dry Wisdom.

When the habits of desire are first dried up but have not yet connected with the Tathāgata’s stream of Dharma-water, one immediately enters the central flow within this very mind, becoming perfectly wondrous and fully blossomed. From that true, wondrous perfection, one again gives rise to true wondrousness; wondrous faith becomes permanently established, and all delusive thoughts are extinguished without remainder. This state of pure truth in the Middle Way is called the Abode of Faith.

With true faith and clear understanding, one realizes all-encompassing penetration; the three categories of aggregates, sense-fields, and elements can no longer act as obstructions. Thus, even throughout countless kalpas of past and future, from the casting off of one body to the receiving of another, all habitual tendencies manifest before them. These good sons are able to recollect them all without any omission; this is called the dwelling of the mind in mindfulness.

The wondrous, perfect, and pure reality gives rise to transformation through its true essence; beginningless habitual tendencies merge into a single luminous clarity. To advance toward true purity solely by means of this luminous clarity is called the mind of diligence; when the essence of the mind manifests before one, being purely characterized by wisdom, it is called abiding in the mind of wisdom.

When one maintains the clarity of wisdom so that it is all-pervasive, tranquil, and profound, and this tranquility is wondrously and eternally concentrated, it is called the "abiding of the settled mind.
When the light of concentration radiates forth and the luminous nature penetrates deeply, advancing alone without retreat, it is called the "non-retrogressive mind."
The mind advances with serenity, maintaining its state without loss; as the vital energies of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions interconnect, this is called the Mind that Protects the Dharma.

Through the maintenance of awakened clarity, one is able to use wondrous power to turn the Buddha’s compassionate light back toward the Buddha and abide therein; like two mirrors reflecting each other’s radiance, their wondrous reflections enter into one another in infinite layers—this is called the Mind of Dedication.

When the light of the mind turns inward in secret, one attains the Buddha’s eternally concentrated, supreme, wondrous purity; abiding in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) without loss, this is called the "abiding of the mind in ethical discipline" (*śīla-citta-vihāra*).

Abiding in the mastery of ethical discipline, one is able to travel throughout the ten directions, proceeding wherever one wishes according to one's vows; this is called the "abiding of the mind in aspiration" (*praṇidhāna-citta-vihāra*).

“Ānanda! This good man, by means of true skillful means, gives rise to these ten minds; the essence of his mind manifests and exerts itself as ten functions that interpenetrate one another, perfectly completing the One Mind. This is called the Dwelling of the Initial Resolve.”

When the mind illuminates itself like pure lapis lazuli, with refined gold appearing within, and one treads upon this wondrous prior mind to form the ground, it is called the Dwelling of Cultivating the Ground (*bhūmi-karman*).
When the mind-ground and its cognitive engagement both attain clarity, and one traverses the ten directions without obstruction, it is called the Dwelling of Cultivation (*caryā-bhūmi*).

Their practice is identical to that of the Buddha, and they receive the Buddha’s spiritual essence; like an intermediate state being seeking parents, their subtle faith communicates with the hidden realm as they enter the lineage of the Tathāgata—this is called the Dwelling of Noble Birth.

Having already wandered within the womb of the Way and personally received the lineage of the Awakened One, like a fetus that has already formed its human features without deficiency, this is called the Stage of Abiding in the Perfection of Expedient Means.
With a countenance like that of a Buddha and a mental state likewise identical, this is called the Stage of the Rectified Mind.
When body and mind have merged and increase day by day, it is called the Stage of Non-retrogression (*avinivartana-vihāra*).
When the ten spiritual marks of the body are simultaneously perfected, it is called the Stage of Youthful Truth (*kumārabhūta-vihāra*).
When the physical form has emerged from the womb and one becomes a true son of the Buddha, it is called the Stage of the Dharma Prince (*dharmarāja-putra-vihāra*).

Just as a great king of a country entrusts all state affairs to his crown prince once he has reached adulthood, so too when a Kṣatriya king’s eldest son has grown up and is consecrated with the ceremonial sprinkling of water, this is called the stage of consecration (abhiṣeka-vihāra).

“Ānanda! Once these good men have become sons of the Buddha, they are endowed with the immeasurable, wondrous virtues of the Tathāgatas and act in accordance with the ten directions; this is called the Practice of Joyful Conduct.”
Skillfully benefiting all sentient beings is called the practice of benefitting others.
Self-awakening and awakening others such that no opposition or rejection occurs is called the practice of freedom from resentment.

Producing [beings] of various kinds until the end of the future, with equality throughout the three periods of time and penetration throughout the ten directions, is called the inexhaustible practice.
When all things are unified and the various dharma-gates are attained without error, it is called the practice of being free from delusion and confusion.
When diversity is manifested within unity, such that each distinct characteristic is seen as identical to every other, it is called the practice of skillful manifestation.

In this way, even unto the atoms that fill the empty space of the ten directions, within each and every atom the worlds of the ten directions appear; the appearance of the atoms and the appearance of the worlds do not obstruct or hinder one another—this is called the practice of non-attachment.
The various manifestations that appear before one are all the foremost *pāramitā*; this is called the practice of reverence (*gurukāra-caryā*).
Such perfect integration is able to establish the norms for the Buddhas of the ten directions; this is called the practice of wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-caryā*).
Each and every one is pure and free from outflows; because their nature is fundamentally one true and unconditioned state, it is called "True Practice. "Ānanda!

When these good men have perfected their supernormal powers and fulfilled the task of attaining Buddhahood, being purely clean and refined, they distance themselves from all lingering afflictions. They shall deliver sentient beings while eliminating the very notion of 'delivering,' turning their unconditioned minds toward the path of Nirvana. This is called the Dedication for the Rescue and Protection of All Sentient Beings while Remaining Free from the Notion of Sentient Beings."
To destroy that which is destructible while remaining far removed from all forms of detachment is called the "indestructible dedication.
For fundamental awakening to be profoundly still, its realization equaling that of the Buddhas, is called the "dedication equal to all Buddhas."
When the essence of purity and truth is brilliantly manifested such that the ground is like the ground of a Buddha, it is called the dedication reaching all places.
When worlds and Tathāgatas mutually penetrate one another without obstruction, it is called the dedication of the inexhaustible treasury of merit.

Within the same Buddha-ground, each stage gives rise to its own cause of purity; by relying on these causes, one manifests and attains the path to nirvana—this is called the dedication of roots of goodness that accord with equality.

Once the true roots have been established, the sentient beings of the ten directions are all my own fundamental nature; as this nature is perfectly accomplished, one does not lose sight of sentient beings—this is called the dedication of merit through the contemplation that accords with the equal observation of all sentient beings.
That all phenomena are free from all marks, and that one is neither attached to "being" nor "leaving," is called the dedication of the mark of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Truly attaining that which is such, unimpeded throughout the ten directions, is called the dedication of liberation without bondage.
When the inherent virtues are perfectly fulfilled and the dimensions of the dharma-realm are extinguished, it is called the "Infinite Dedication of the Dharma-realm. Ānanda!
These good sons, having fully perfected these forty-one pure minds, next accomplish the four kinds of wondrous and perfect preparatory practices.

Taking the Buddha’s awakening as one's own mind, whether it has emerged or not yet emerged, is like drilling wood to produce fire when the wood is about to ignite; this is called the Stage of Warmth (*uṣmagata*).

Furthermore, taking one's own mind as that which the Buddha treads upon, whether relying on it or not, is like ascending a high mountain where the body enters empty space but there is still a slight obstruction below; this is called the Stage of the Summit (*mūrdhan*).

When the mind and the Buddha are identical and one rightly attains the Middle Way—like enduring a person, neither harboring resentment nor venting anger—it is called the Ground of Patience (*kṣānti-bhūmi*).
When numerical distinctions are extinguished and both delusion and awakening are no longer objects of reference within the Middle Way, it is called the World-First Ground (*laukikāgra-dharma-bhūmi*).

“Ānanda! This son of good family has attained thorough penetration into great bodhi; his awakening penetrates the realm of the Tathāgata and the ultimate limit of the Buddha’s domain, and it is called the Stage of Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi).”
When the dissimilar enters the same and that sameness also ceases, it is called the Ground of Freedom from Defilement (vimalā-bhūmi).
When purity reaches its limit and luminosity arises, it is called the Ground of Radiant Light (prabhākari-bhūmi).
When luminosity reaches its limit and awakening is fulfilled, it is called the Ground of Blazing Wisdom (arciṣmatī-bhūmi).
That which cannot be reached by any sameness or difference is called the Ground Difficult to Conquer (Duranjaya-bhūmi).
That in which the unconditioned nature of true suchness (tathatā) is pure and luminously manifest is called the Ground of Presence (Abhimukhi-bhūmi).
Reaching the ultimate limit of true suchness is called the Ground of Far-Going (Dūraṅgama-bhūmi).
The single mind of true thusness is called the Immovable Ground (Acalā-bhūmi).
The manifestation of the function of true thusness is called the Ground of Excellent Wisdom (Sādhumatī-bhūmi). "Ānanda!

From this point onward, these bodhisattvas complete their cultivation and bring their merits to perfection; this stage is also called the Stage of Cultivation. As the wondrous cloud of compassion covers the ocean of nirvāṇa, it is named the Dharma Cloud Stage (Dharmameghā-bhūmi).

The Tathāgata flows against the current; likewise, when a Bodhisattva proceeds with the current until reaching the boundary of enlightenment where they enter into union, they are called an Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi) being.

"Ānanda! From the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*) up to Equal Enlightenment, this awakening first attains the initial stage of Dry Wisdom within the Diamond Mind (*vajra-citta*). Thus, through these successive layers—twelve in total, both single and repeated—one finally exhausts the Sublime Awakening and achieves the Unsurpassed Way. All these various stages employ the diamond-like observation of the ten profound metaphors for the illusory nature of phenomena; within *śamatha*, one utilizes the *vipaśyanā* of all Tathāgatas to purify, cultivate, and realize, gradually entering deeper."

Ānanda! It is precisely because of these three progressive advancements that one is well able to accomplish the fifty-five stages of the true path to Bodhi. One who contemplates in this manner is said to have right contemplation;
if one contemplates otherwise, it is called wrong contemplation.
At that time, Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What should this sutra be named?"
"How should I and all sentient beings uphold it?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"The name of this sutra is 'The Great Buddha-Crown Sitatapatra, the Unsurpassed Jewel Seal, the Pure Ocean-Eye of the Tathāgatas of the Ten Directions'."
It is also titled “Saving and Protecting One’s Kinsmen and Causes, Delivering Ānanda and the Bhikṣuṇī of this Assembly by Nature, Attaining Bodhicitta, and Entering the Ocean of Universal Knowledge”;

it is also titled “The Tathāgata’s Secret Cause: The Definitive Meaning of Cultivation and Realization”; it is also titled “The Great Vaipulya Wondrous Lotus King, the Dhāraṇī Mantra of the Mother of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions”;
and it is also titled “The Consecrated Phrases: The Śūraṅgama Samādhi, the Foremost of the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas.”
“You should uphold this.

Having spoken these words, Ānanda and the great assembly immediately received the Tathāgata’s revelation of the meaning of the secret seal, the *Paṭala*, as well as the definitive titles of this sutra. They suddenly awakened to the stages of holy progress in *dhyāna*; their minds became refined through the supreme, wondrous principle, becoming empty and tranquil. They severed the six grades of subtle afflictions cultivated within the three realms. Thereupon, they rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“O World-Honored One of Great Majestic Virtue!
Your compassionate voice is unobstructed, skillfully opening the subtle, deep-seated delusions of sentient beings, so that today my body and mind are refreshed and I have attained great benefit.
World-Honored One!

If this wondrously luminous, truly pure, and wondrous mind is fundamentally all-pervasive and perfect, then even the great earth, grasses, trees, crawling insects, and sentient beings—the original source of True Suchness—is itself the true essence of the Tathāgata’s attainment of Buddhahood.
The Buddha-body is the ultimate reality; how can there still be the paths of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, and devas?
World-Honored One!
"Does this path exist inherently from the beginning,
or does it arise from the deluded habitual tendencies of sentient beings?
World-Honored One!"

For example, the bhikṣuṇī Ratnapadmagandhā upheld the bodhisattva precepts yet secretly engaged in sexual misconduct. She falsely claimed that sexual conduct was not killing, not stealing, and carried no karmic retribution. Having uttered these words, a great, fierce fire first arose from her female organ, and subsequently, fierce fires burned through every joint of her body; she then fell into the Avīci Hell.

King Virūḍhaka and the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra: because King Virūḍhaka slaughtered the Gautama clan, and because Sunakṣatra falsely proclaimed that all phenomena are empty, they both fell alive into the Avīci Hell.
Are these various hells fixed in specific locations,
or do they arise spontaneously?

Since each person generates their own karma and experiences its results individually, we pray that you will extend great compassion to dispel our ignorance, so that all sentient beings who uphold the precepts may hear this definitive meaning, receive it with joy and reverence, and maintain purity without transgression.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"How excellent is this question!
It shall cause all sentient beings not to enter into false views."
Listen attentively now!
I shall explain it for you, Ānanda.

All sentient beings are in truth fundamentally true and pure; it is because of their deluded views that deluded habits arise, and because of these, they distinguish between the internal and the external. Ānanda!

The internal division refers to the realm of sentient beings. Due to various attachments and defilements, deluded sentiments are aroused; as these sentiments accumulate without ceasing, they can produce the water of craving. Therefore, when a sentient being’s mind recalls delicacies, saliva flows from the mouth; when the mind recalls a former person, whether with pity or resentment, tears fill the eyes; when greedily seeking wealth and treasures, the heart produces a flow of craving that makes the entire body glisten and moist; and when the mind is attached to sexual conduct, the two organs of male and female naturally discharge fluids.
"Ānanda! Although various cravings differ, their flowing and binding are the same; they moisten and do not ascend, but naturally fall downward—this is called the internal constituent. Ānanda!"

The external factors are those beyond the realm of sentient beings; because of their yearning and aspiration, they give rise to illusory conceptions. When these conceptions accumulate without ceasing, they can produce a superior vital energy (*vīrya*). Therefore, when sentient beings maintain prohibitive precepts in their minds, their entire bodies become light and pure; when they maintain mantras and mudrās in their minds, their gaze becomes heroic and resolute; when they desire to be born in the heavens, they dream of soaring upward; when they fix their minds on the Buddha-lands, sacred realms manifest in the darkness; and when they serve spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), they regard their own bodies and lives as insignificant.

"Ānanda! Although various perceptions differ, their lightness and buoyancy are the same; they fly and move without sinking, naturally transcending [their objects]. This is called the external constituent. Ānanda!"

In all worlds, birth and death continue in succession: birth follows from habitual tendencies, and death proceeds from the flux of transformation. At the moment of death, before warmth and sensation have been abandoned, the good and evil of one’s entire life manifest simultaneously. As the two habits of death (the inverse) and birth (the conformative) intersect, those whose thoughts are purely conceptual will immediately fly upward and be born in the heavens. If their flying mind is further endowed with merit, wisdom, and pure vows, their minds will naturally open, they shall behold the Buddhas of the ten directions, and they will be reborn in any pure land according to their wishes.

If their emotions are few and their thoughts many, they will lightly ascend but not reach far; they shall become flying immortals, powerful ghost-kings, flying yakṣas, or earth-walking rākṣasas, roaming through the four heavens with unimpeded movement. Among them, if there are those with virtuous vows and virtuous minds who protect my Dharma—whether protecting the prohibitions and precepts in accordance with those who uphold them, or protecting divine mantras in accordance with those who recite them, or protecting meditative concentration and sustaining the patience of the Dharma—these shall personally dwell beneath the seat of the Tathāgata.
If emotion and thought are equal, one neither flies nor falls, but is born among humans; if thought is clear, one is intelligent, while if emotion is deep, one is dull.
If emotion is predominant and thought is scarce, one flows into the realm of horizontal birth, becoming heavy as a member of the fur-bearing herd or light as a member of the feathered tribes.

With seven emotions and three thoughts, one sinks into the water-wheel and is born at the boundary of fire, receiving the breath of fierce flames; as a hungry ghost, one is constantly burned, and even water harms oneself, remaining without food or drink for hundreds of thousands of kalpas.

With nine emotions and one thought, one descends through the fire-wheel and enters the ground where wind and fire intersect; there are two kinds of hells: the *Sāntara* (with intervals) and the *Avīci* (without intervals).

If one is purely emotional, one sinks directly into the Avīci hell. Furthermore, if within that sinking heart one slanders the Mahayana, destroys the Buddha’s prohibitive precepts, speaks deceptive and false teachings, vainly covets offerings of faith, unworthily receives respect, or commits the five heinous crimes and ten grave offenses, one will be reborn in the Avīci hells throughout the ten directions.
"Although these evil karmas are brought upon oneself through one's own actions, within the commonality of sentient existence (nikāya-sabhāga), there are also underlying grounds. Ānanda!
All of these are what those sentient beings have induced by their own karma; having created the ten causes of habituation, they undergo the sixfold intersecting retributions."
What are the ten causes? "Ānanda!

First, the habit of sexual intercourse arises from mutual friction; as this grinding continues without ceasing, a great and fierce fire is thereby ignited within. It is like a person rubbing their hands together, where the sensation of warmth immediately appears."
As these two habits fuel one another, there arise such matters as the iron bed and the copper pillar.
Therefore, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate sexual misconduct by the same name: the fire of desire;
Bodhisattvas view desire as they would avoid a pit of fire.

"Second, when the habit-energy of greed intermingles with mental calculations, it arises from mutual attraction; as this attraction and grasping do not cease, there consequently come to be accumulated cold and solid ice that freezes within, just as when a person draws in air through the mouth, a sensation of cold arises.
Because these two habits mutually oppress one another, there are the phenomena of the *ṭaṭa*, *paṭa*, and *raṭa* hells, as well as the blue, red, and white lotus hells of frozen ice."
Therefore, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate excessive seeking with the same name as "the water of greed";
Bodhisattvas view greed as they would avoid a sea of miasma.

Third, the habit of pride involves mutual arrogance, arising from mutual reliance; it flows and surges without ceasing. Because of this, there are surging waves and rushing currents where accumulated waves form water, just as when the mouth and tongue taste each other repeatedly, water is thereby produced.
Because these two habits strike against one another, there arise such phenomena as rivers of blood, rivers of ash, hot sands, poisonous seas, and the pouring down and swallowing of molten copper.
For this reason, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions characterize *māna* (conceit) as "drinking the water of delusion";
Bodhisattvas view conceit as they would avoid a great drowning.

"Fourth, the habit-energy of anger clashes and conflicts; arising from mutual opposition, this opposition knots together without ceasing. The heat of the mind ignites fire, forging the vital breath into metal. For this reason, there exist mountains of knives, iron stakes, sword-trees, sword-wheels, axes, halberds, spears, and saws—like a person harboring a grievance whose murderous energy flies and stirs.
As these two habits strike one another, there arise all manner of punishments: impaling, cutting, beheading, hacking, mincing, piercing, beating, and striking."
Therefore, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions characterize anger as the "sharp sword";
when Bodhisattvas see anger, they avoid it as they would an execution.

Fifth is the habit of deceitful enticement, which originates from mutual teasing and gives rise to restless attachment; because of this, there are bonds, wooden stocks, and strangulation, like water soaking a field where grasses and trees grow.
As these two habits perpetuate one another, there arise such matters as handcuffs, fetters, shackles, whips, staves, clubs, and cudgels.
For this reason, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate deceit and falsehood with the same name: "slanderous thieves.
Bodhisattvas view fraudulence as they would fear a jackal or a wolf.

"Sixth, the habit-energy of deception arises from mutual delusion; when such false and deceptive practices cease not, the mind takes flight to create villainy. For this reason, there are dust, excrement, urine, filth, and impurities—just as dust follows the wind so that nothing can be seen.
When these two habits combine, there arise various occurrences such as drowning, being cast up, flying and falling, or drifting and sinking."
Therefore, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate deception as "killing by calamity" (kalpa-ghāta);
when Bodhisattvas see deception, they regard it as treading upon a venomous snake.

Seventh, the habit-energy of enmity arises from mutual resentment; because of this, there are flying stones, hurled rocks, wooden boxes, carriage cages, jars, and sacks used for crushing—just as a person harboring malice inwardly nurtures evil within their breast.
As the two habits devour one another, there arise various acts such as hurling, seizing, striking with projectiles, and grappling.
For this reason, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate an enemy as a "hostile and harmful ghost" (viheṭhaka-guhyaka);
a Bodhisattva views an enemy as if drinking poisoned wine.

"Eighth, the habitual practice of views becomes mutually manifest, such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and various karmas born of false awakening. These arise from opposition and contradiction, giving rise to mutual conflict; thus there exist kings, messengers, magistrates, and officials who testify and uphold written records.

Just as travelers on a road meet one another in their coming and going, these two habits intersect; therefore, there exist interrogations, deceptions, examinations, cross-examinations, investigations, and thorough inquiries, where the children who illuminate good and evil hold registers in their hands to adjudicate all matters through eloquence."
Therefore, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate evil views with the same term: "the pit of views.
When Bodhisattvas encounter various delusions and cling to them universally, it is as if they have entered a valley of poison.

"Ninth, the habit-energy of oppression intermingles and issues forth as false accusations and slanders; for this reason, there are mountains closing in, rocks closing in, grinding mills, and plowing and crushing, just as slanderous thieves oppress and wrongfully persecute the virtuous.
Because these two habits mutually repel one another, there are various occurrences such as being pressed down, crushed, squeezed, strained, and measured across."
Therefore, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate those who harbor resentment and slander as "slanderous tigers" by the same name;
when a Bodhisattva is falsely accused, it is like encountering a thunderbolt.
Tenth, the habit of litigation arises from concealment and hiding; because of this, there is the illumination of clear vision, such that one cannot hide one's shadow in the midst of the sun.
Therefore, there are such things as evil friends, the karma-mirror, and the fire-jewel, which reveal past karmas and provide direct verification of one's deeds.
For this reason, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate the concealment [of one's faults] by the same name: the "hidden thief.
Bodhisattvas view concealment as if wearing a mountain upon their heads while treading upon a vast ocean.
"What are the six retributions? Ānanda!
All sentient beings create karma through the six consciousnesses; the evil retributions they thereby attract emerge from the six sense organs."
"How do retributions for evil emerge from the six sense faculties?
First, the retribution of seeing brings forth evil fruits.

When this karma of seeing intersects with other factors, at the time of death one first sees fierce fires filling the ten directions. The deceased’s consciousness flies and falls, riding upon the smoke to enter the Avīci Hell, where two distinct appearances manifest: [...]"
"First is seeing clearly, whereby one sees various evil things everywhere and gives rise to immeasurable fear;
second is seeing in darkness, wherein nothing is seen in stillness and one gives rise to immeasurable dread."
Thus, seeing fire can become boiling cauldrons of molten copper;
smelling it can become black smoke and purple flames;
tasting it can become scorched pellets and iron gruel.
When burned by touch, it can become hot ashes, embers, and charcoal;
when burned within the mind, it can produce sparks that scatter and flare, fanning through the realm of space.
Second, hearing reports [of others' misdeeds] invites and draws forth evil retributions.

When this faculty of hearing and karma interact, at the time of death one first perceives waves that submerge heaven and earth; the deceased’s consciousness descends and flows along with them, entering the Avīci Hell and manifesting two signs:
first, "open hearing," where one hears various clamors and the spirit becomes bewildered and confused;
second, "closed hearing," where all is silent and nothing is heard, as the dark soul sinks into oblivion.
Thus, when the waves of hearing enter the ears, they can act as reproach and interrogation;
when they enter the eyes, they can act as thunder and roars, and as noxious poisonous vapors;
when they enter the breath, they can act as rain and mist, sprinkling poisonous insects all over the body.
If one pours it upon taste, it can become pus, blood, and various kinds of filth;
if poured upon touch, it can become animals, ghosts, excrement, or urine;
if poured upon thought, it can become lightning and hail that shatter the heart and soul.
"Third, the retribution of smelling invites and draws forth evil fruits.

When this smelling karma intersects, at the time of death, one first sees poisonous vapors filling the near and far surroundings. The deceased's spirit-consciousness surges up from the earth and enters the Avīci Hell, manifesting two signs:
first, pervasive hearing, whereby one is overwhelmed by various foul vapors that intensely disturb the mind."
Second, if the sense of hearing is blocked and the vital breath is stifled so that it cannot pass through, one faints and falls to the ground.
When inhaling such vapors, if they strike the breath, they can become a solid substance or a shoe;
if they strike the sight, they can become fire or a torch.
When it encounters sound, it can become drowning, submersion, surging, and boiling;
when it encounters flavor, it can become hunger and refreshment;
when it encounters touch, it can become bursting and rotting, becoming a great mountain of flesh with hundreds of thousands of eyes that devour immeasurably.
When these thoughts collide, they can turn into ash and miasma, or into flying sand and gravel that shatter the body.
"Fourth, the retribution of flavors invites evil fruits.

When this karmic activity of flavors intersects, at the moment of death, one first sees an iron net with fierce, blazing flames completely covering the world; the deceased's consciousness passes through and hangs upside down from the net with its head downward, entering the Avīci Hell where two manifestations appear:
First, when inhaling, it forms freezing ice that cracks the flesh of the body;
second, when exhaling, it flies forth as a fierce fire that scorches and rots the marrow and bones.
Thus one experiences these flavors; by experiencing them repeatedly, one becomes able to receive and endure them.
By experiencing it through sight, one can manifest as molten gold and stone;
by experiencing it through hearing, one can manifest as sharp weapons;
by experiencing it through breathing, one can manifest as a vast iron cage covering the entire land.
When experienced through touch, it can become bows, arrows, crossbows, and projectiles;
when experienced through thought, it can become flying red-hot iron raining down from the sky.
Fifth, the retribution of touch invites and draws forth evil fruits.

When these karmic contacts intersect, at the moment of death, one first sees great mountains closing in from all four sides with no way out. The deceased’s consciousness perceives a great iron city filled with fire-serpents, fire-dogs, tigers, wolves, and lions, as well as ox-headed hell-wardens and horse-headed rākṣasas holding spears and halberds, who drive them through the city gates toward the Avīci Hell. There, two types of contact manifest:
first, contact by convergence, where the closing mountains press against the body until the flesh and bones crush and the blood flows;
second, contact by separation, where knives and swords strike the body and mind, slicing and tearing the liver and heart.
Thus, when combined with touch, as it passes through the sense of touch, it can act as a path, a contemplation, a hall, or a table;
when passing through sight, it can act as burning or incinerating;
and when passing through hearing, it can act as clashing, striking, stabbing, or shooting.
When it passes through the breath, it can become a cangue, a sack, a cross-examination, or a binding;
when it passes through the sense of taste, it can become plowing, tongs, cutting, or slicing;
when it passes through thought, it can become falling, flying, frying, or roasting.
"Sixth, the retribution of thought invites evil fruits.

When this karma of thought intersects with other conditions, at the moment of death, one first sees an evil wind blowing away and destroying the land. The deceased’s spirit-consciousness is blown upward into the air, where it whirls and falls, driven by the wind, into the Avīci Hell. There, two appearances manifest:
first, a state of non-awakening; when delusion reaches its extreme, one runs about wildly and incessantly."
Second is non-delusion: one realizes that suffering is an immeasurable burning and its pain is so profound it is difficult to endure.
Such perverse thoughts, when bound together, can act as the means and the object;
when bound together as views, they can act as the mirror and the witness.
When concentration is focused on hearing, one can become a great boulder, ice, frost, earth, or mist;
when concentration is focused on breathing, one can become a great fire-chariot, a fire-boat, or a fire-cage;
when concentration is focused on tasting, one can become a great cry of lamentation, or remorse, or weeping.
Through the conjunction of contact, one can become large or small; undergo ten thousand births and ten thousand deaths within a single day; and be turned face down or face up. "Ānanda!
These are called the ten causes and six effects of hell, all of which are created by the deluded ignorance of sentient beings."
If sentient beings fully commit evil karma, they enter the Avīci Hell and undergo immeasurable suffering for immeasurable kalpas;
if they commit [evil] through each of the six sense organs, or if their actions involve both the objects and the organs, such persons enter the eight hells of uninterrupted suffering;
if they commit killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct through the three of body, speech, and mind, such persons enter the eighteen hells.

If one does not engage in all three types of karma simultaneously, but instead commits either one instance of killing or one instance of stealing during the interim, such a person will enter thirty-six hells;
if one sees with the eyes and commits a single transgression through a single faculty and a single type of karma, such a person will enter one hundred and eight hells.
Thus, sentient beings act and create individually, entering the stage of homogeneity within the world; these deluded thoughts arise and do not exist from the beginning.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

These sentient beings have not violated the codes of discipline, nor have they transgressed the Bodhisattva precepts, nor have they defiled the Buddha’s Nirvana; yet, through various other miscellaneous karmas that have burned them throughout kalpas, their offenses are eventually exhausted, and they receive the forms of various ghosts.
If their original offense was due to greed for material things, when their retribution ends, they encounter matter and take form, being called "strange ghosts" (kuei-kuei).
If their offense was due to greed for sensual beauty, when their retribution ends, they encounter wind and take form, being called "drought ghosts" (p'o-kuei).
If greed and delusion constitute their offense, when that person’s retribution is exhausted, they encounter the form of a beast and become known as a *māyā* ghost;
if greed and resentment constitute their offense, when that person’s retribution is exhausted, they encounter the form of an insect and become known as a *gūdu* poison-ghost;
if greed and obsessive recollection constitute their offense, when that person’s retribution is exhausted, they encounter the form of a decaying corpse and become known as a *rākṣasa* plague-ghost.
Greed and arrogance constitute an offense; when such a person’s retribution for this offense is exhausted, they encounter atmospheric vapors to form a body, and are called a *preta* (hungry ghost).

Greed and deception constitute an offense; when such a person’s retribution for this offense is exhausted, they encounter darkness to form a body, and are called a *yāma* (demon of sleep-inducing oppression).

Greed for brilliance constitutes an offense; when such a person’s retribution for this offense is exhausted, they encounter refined essences to form a body, and are called a *māṇibhadra* (or *vaṃśa*) ghost.
When greed constitutes an offense, once that person’s retribution is exhausted, they encounter a luminous form as their manifestation; this is called a *yǐshǐ guǐ* (servant-demon).

When greed for factionalism constitutes an offense, once that person’s retribution is exhausted, they encounter a human form as their manifestation; this is called a *chéngzòng guǐ* (messenger-demon).

Ānanda! These people have all fallen due to their pure delusion; scorched by the fires of karma until they are dried up, they emerge above as ghosts. All such beings are summoned and led forth by the karma of their own false imaginings.
If one awakens to Bodhi, then it is wondrous, perfect, and luminous, fundamentally having nothing at all.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

When the karma of a hungry ghost has been exhausted, both emotion and thought become empty; only then, encountering the person they originally wronged in this world, do they take birth as an animal to repay their past debts."
The ghosts of strange objects, when their retribution is exhausted, are mostly reborn in the world as owls;
the ghosts of wind-demons, when their retribution is exhausted, are mostly reborn in the world as all manner of ill-omened anomalies;
the ghosts of domestic spirits, when their retribution for the death of livestock is exhausted, are mostly reborn in the world as foxes.
When the retribution of the *chónggǔ* ghosts is exhausted, they are extinguished; being born into the world, they mostly become poisonous species.
When the retribution of the *shuāilì* ghosts is exhausted, they are impoverished and depleted; being born into the world, they mostly become *huí* (roundworms).
When the retribution of the *shòuqì* ghosts is exhausted, their vital energy dissolves; being born into the world, they mostly become food.
When the subtle and obscure ghosts have their retribution exhausted through subtle dissolution, they are mostly reborn in the world as types of clothing;
when the harmonious and refined ghosts have their retribution exhausted through harmonious dissolution, they are mostly reborn in the world as types of responsive phenomena;
when the bright and spiritual ghosts have their retribution exhausted through the extinction of brightness, they are mostly reborn in the world as all various types of auspicious omens.
When those who were ghosts among humans die and their retribution is exhausted, they are mostly reborn in the world as members of their own species.

Ānanda! All these beings have been dried up by the fire of karma; having repaid their past debts, they become animals as a side effect. These, too, are all summoned and drawn forth by their own false and delusive karma.
If one awakens to Bodhi, then these deluded conditions are fundamentally non-existent.

As you have said regarding Jewel-Lotus Fragrance and others, as well as King Vaidūrya and the Bhikṣu Sunakṣatra—such evil karma was originally produced by themselves; it did not descend from heaven, nor emerge from the earth, nor was it bestowed by humans. It was summoned by their own delusions and must be received back by themselves;
within the mind of Bodhi, they are all merely the solidification of floating, false, and empty conceptions.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

When these animals repay their prior debts, if the debtor pays more than what was owed, these beings will again become human and demand back the excess. If that person possesses both power and merit, they will not relinquish their human form while among men to repay that power;
if they lack merit, they will again become animals to repay the remaining balance."

Ānanda! You should know that if one uses money or goods, or employs their labor, the debt is settled once repaid and the matter ceases; however, if in the interim one takes another's life or eats their flesh, then even for as many eons as atoms in the dust, they will continue to devour and slaughter one another like a turning wheel, alternating between being the superior and the inferior without rest.
Only through the attainment of *śamatha* or the appearance of a Buddha in the world can this cycle be brought to a halt. It cannot otherwise be stopped.
You should now know this: those of the owl class, having completed their retribution and regained their physical forms, are born into the human realm among the dull-witted;
those of the ill-omened class, having completed their retribution and regained their physical forms, are born into the human realm among the foolish;
and those of the fox class, having completed their retribution and regained their physical forms, are born into the human realm among the perverse.
Those of the insect class, having fulfilled their retribution and regained their forms, are born among human beings as members of the common class;
those of the worm class, having fulfilled their retribution and regained their forms, are born among human beings as members of the lowly class;
those of the food-eating class, having fulfilled their retribution and regained their forms, are born among human beings as members of the gentle class.
Those who followed the worldly path, having received their full retribution and resumed their forms, were born among human beings as members of the class of laborers;
those who responded to the Way, having received their full retribution and resumed their forms, were born among human beings as members of the class of scholars;
and those who possessed auspicious signs, having received their full retribution and resumed their forms, were born among human beings as members of the class of the enlightened.
Those various beings, having fully repaid their debts and returned to human form, are born among the human race and join the ranks of the enlightened. Ānanda!

All of these have, through the completion of their past karmic debts, returned to the human state; yet from time immemorial, they have been governed by inverted karmic calculations, giving rise to one another and killing one another. Having failed to encounter the Tathāgata or hear the True Dharma, they naturally revolve within the midst of worldly afflictions; such as these are called "those worthy of compassion."

“Ānanda! Furthermore, there are followers who do not rely on perfect enlightenment to cultivate *samādhi*, but instead cultivate deluded thoughts to preserve their forms through visualization, wandering in mountain forests where humans do not reach; there are ten classes of such seers.
Ānanda! Those sentient beings who, with steadfast resolve, consume medicinal elixirs without ceasing until the path of food is perfected, are called earth-walking immortals (*bhūmicara-ṛṣi*).
Those who, with steadfast resolve, ingest herbs and trees without ceasing until the path of medicine is perfected, are called flying immortals (*khecara-ṛṣi*).
If one is firm as metal and stone without ceasing, the Way of Transformation is perfected, and one is called a "Wandering Immortal" (Cāraṇa-ṛṣi);
if one is firm in movement and stillness without ceasing, the Vital Essence is perfected, and one is called a "Sky-Walking Immortal" (Ākāśa-gāmin-ṛṣi);
if one is firm in the bodily fluids without ceasing, the Virtue of Moistening is perfected, and one is called a "Heaven-Walking Immortal" (Divya-gāmin-ṛṣi).
If one is firm and resolute in refining the essence without ceasing, and attains perfection therein, they are called a Perfected Being of Penetrating Conduct;
if one is firm and resolute in incantations and prohibitions without ceasing, and attains perfection in their ritual arts, they are called a Perfected Being of Path-Conduct;
if one is firm and resolute in contemplation without ceasing, and attains perfection in mindfulness and recollection, they are called a Perfected Being of Illuminating Conduct.
When firm and stable union continues without ceasing, and the resonance and response reach perfect fulfillment, one is called a "Rishi of Refinement" (jingxing xian).
When firm and stable transformation continues without ceasing, and awakening reaches perfect fulfillment, one is called a "Rishi of Transcendence" (juexing xian).

Ānanda! These individuals all refine their minds among human beings, yet they do not follow the path of right awakening; instead, they attain a distinct mode of existence with a lifespan of ten million years, dwelling in deep mountains or on remote ocean islands far from the realm of men. This, too, is merely the circulation of deluded thoughts within saṃsāra; failing to cultivate samādhi, when their retribution is exhausted, they return once more to be scattered among the various realms of existence.

“Ānanda! Those people of the world do not seek the permanent and abiding; they are unable to relinquish their affection and love for their wives and concubines. Yet, regarding sexual misconduct, their minds do not flow into dissipation, and through clarity and purity, luminosity arises. After the end of their lives, they dwell in proximity to the sun and moon; such a class is called the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.

As for those whose lustful attachment to their own wives and chambers is slight, yet who cannot fully savor the state of pure dwelling, after the end of their lives, they transcend the brilliance of the sun and moon and dwell at the summit of the human realm; such a class is called the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.”

When encountering desire, they engage briefly and then depart without lingering thought; in the human world, their movement is slight and their stillness is great. After the end of life, they dwell serenely in the void, where the light of the sun and moon cannot reach above them. These beings possess their own radiance; such a class is called the Suyāma Heaven. They are tranquil at all times, and though sensory contacts may arise, they are unable to disturb them.

After the end of life, they ascend to a realm of subtle refinement, no longer reaching the levels of the humans or devas of the lower realms, and even when the kalpa ends, they are not affected by the three calamities.

Such a class is called the Tuṣita Heaven. I have no lustful mind and respond to your actions only as a matter of circumstance; when we lie together, the flavor is like chewing wax. After the end of life, I am reborn beyond the Realm of Transformation. Such a class is called the Nirmāṇarati Heaven.

Without a worldly mind, they engage in worldly affairs, yet in their interaction with such activities, they clearly transcend them; after the end of life, they are universally able to emerge and transcend both realms of transformation and non-transformation—this class of beings is called the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Transformations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin).
Ānanda! Thus, although the forms of these six heavens move about, the traces of their minds still intermingle; from this point downward, it is called the Desire Realm.
