*The Great Buddha-Usnīṣa Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Myriad Practices*, Scroll Eight.
The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata’s Attainment of Enlightenment through the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas,
Revealed from the Great Uṣṇīṣa; also known as the Scripture of the Great Maṇḍala of Nālandā in Central India,
excerpted for separate circulation from the Abhiṣeka Section, Scroll Nine.
Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Prajñāmitra of the Tang Dynasty: “Ānanda!

Among all those in the world who cultivate the mind, if they do not rely on *dhyāna* (meditative concentration) and lack wisdom, yet are able to restrain their bodies from practicing sexual desire—whether walking or sitting—with no thoughts of passion arising and no lingering attachment to the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*)—such persons should consider themselves companions of Brahmā. This class of beings is called the Heaven of the Retinue of Brahmā (*Brahmapārṣadya*).

When the habit of desire is eliminated and the mind of detachment manifests, such that they delight in and accord with the various codes of discipline (*vinaya*), these persons are then able to practice the virtues of Brahmā. This class of beings is called the Heaven of the Ministers of Brahmā (*Brahmapurohita*).”

With body and mind wondrously perfect and majestic deportment unimpaired, and having augmented their pure precepts with clear awakening, such persons are able at that time to preside over the Brahma assembly as Great Brahma Kings; this class of beings is called the Mahābrahmā Heaven.

Ānanda! These three superior streams cannot be oppressed by any suffering or affliction; although they are not the true, authentic Samādhi of right cultivation, because the various outflows do not disturb the pure mind, they are called the First Dhyāna.

“Ānanda! Next, there are Brahmā gods who govern the Brahmā people and perfect the Brahma-conduct; with their minds clarified and unmoving, they give rise to a tranquil radiance—this class is called the Heaven of Limited Light (Parīttābha).

Their lights shine upon one another in an inexhaustible brilliance, reflecting throughout the ten directions so that the entire world-system becomes like lapis lazuli—this class is called the Heaven of Infinite Light (Apramāṇābha).”

Sustaining the circular radiance, they accomplish the essence of the teaching; they manifest pure transformations and their applications are inexhaustible. This class of beings is called the Heaven of Luminous Sound (Ābhāsvara). Ānanda!

These three superior types of practitioners cannot be assailed by any anxieties or worries; although they have not yet attained the true, correct samādhi, coarse outflows have been suppressed within their pure minds, and this is termed the Second Dhyāna.

“Ānanda! Thus, when these devas and humans have perfected their radiant halos, mastered their sounds, and revealed their subtleties; when they give rise to refined practice and attain the bliss of tranquil extinction—this class of beings is called the Heaven of Limited Purity (Parīttābha).

When the pure void manifests before them, triggering boundlessness, and their bodies and minds achieve lightness and ease, attaining the bliss of tranquil extinction—this class of beings is called the Heaven of Infinite Purity (Apramāṇābha).”

When the world, body, and mind are all perfectly pure, and the accomplishment of pure virtues brings forth a supreme reliance that manifests as the bliss of quiescent extinction—this class of beings is called the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven (the Heaven of Universal Purity).

Ānanda! These three superior streams possess great conformity; body and mind are tranquil and secure, attaining immeasurable bliss. Although they have not yet truly attained genuine *samādhi*, within their tranquil minds, joy is fully present; this is called the third *dhyāna*.

“Ānanda! Furthermore, there is a class of devas and humans whose afflictions no longer constrain body or mind, for whom the causes of suffering have been exhausted, and who realize that pleasure is not permanent and will inevitably perish. They simultaneously and instantaneously relinquish both the minds of suffering and pleasure; their coarse and heavy characteristics are extinguished, and a nature of pure merit arises. This class is called the Heaven of Merit-Born (Puṇyaprasava).

Their minds of equanimity are perfectly integrated, their resolute understanding is pure, and within this unobstructed merit they attain wondrous compliance that extends to the end of the future. This class is called the Heaven of Merit-Loved (Puṇyaprasādika).”

Ānanda! From this Heaven of the Pure Abodes there are two diverging paths. If, based on their previous state of mind, they dwell in the cultivation and realization of immeasurable pure light with perfected and brilliant merit, such a class is called the Heaven of Vast Results (Bṛhatphala).

If, based on their previous state of mind, they simultaneously loathe both suffering and pleasure, diligently cultivating a continuous state of equanimity without interruption, and thoroughly exhausting the path of equanimity until body and mind are both extinguished—such that their mental deliberations become ashen and solid for five hundred kalpas—this person, having taken birth-and-death as their cause, is unable to manifest the nature of non-birth-and-death; they undergo extinction during the first half-kalpa and rebirth during the second half-kalpa. Such a class is called the Heaven of No-Thought (Asaṃjñisattva).

Ānanda! These four superior streams cannot be moved by any worldly objects of suffering or pleasure; although they are not the unconditioned truly immovable stage, because the mental effort of those who still possess a grasping mind has reached full maturity, they are called the four dhyānas.

“Ānanda! Furthermore, there are five types of non-returner devas (*anāgāmin*) who, within this realm, simultaneously extinguish the nine grades of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the lower world. Since both suffering and pleasure have perished and they no longer dwell below, they establish their abodes within the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) of equanimity (*upekṣā*).”
Ānanda! When both suffering and pleasure have ceased and the conflicting mind no longer engages, such a class of beings is called the Heaven of No Affliction (Avṛha).
When the mechanism of the mind moves alone and there is no ground for the friction of engagement, such a class of beings is called the Heaven of No Heat (Atapa).

When the wondrous vision throughout the worlds of the ten directions is perfectly clear and limpid, such that no further dust-like forms or any defilements remain, those of this class are called the Heaven of Good Vision (*Sudṛśa*).
When the refined vision manifests before them, forging all things without obstruction, those of this class are called the Heaven of Good Manifestation (*Sudarśana*).
When they have ultimately fathomed the subtle principles and exhausted the nature of form until entering the boundless limit, those of this class are called the Heaven of Ultimate Form (*Akaniṣṭha*).

“Ānanda! As for these Non-returner devas and those Four Dhyāna Heavenly Kings of the four stations, they can only hear of them with admiration but cannot know or see them. It is just as in this world where vast wildernesses, deep mountains, and sites of the holy path are all sustained by Arhats; therefore, they cannot be seen by ordinary, coarse people of the world.”
"Ānanda!
These eighteen heavens are solitary and without companions, yet they have not yet exhausted the burden of physical form; from here downward, they are called the Realm of Form (rūpadhātu).
Furthermore, Ānanda!"
From within this limit of form at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), there are further two divergent paths.

If one illuminates wisdom through the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā-citta*), and the light of wisdom becomes perfectly pervasive, one then transcends the realm of dust, attains the state of an Arhat, and enters the Bodhisattva vehicle; such a class is called a "Great Arhat who has turned the mind."

If, through the mind of equanimity, one achieves the relinquishing of aversion and perceives the body as an obstruction, such that obstructions dissolve and one enters emptiness—this class of beings is called the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).

When all obstructions have dissolved, there is neither obstruction nor cessation; therein remains only the *ālaya-vijñāna*, together with the subtle half-portion of the *manas*—this class of beings is called the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).

When both emptiness and form have vanished and the conscious mind has entirely ceased, the ten directions are silent and utterly devoid of any destination—this class of beings is called the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

The nature of consciousness is immovable; by investigating it through its cessation until one reaches its ultimate limit, one proclaims the nature of exhaustion within that which is inexhaustible. Thus, existing yet not existing, exhausting yet not exhausting—this class of beings is called the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception.

These individuals exhaust emptiness but do not exhaust the principle of emptiness; those who have reached the end of the holy path from the Heaven of No-Return are this class known as the dull Arhats whose minds do not turn back.
If those from among the non-Buddhist heavens of the Unconscious (asaṃjñin) exhaust their emptiness without returning, being deluded, leaking, and ignorant, they will enter the cycle of rebirth.
"Ānanda! These various devas in each of these heavens are all ordinary beings for whom the fruits of karma have been repaid; once that repayment is exhausted, they enter the cycle."
That Heavenly King is a bodhisattva who, through the progressive advancement of his practice in samādhi, turns toward the path of cultivation followed by the assembly of noble ones.

Ānanda! In these four heavens of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), body and mind have ceased; the nature of concentration manifests before them, and there is no corporeal form resulting from karma. From this point until the end, it is called the Formless Realm.

All of this arises from failing to comprehend the wondrously enlightened and luminous mind; through the accumulation of delusions, the false three realms come into being. Within these realms, beings falsely follow the seven destinies and sink into them, with each *pudgala* falling according to their own kind.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
Within these three realms, there are four classes of asuras.

Those who, within the realm of hungry ghosts, attain supernatural powers through the power of protecting the Dharma and enter the void—these asuras are born from eggs and are categorized within the destiny of hungry ghosts."
If they descend from the heavens due to a loss of merit and fall into a degraded state, their dwelling place is adjacent to the sun and moon;
these asuras are born from a womb and are categorized within the human realm.

There are asura kings who uphold the world with power that penetrates all and is free from fear, able to contend for authority with Brahmā, Śakra Devendra, and the Four Heavenly Kings; these asuras arise through transformation and are categorized within the celestial realm.

Ānanda! There is another class of inferior asuras who are born in the depths of the great ocean and dwell at the mouths of underwater caverns; they roam through the void by day and return to their watery lodgings by night. These asuras exist due to moisture and are categorized within the realm of animals.

"Ānanda! Thus, these seven realms—the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, seers and immortals, devas, and asuras—are all investigated and found to be merely the deluded thoughts of the various conditioned states of existence. They are born of false imagination and follow according to karma. Within the wondrous, perfect, and luminous mind that is inherently unconditioned, they are all like flowers in the sky, fundamentally non-existent; they are but a single falsehood, with no further root or source."

Ānanda! These sentient beings do not recognize their original mind and thus undergo this cycle of rebirth; having passed through immeasurable kalpas without attaining true purity, it is entirely due to their compliance with killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct. By reversing these three, one gives rise to the absence of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct: that which is called "existence" belongs to the realm of ghosts, while that which is called "non-existence" pertains to the celestial realms.

As existence and non-existence mutually oppose one another, the nature of saṃsāra arises. If one attains the wondrous arousal of samādhi, then there is wondrous, eternal stillness; both existence and non-existence are absent, and even the absence of duality is extinguished. Since there is not even the state of non-killing, non-stealing, and non-sexual misconduct, how could one further follow the affairs of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct?

Ānanda! The three karmas are not severed; each has its own private tendencies. Because of these individual privacies, the collective category of privacies arises. This occurs through the spontaneous delusion of the self, though it has no fixed location. This arising of delusion is without cause and cannot be traced. You must exhort yourself in practice if you wish to attain Bodhi; you must eliminate the three delusions. If you do not exhaust the three delusions, even if you obtain supernatural powers, they will all be worldly, conditioned functions. If habitual tendencies are not extinguished, you will fall into the path of Māra. Though you wish to eliminate delusion, you will instead increase your hypocrisy. The Tathāgata says such people are to be pitied.
"You have falsely created this fault of non-enlightenment for yourself;
to speak thus is called speaking correctly, whereas for anyone else to say so would be the speech of Māra.

At that moment, as the Tathāgata was about to conclude his session on the Dharma seat, he took up a seven-jeweled desk from his lion throne, turned toward the Purple Gold Mountain, and leaned against it once more, addressing the great assembly and Ānanda, saying:

“You who are still in training—whether pratyekabuddhas or śrāvakas—have today turned your minds toward the great bodhi and the unsurpassed, wondrous enlightenment. I have now already taught you the method for true practice, yet you still do not recognize the subtle demonic activities involved in cultivating *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. When demonic realms manifest before you, you fail to recognize them; your purification of mind is not correct, and you fall into false views. Whether it be the *skandha-māra*, the celestial *māra*, attachment to ghosts and spirits, or encounters with malevolent demons, your mind lacks clarity and you mistake a thief for your own son. Furthermore, you consider a small attainment to be sufficient, like the unlearned bhikṣu in the fourth dhyāna who falsely claimed to have realized sainthood. Once his heavenly retribution was exhausted and the signs of decline appeared, he slandered the arhats and, undergoing further existence, fell into the Avīci Hell.”
"You should listen attentively; I shall now analyze this for you in detail.
Ānanda rose together with the other students in the assembly, and with joy they prostrated themselves, bowing to listen to his compassionate instruction.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda and the great assembly:

"You should know that the twelve classes of sentient beings in this world of outflows share the same fundamentally awakened, wondrously luminous, and perfectly enlightened essence of mind as the Buddhas of the ten directions; they are neither two nor different.

Yet, due to your deluded thoughts, you have mistaken the fundamental principle for a fault, giving rise to ignorance and craving. From this arising of pervasive delusion, the nature of space emerged; as this deluded transformation did not cease, the world came into being. Thus, these microdust-like lands of the ten directions are not free from outflows; they are all established through stubborn, deluded, and false conceptualization."

You should know that empty space arises within your own mind, like a fragment of cloud appearing in the vast clarity of the great sky; how much more so must the various worlds within that space be subject to change?

If even one person among you awakens to the truth and returns to the source, all this emptiness of the ten directions will utterly dissolve and vanish; how then could the lands existing within that space not tremble and shatter?

As you cultivate dhyāna and adorn your samādhi, the minds of the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions and the various untainted Great Arhats become profoundly attuned and unified, remaining serene in their respective states.

Consequently, all Māras, spirits, ghosts, and ordinary devas see their palaces collapse and crack for no apparent reason; the great earth quakes and splits, and all creatures of land, water, and air are struck with terror.
Ordinary beings are mired in darkness and do not perceive their own gradual transformation.

Although they all possess the five supernormal powers, they lack the power of the exhaustion of outflows; being attached to these worldly defilements, how could I cause you to shatter that very place?
For this reason, spirits, ghosts, celestial Māras, and various demons and goblins will all come to harass you during your samādhi.

However, although those Māras may be filled with great rage, within their afflictions and amidst your wondrous enlightenment, they are like wind blowing against light or a sword cutting through water—they cannot touch you at all. You are like boiling water and they are like solid ice; as the warmth gradually approaches, the ice will melt away before long. They merely rely on their supernatural powers and are but guests; that they succeed in creating confusion and disorder depends on the master of the five skandhas within your own mind. If the master is deluded, the guests will find their opportunity;
if you remain in *dhyāna* and awaken to it without confusion, then those demonic affairs will be powerless against you.

When the darkness dissolves and enters into clarity, those various malevolent spirits will all receive only the subtle qi; since clarity can destroy darkness, they will perish on their own when drawing near—how then would they dare remain to disturb meditative concentration?
If you do not attain clear awakening and remain deluded by the *skandhas*, then you, Ānanda, will surely become a son of Māra and accomplish the work of a Māra-man.

Consider, for instance, how the Mataṅga woman was utterly lowly and inferior; though she used incantations to violate your Buddhist precepts, she destroyed but one among the eighty thousand rules of conduct. Because your mind remained pure, you had not yet fallen into ruin. But this [present danger] would destroy your entire body of precious enlightenment, like a high minister’s family suddenly being seized and confiscated—utterly ruined and scattered, beyond all hope of rescue.
“Ānanda, you should know this!

When you sit at the site of enlightenment and cause all thoughts to fall away, once those thoughts are exhausted, then all that is luminous and penetrating, free from thought, remains unshaken by movement or stillness, and recollection and forgetfulness become as one. Abiding in this state, you shall enter samādhi. It is like a person with clear vision standing in deep darkness: though the essential nature is wondrously pure, the mind has not yet emitted light. This is called the realm of the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha).

If the eyes become bright and clear, and the ten directions open up so that there is no longer any darkness, this is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of form; such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of the kalpa.”
Observe its origin: it takes solidified false imagination as its root. "Ānanda!

If, within this state, you investigate with refined clarity and brilliance, such that the four elements no longer entwine and for a brief moment your body can pass through obstructions, this is called the overflowing of refined spirit before the objective field."
This is merely a temporary attainment through the power of practice; it is not a realization of sainthood. If you do not regard it as a state of sainthood, it is called a "wholesome realm";
if you take it to be a realization of sainthood, you will immediately fall prey to various demonic influences.

“Ānanda! Furthermore, when one uses this mind to investigate the subtle brilliance until it penetrates deep within the body, this person may suddenly pick out roundworms or maggots from within their own body; yet their physical form remains intact, without any injury or damage. This is called the overflowing of refined spirit throughout the physical body.”
This is merely a temporary attainment resulting from refined practice; it is not a realization of sainthood. If one does not conceive of it as a state of sainthood, it is called a "wholesome realm";
if one interprets it as a realization of sainthood, one will immediately fall prey to various demonic influences.

Furthermore, when this mind is investigated with refined precision both internally and externally, the *po* (souls), *hun* (spirits), will, and consciousness—excluding the body they grasp and sustain—all enter into one another, alternating as guest and host. Suddenly, one hears the sound of the Dharma being preached in the air, or hears the profound meanings of the mysteries being expounded throughout the ten directions; this is called the successive separation and union of the refined souls.

Having accomplished the seeds of goodness, one may temporarily attain such states; yet these do not constitute the realization of a sage, nor should one harbor the thought that they are the realization of a sage—these are called "wholesome realms.
If one interprets them as the realization of a sage, one will immediately fall prey to various forms of heterodoxy.

Furthermore, when this mind is clear, luminous, and penetrating, with inner radiance shining forth, the ten directions everywhere take on the color of Jāmbūnada gold, and all species are transformed into Tathāgatas. At that moment, one suddenly beholds Vairocana seated upon a terrace of celestial light, surrounded by a thousand Buddhas; a billion lands and lotus flowers appear simultaneously. This is called the influence of the soul’s spiritual awakening.

The radiance of the mind is refined and bright, illuminating all worlds; to attain this temporarily is a wholesome state, provided one does not regard it as a holy realization or harbor thoughts of being a sage.
If one mistakes it for a holy attainment, one will immediately fall prey to various demonic influences.

Furthermore, as this mind investigates the subtle brilliance with ceaseless observation, suppressing, subduing, restraining, and transcending it, there suddenly comes a time when the empty space of the ten directions becomes the color of seven treasures or a hundred treasures; these fill all at once without obstructing one another, and blue, yellow, red, and white each appear in their pure intensity. This is called the power of suppression exceeding its proper measure.
To temporarily attain such a state is not yet a holy realization; if one does not conceive of it as a holy attainment, it is called a "wholesome realm.
If, however, one interprets it as a holy realization, one will immediately be possessed by various demons.

Furthermore, if with this mind one investigates until it becomes transparent and its refined radiance is undisturbed, suddenly at night when darkness falls, while in a dark room one may see all manner of objects no differently than in broad daylight, and the objects in the dark room do not vanish—this is called the mind becoming subtle and dense, clarifying its vision so that what is seen penetrates even the profound obscurity.
To temporarily attain such a state is not yet a holy realization; if one does not conceive it as a holy attainment, it is called a "wholesome realm.
If, however, one interprets it as a holy realization, one will immediately be possessed by various demons.

Furthermore, when this mind enters the sphere of perfect, empty fusion, the four limbs suddenly become like grass and wood; even if burned by fire or hacked with a blade, there is no sensation at all. Moreover, the flames cannot burn them, and even if their flesh is cut, it is as if wood were being pared away. This is called the "dusts" (sensory objects) being cast aside, and the nature of the four great elements entering exclusively into purity.
To attain such a state for a time does not constitute a holy realization; if one does not conceive of it as a holy attainment, it is called a "wholesome realm.
If, however, one interprets it as a holy realization, one will immediately be possessed by various demons.

Furthermore, when this mind achieves purity and the power of that pure mind reaches its peak, one may suddenly see the great earth and the mountains and rivers of the ten directions all become Buddha-lands, replete with the seven treasures and filled with radiant light. One may also see countless Buddhas and Tathāgatas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, filling the void of space within magnificent palaces and towers. Looking down, one sees the hells; looking up, one observes the celestial palaces, perceiving them all without obstruction. This is called the deepening of focused contemplation through longing and aversion; after long practice, these thoughts transform into actual manifestation.
If you do not mistake this for a realization of sainthood nor give rise to the thought that you have attained sainthood, it is called a "wholesome state.
If you take it to be a realization of sainthood, you will immediately fall prey to various demonic influences.

Furthermore, if you use this mind to investigate the profound and far-reaching, suddenly in the middle of the night you may see distant places from afar—marketplaces, streets, alleys, relatives, and kin—or even hear their voices. This is called the "pressing of the mind," where the mind flies out due to extreme intensity, resulting in many such visions across great distances.
If you do not mistake this for a realization of sainthood nor give rise to the thought that you have attained sainthood, it is called a "wholesome state.
However, if you take it as a realization of sainthood, you will immediately fall prey to various demonic influences.

Furthermore, if you investigate this mind with such extreme intensity that you perceive the physical form of a spiritual teacher shifting and changing—undergoing various transformations in an instant without apparent cause—this indicates that a malevolent mind harbors demons, or that a celestial Mara has entered your heart and belly, causing you to preach the Dharma and master wondrous meanings without any basis.
"If you do not regard this as a realization of sainthood nor give rise to the thought that you have attained sainthood, the works of Māra will subside;
however, if you take it to be a realization of sainthood, you will immediately fall under the sway of various demons. Ānanda!"

These ten kinds of visionary states appearing during dhyāna are all manifestations resulting from the interaction between the physical aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and the application of the mind; thus these phenomena appear. Sentient beings, stubborn and deluded, fail to reflect upon themselves; encountering these conditions, they remain confused and fail to recognize them for what they are, claiming instead that they have attained sainthood. Having committed this great falsehood, they fall into the Avīci Hell.

After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, you should rely upon this teaching to proclaim its meaning during the period of the Final Dharma; do not allow celestial Māras to find any opportunity, but maintain and protect it so that they may achieve the Unsurpassed Way.

“Ānanda! When that son of good family practices samādhi within śamatha and the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) is exhausted, he perceives the minds of all Buddhas as images appearing in a clear mirror. Although he has attained something, he is not yet able to employ it; it is like a person suffering from a nightmare whose hands and feet are perfectly intact and whose sight and hearing are unconfused, yet whose mind is touched by an external malevolent spirit so that he cannot move. This is called the domain of the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha).

If the affliction of the nightmare ceases, his mind detaches from the body and turns back to observe its own face; going and staying become free, and there is no longer any obstruction. This is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of sensation, and such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of views (dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya).”
Contemplating its origin, one finds that empty, luminous delusion constitutes its root.

"Ānanda! When that virtuous man is within this state, he attains a great radiance. As his mind becomes brilliantly clear, if he suppresses it internally to an excessive degree, he will suddenly give rise to boundless compassion at that moment. Thus, even upon seeing a mosquito or a gnat, he regards them as his own infant; his heart is filled with such pity that he unconsciously sheds tears. This is called the overreaching suppression and subduing of one's spiritual effort."
To awaken is to be without fault; this is not yet the realization of a sage. Once one has attained clear understanding and is no longer deluded, [the afflictions] will naturally dissipate over time.

If, however, you mistake this for the realization of a sage, the demon of sorrow will enter your heart-mansion; you will feel grief upon seeing others and weep boundlessly, losing your correct meditative absorption and inevitably falling into ruin.

"Ānanda! Furthermore, within that meditative concentration, those good sons see the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) dissolve and the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) become clear. As superior signs manifest before them, they are moved by an excess of emotion; suddenly, within this state, they give rise to limitless courage. Their minds become fierce and sharp, their resolve equaling that of all Buddhas, and they claim that the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* can be transcended in a single thought-moment. This is called 'the function of overreaching and transgressing through forceful exertion.'"
Awakening brings no fault, yet this is not the realization of a sage; through clear understanding and freedom from delusion, [the afflictions] will naturally dissipate over time.

If you mistake this for the attainment of sainthood, then mad demons will enter your heart and viscera; you will boast whenever you see others, possessing incomparable arrogance, such that your mind looks neither upward to the Buddhas nor downward to men. Having lost right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*), you shall surely fall into ruin.

Furthermore, among those good sons in that state of meditative concentration, when the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has dissolved and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes clear, they find no new realization before them while losing their former abode. Their power of wisdom declines, and as they fall into the midst of this state, they see nothing at all. Suddenly, a great parching thirst arises within their hearts; at all times, they sink into recollection without dispersal, taking this to be the mark of diligent vigor. This is called "cultivating the mind and losing oneself through a lack of wisdom."
To awaken to this is to be without fault, yet it does not constitute the realization of a sage.

If you take this to be the realization of a sage, then the demon of recollection will enter your heart and viscera; morning and evening it will seize your mind and suspend it in one place, causing you to lose right concentration and leading you inevitably to fall into ruin.

"Furthermore, among those good sons within that samādhi, when the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has dissolved and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes clear, their power of wisdom exceeds their concentration and they lose its sharp intensity. Holding various superior natures within their minds, they themselves suspect they are Vairocana; taking little as sufficient, this is called losing constant discernment through the application of the mind, thereby drowning in intellectual views."
To awaken in this way is to be without fault, yet it does not constitute the realization of a sage;
if one takes this awakening to be the realization of a sage, then the demons of inferiority and complacency will enter one’s heart and viscera, leading one to say upon seeing others:
"I have attained the unsurpassed, primary truth."
"Losing right concentration, they shall fall into ruin.

Furthermore, among those sons of good family within that state of meditative absorption, when the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has dissolved and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes clear, because they have newly realized what they had not yet attained, their former mind has already perished. As they survey these two boundaries, difficulties arise spontaneously; suddenly, an inexhaustible sorrow wells up within their hearts, like sitting upon an iron bed or drinking a lethal poison. Their hearts no longer desire to live, and they constantly seek someone to end their lives so that they may quickly attain liberation. This is called losing the skillful means in one's practice."
To awaken to this is to be without fault, yet it does not constitute the realization of a sage.

If you mistake this for the realization of a sage, then a demon of "constant anxiety" will enter your heart and viscera to the extent of one part; with sword or blade in hand, you will cut your own flesh, rejoicing in the relinquishing of your life-span, or you will wander into mountain forests in constant anxiety, unable to bear being seen by others. Having lost right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*), you shall surely fall into ruin.

Furthermore, within that samādhi, when those good sons perceive the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) dissolving and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becoming clear and bright, and after their minds have become peaceful and secure in this state of purity, suddenly an infinite joy arises within them. Their hearts are so filled with rapture that they cannot restrain themselves; this is called "light ease" (*praśrabdhi*) without wisdom, leading to self-restraint through delusion.
To realize this is to be without fault, yet it does not constitute the realization of a sage.

If you take this to be the realization of a sage, then a portion of the "demon of fondness for joy" will enter your heart and viscera; upon seeing others, you will laugh, and by the roadside you will sing and dance to yourself, claiming that you have already attained unimpeded liberation. Having lost right concentration, you shall surely fall into ruin.

Furthermore, among those good sons within that state of concentration, when the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has dissolved and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes clear, they may consider themselves sufficient. Suddenly, a groundless and great conceit (*māna*) arises; thus, from conceit (*māna*) and excessive conceit (*atimāna*), as well as conceit beyond conceit (*mānātimāna*), or overweening conceit (*adhimāna*), or even inferiority complex (*ūnamāna*), these may all erupt at once. In their hearts, they still hold the Tathāgatas of the ten directions in contempt, let alone the lower-ranking Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. This is called "seeing oneself as superior while lacking the wisdom to save oneself."
To realize this is to be free from fault; it does not constitute the realization of a sage.

If you take this to be the realization of a sage, then a portion of the great demon of pride will enter your heart and viscera. You will cease to pay homage to stupas and temples and destroy scriptures and images, saying to donors:

"These are merely gold, copper, earth, or wood; these scriptures are but leaves or folded flowers. Since the true and eternal reality resides in the physical body, one need not show reverence to them; instead, to venerate earth and wood is truly perverse."

Those who have deep faith will, by following such destruction and burying [the scriptures] in the earth, cause deluded sentient beings to enter the Avīci Hell; they shall lose right concentration and fall into ruin.

"Furthermore, within that samādhi, those good sons see the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) dissolve and the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) become clear. Within their refined brilliance, they perfectly realize the principle of essence and attain great compliance. Suddenly, their minds give rise to immeasurable lightness and tranquility, and they claim to have attained sainthood and great mastery; this is called attaining various states of lightness and purity through wisdom."
To realize this is to be free from fault, yet it does not constitute the realization of a sage.

If you take it as proof of sainthood, then a degree of the "delightful, pure, and light" demon will enter your heart and viscera; you will then consider yourself satisfied and no longer seek further progress. Such people mostly become monks who lack learning, who harbor doubts and slander others in later generations, falling into the Avīci Hell. Having lost right concentration, they shall surely sink into ruin.

Furthermore, within that meditative concentration, those good sons see the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) dissolve and the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) become clear. Within this state of luminous awakening, they attain a nature of empty clarity; therein, they suddenly turn toward eternal extinction, repudiating cause and effect and entering exclusively into emptiness. With the mind of emptiness manifest before them, their minds eventually give rise to the view of perpetual annihilation.
To awaken is to be without fault, yet this is not yet the realization of a sage;

if you take this awakening to be the proof of sainthood, then the "demon of emptiness" will enter your heart and inner organs, leading you to slander those who uphold the precepts as being of the Lesser Vehicle, claiming: "How can a Bodhisattva who has realized emptiness have anything to uphold or transgress?"

Such a person constantly frequents faithful donors to drink alcohol, eat meat, and engage extensively in sexual misconduct; yet, due to the power of Māra, they cause those before them to harbor no suspicion or slander. Once the ghostly mind has long entered them, they may even consume excrement, urine, wine, meat, and the like—all equally empty—thereby violating the Buddha’s disciplinary code and leading others into sin. Having lost right mindfulness, they shall surely fall into ruin.

"Furthermore, within that state of concentration, when the sons of good family perceive that the aggregate of form has dissolved and the aggregate of sensation becomes clear, they relish its empty luminosity until it penetrates deep into the marrow of their bones. Suddenly, infinite craving arises in their hearts; when this craving reaches its peak, it gives rise to madness, which then becomes lustful desire. This is called the meditative state being so peaceful and harmonious that it enters the heart, where, lacking the power of wisdom to sustain themselves, they mistakenly fall into various desires."
To awaken [to this] is to be without fault; it does not constitute the realization of a sage.

If you take this to be the realization of a sage, then the demon of desire will enter your heart and viscera, leading you to claim that desire itself is the path to Bodhi. You will then transform laypeople into practicing desire with equality, declaring that those who engage in sexual intercourse are "sons upholding the Dharma. By the power of spirits and ghosts, you will gather the ignorant and foolish in the final age, numbering as many as a hundred, or even two hundred, five, six, or seven hundred, or reaching many millions. When the demon’s mind becomes weary and leaves his body, he will lose his majestic power and fall into royal peril. Having misled sentient beings, they will enter the Avīci Hell; having lost right concentration, they shall surely sink into ruin.

“Ānanda! These ten kinds of manifestations that appear during dhyāna are all produced because the mind is applied in a conflicted manner within the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). Sentient beings are stubbornly deluded and fail to reflect upon themselves; encountering these conditions, they are confused and do not recognize them for what they are, claiming instead that they have attained the state of a sage. Having committed this great falsehood, they fall into the Avīci Hell.”

"You all should likewise carry the words of the Tathāgata and, after my parinirvāṇa, transmit them during the Final Dharma period, causing all sentient beings everywhere to awaken to this meaning. Do not allow celestial Māras to find any opportunity; maintain and protect [these teachings] so that they may achieve the Unsurpassed Way."

“Ānanda! When that son of good family has cultivated *samādhi* and exhausted the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), although his outflows (*āsrava*) are not yet exhausted and his mind has not yet separated from its physical form, he is already like a bird that has escaped from a cage. He is able to achieve this and, proceeding from this ordinary body, traverse the sixty holy stages of a Bodhisattva. Attaining the *manomaya-kāya* (mind-made body), he moves everywhere without obstruction. It is like a person who is sound asleep and speaks in a dream; though that person has no conscious awareness of it, the words spoken possess rhythmic cadence and sequential order, causing those who are awake to fully understand their meaning. This is called the domain of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).

If the movement of thought ceases and floating perceptions are eliminated, so that the mind of awakened clarity is like a mirror free of dust and grime, and one perceives the beginning and end of a single cycle of birth and death with total illumination, this is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of perception. Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*).”
If one examines its origin, it is based on pervasive delusive conceptions. "Ānanda!

That good man, whose aggregate of sensation is void and subtle, having not encountered perverse thoughts and having manifested a perfect concentration, within this samādhi comes to cherish that perfect clarity; he sharpens his refined contemplation and greedily seeks out skillful means."

At that time, a celestial demon (māra) watches for an opportunity; his refined spirit flies into a person who speaks the sutras and the Dharma. That person does not realize they are possessed by a demon, and claims for themselves that they have attained unsurpassed nirvana. He comes to the place of a seeker of skillful means—a son of good family—and spreads out a seat to preach the Dharma.
In an instant, his form may manifest as a bhikṣu for that person to see, or he may become Śakra, or a woman, or a bhikṣuṇī; or, while lying in a dark room, his body emits radiance.

Such people are deluded by folly and mistake him for a Bodhisattva; they believe his teachings and allow their minds to be shaken. They violate the Buddha’s Vinaya and secretly practice lustful desires. With mouths skilled at speaking of calamities, auspicious signs, and strange portents, they may say that the Tathāgata has appeared in such-and-such a place, or speak of the kalpa-fire or of weapons and war. They terrify people, causing their family wealth to dissipate without cause. This is known as a "strange ghost" who, having grown old, becomes a demon to harass and disturb these people.
Once he becomes satiated and the thought of departure arises, he leaves the person's body; both the disciple and the teacher then fall into royal peril.
"You should awaken first so as not to enter saṃsāra;
if you remain deluded and ignorant, you will fall into the Avīci Hell. Ānanda! "

Furthermore, son of good family, when the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is empty and subtle, and one is not beset by perverse thoughts as the perfect concentration (*samādhi*) gives rise to illumination, yet within this *samādhi* the mind loves to wander and rove, causing its refined reflections to fly forth in a greedy quest for experience.

At that time, a celestial Mara, watching for an opportunity, sent a flying spirit to possess a person who would orally preach the sutras and dharmas. That person, unaware that he was possessed by a Mara, would also claim to have personally attained unsurpassed Nirvana, and would come to the place of the seeker of the Way—a son of good family—to arrange his seat and preach the Dharma.

While their own forms remained unchanged, those listening to the Dharma suddenly saw themselves sitting upon precious lotus flowers; their entire bodies were transformed into masses of purple-gold light, and each member of the assembly experienced this unprecedented phenomenon.

Such people are deluded by folly and mistake him for a Bodhisattva; their minds become licentious and they violate the Buddha’s Vinaya, secretly practicing greed and desire. They take pleasure in saying that various Buddhas have appeared in the world, claiming that a certain person in a certain place must be the incarnation of a certain Buddha come here, or that a certain person is a certain Bodhisattva who has come to transform the human realm. Because these people see him, their hearts develop a longing for him; false views arise in secret and the seeds of wisdom are extinguished. This is called a *pātāla* ghost who, having grown old, becomes a demon to harass and disturb such people.
Once the demon is satiated and its heart turns away from the person's body, both the disciple and the teacher will fall into royal punishment.
"You should awaken first so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth;
if you are deluded and ignorant, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.

Furthermore, O virtuous man, when the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) is empty and subtle, and you have not encountered perverse thoughts, your perfect concentration manifests clarity. Within this samādhi, if your mind becomes fond of continuous, subtle absorption, you clarify your refined contemplation and greedily seek a point of accord."

At that time, a celestial Mara, watching for an opportunity, sends forth his essence to possess a person who speaks of the sutras and the Dharma. That person is truly unaware that they are possessed by a Mara; they also claim to have personally attained unsurpassed Nirvana, and comes to the place where the seeker of harmony—a good man—resides, to arrange seats and preach the Dharma.

While their forms and those who listen to the Dharma remained externally unchanged, the listeners experienced internal transformations before even hearing the Dharma: their minds spontaneously attained awakening, their thoughts shifted moment by moment, some gained knowledge of past lives, some possessed the power of knowing others' minds, some beheld the hells, some knew all manner of good and evil affairs in the human world, some spoke verses aloud, and some recited sutras themselves; each was filled with joy at having attained what they had never experienced before.

Such a person, deluded by folly, mistakes this for a bodhisattva and cherishes it with deep affection. They violate the Buddha’s code of discipline and secretly practice lustful desires. In their speech, they delight in saying that there are "great" and "small" Buddhas, that such-and-such a Buddha was earlier and such-and-such a Buddha was later, and that among them there are true Buddhas and false Buddhas, male Buddhas and female Buddhas; they say the same of bodhisattvas. Because the person sees these things, their original mind is washed away and they easily fall into heterodox enlightenment. This is called a possessing ghost who, having grown old, becomes a demon to harass and disturb this person.
Once its desire is satisfied, the spirit leaves the person's body, and both the disciple and the teacher fall into royal punishment.
"You should awaken first so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth;
if you are deluded and ignorant, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.

Furthermore, O virtuous man, when the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) is empty and subtle, and you have not encountered perverse thoughts, your perfect concentration (samādhi) will bring forth illumination. Within this samādhi, if your mind becomes attached to the fundamental source and you exhaustively investigate the beginning and end of the nature of all transforming things, your spirit will become refined and you will greedily seek analytical discernment."

At that time, a celestial demon, watching for an opportunity, sent forth his essence to possess a person who would orally preach the sutras and dharmas. That person was unaware beforehand that he was possessed by a demon; he also claimed to have personally attained unsurpassed nirvana and came to the place of the virtuous man who sought the source, where he spread out a seat and preached the Dharma.

His body possessed such majestic power that it subdued those who sought him; even without hearing the Dharma, they were naturally humbled in his presence. These people regarded the Buddha’s Nirvana and Bodhi-Dharmakāya as being none other than their own present physical bodies. They saw the successive generation of fathers and sons as the eternal, uninterrupted Dharmakāya. Pointing directly to the present world, they declared it to be the Buddha-land, seeing no separate Pure Abodes or golden marks. Having accepted this with faith, they forgot their former minds; they took refuge in his person and life, attaining what they had never experienced before.

These deluded fools imagine themselves to be Bodhisattvas; yet when their minds are scrutinized, they are found to have violated the Buddha’s discipline and secretly practice lust. They delight in saying that the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue are all pure lands, and that the male and female organs are the true locus of Bodhi and Nirvana. Those ignorant ones believe these foul words; this is known as being possessed by evil spirits such as *gudu* and *yan-sheng*, who, having grown old, become demons to harass and disturb these people.
When a sense of satiety arises, they depart from the person's body;
both the disciple and the teacher will fall into royal calamity.
You should attain prior awareness so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth.
Deluded and ignorant, they fall into the Avīci Hell.

Furthermore, son of good family, when the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) is empty and subtle, and one has not encountered perverse thoughts, the perfect concentration gives rise to illumination. Within this samādhi, the mind develops a longing for responsive resonance; it circulates and investigates exhaustively, greedily seeking a hidden response.

At that time, a celestial Mara, watching for an opportunity, will dispatch a refined spirit to possess a person who speaks the sutras and dharmas. That person has no prior awareness of being possessed by a Mara, and they also claim to have personally attained unsurpassed nirvana; they come to the place of a virtuous man seeking a response, arrange their seat, and preach the Dharma.

He enables the audience to behold his body for a brief moment as if for hundreds of thousands of years; their hearts give rise to such deep attachment that they cannot bear to part from him. They serve as his slaves, providing the four requisites of life without ever feeling weary. He causes each person in the assembly to realize that he was originally their teacher and good spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), thereby giving rise to a distinct dharma-love that adheres like glue or lacquer—a state they have never experienced before.
Such people are deluded by folly and take them to be bodhisattvas; they draw near to their minds, violate the Buddha’s code of discipline, and secretly practice lust.

They delight in saying: "In a previous life, during such-and-such a birth, I first delivered such-and-such a person; at that time, they were my wife, concubine, or brother. Now I have come to deliver them and accompany you back to such-and-such a world to make offerings to such-and-such a Buddha."
Or some may say that there is a separate realm of the Great Luminous Heaven where a Buddha dwells, a place where all Tathāgatas rest and reside.
Those who lack wisdom believe this falsehood and lose their original mind; this is called a malevolent ghost who, having grown old, becomes a demon to harass and disturb such a person.
When the mind of satiety arises, it departs from that person's body;
both the disciple and the teacher will fall into royal peril.
You should awaken first, so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth.
Deluded and ignorant, they fall into the Avīci Hell.

Furthermore, O good man, when the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is void and subtle, and one has not encountered perverse thoughts, the perfect samādhi brings forth illumination. Within this state of *samādhi*, the mind cherishes deep penetration; through diligent self-discipline, one delights in dwelling in the stillness of the aggregates and greedily seeks tranquil serenity.

At that time, a celestial Māra, watching for an opportunity, sends forth his essence to possess a person who speaks the teachings of the sūtras. That person does not originally realize they are possessed by a Māra, yet claims to have personally attained unsurpassed nirvāṇa; he comes to the place of the good man seeking the aggregates, spreads out his seat, and preaches the Dharma.
He caused those listening to each recognize their own past karma; at times, he would say to one person in that assembly, "Though you have not yet died, you have already become an animal.
He then commanded another to step on the person's tail, causing him to be instantly unable to rise. Thereupon, the entire assembly bowed their hearts in humble reverence.

There is a person who, as soon as they give rise to a thought, is already known by its inception; outside of the Buddha’s Vinaya discipline, they undergo excessive asceticism, slander bhikṣus, revile their followers, and expose private affairs without avoiding public censure. They delight in speaking of future calamities and blessings, and when the time arrives, not even a hair's breadth of error occurs. This is a powerful ghost who has grown old and become a māra, coming to vex and disturb this person.
When a sense of satiety arises and the spirit departs from the person's body,
both the disciple and the teacher will often fall into royal punishment.
You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth.
Deluded and ignorant, they fall into the Avīci Hell.

Furthermore, O son of good family, when the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) is empty and subtle, and one is not beset by deviant thoughts but has manifested clarity through perfect concentration, within this samādhi one may develop a fondness for knowledge and insight, diligently and painfully investigating and seeking after past lives.

At that time, a celestial Mara, watching for an opportunity, dispatches a refined spirit to possess a person who speaks of the sutras and the Dharma. That person is entirely unaware of being possessed by a Mara, and likewise claims to have personally attained supreme Nirvana; he comes to the place of the seeker of the Way, a son of good family, spreads his seat, and preaches the Dharma.

This person, without cause, obtains a great precious jewel at the place where the Dharma is being preached. That Māra may sometimes transform himself into an animal, with its mouth holding that jewel along with various rare treasures, bamboo slips, talismans, documents, and other extraordinary objects; he first presents these to the person and then attaches them to his body. Or, he entices the listeners by hiding a bright moon-jewel beneath the earth so that it illuminates that spot, and those listeners experience what they have never known before.

They consume many medicinal herbs and abstain from fine delicacies; at times they eat only one sesame seed and one grain of wheat per day. Yet their bodies remain plump and robust because they are sustained by the power of Māra. They slander bhikṣus and revile their fellow practitioners without avoiding public censure. They are fond of speaking of hidden treasures in other lands and the secret dwelling places of sages throughout the ten directions, claiming that those who follow them will often encounter extraordinary persons. These are spirits of mountains, forests, land, city walls, rivers, and peaks who have grown old and become Māras. Some preach licentiousness and violate the Buddha’s precepts, secretly indulging in the five desires with those who serve them. Others appear diligent, consuming only grasses and trees, yet their conduct is erratic as they seek to disturb and confuse those people.
When a sense of satiety arises in the mind, it departs from that person's body;
both the disciple and the teacher will often fall into royal calamity.
You should attain prior awareness so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth.
Deluded and ignorant, they fall into the Avīci Hell.

Furthermore, O virtuous man, when the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha) is empty and subtle, and one has not encountered perverse thoughts, the perfect concentration brings forth illumination. Within this samādhi, if the mind develops a fondness for various supernatural powers and transformations, investigating the source of such manifestations and greedily seeking spiritual might, [one will fall].

At that time, a celestial Mara, waiting for an opportunity, sends forth his essence to possess a person who speaks the sutras and the Dharma. That person truly does not realize they are possessed by a Mara; they also claim to have personally attained unsurpassed nirvana, and comes to the place of the virtuous man seeking spiritual penetration to arrange seats and preach the Dharma.

This person may again take fire in his hand and grasp its light, distributing it over the heads of the fourfold assembly who are listening; the flames atop the heads of these listeners all reach several feet in length, yet they lack the quality of heat and never burn.
Or he may walk upon water as if treading on level ground;
or he may sit cross-legged in mid-air, remaining motionless.
They may enter into a flask or reside within a sack;
they pass through windows and penetrate walls without any obstruction;
yet, regarding weapons and blades, they find no mastery.

They claim to be the Buddha’s body while wearing white robes, accepting prostrations from bhikṣus, slandering dhyāna and the Vinaya, and reviling their followers. They expose private matters without avoiding public censure, constantly speaking of supernatural powers and mastery. Sometimes they cause others to see Buddha-lands by the side; such demonic power deludes people and lacks any reality. They praise sexual misconduct and do not condemn coarse behavior, taking various lewd acts as the transmission of the Dharma. These are known as the great-power mountain spirits, sea spirits, wind spirits, river spirits, and earth spirits of the world; they are the accumulated karmic ghosts of all grasses and trees over many kalpas, or dragon ghosts, or immortals who have ended their lives but returned as ghosts, or those whose immortal term has expired and whose years dictate death, yet whose forms do not decay and who are possessed by other monsters. As they grow old, they become demons that harass and disturb these people.
When a sense of satiety arises in their minds, they leave that person's body;
both the disciple and the teacher often fall into royal calamity.
You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth.
Deluded and ignorant, they fall into the Avīci Hell.

Furthermore, son of good family, when the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) is void and subtle, and one has not encountered perverse thoughts but has instead clarified the mind through perfect concentration, within this samādhi one may develop a fondness for entering cessation (nirodha). One then investigates the nature of transformation and greedily seeks profound emptiness.

At that time, a celestial Mara, watching for an opportunity, sends forth his essence to possess a person who speaks of the sutras and the Dharma. That person does not realize at all that he is possessed by a Mara, and he claims for himself that he has attained unsurpassed Nirvana; he comes to the place where those seeking emptiness dwell, spreads out his seat, and preaches the Dharma.

Within the great assembly, his form suddenly vanished into emptiness so that the multitude could see nothing; then he would emerge abruptly from the void, appearing and disappearing at will. At times he manifested his body as transparent as lapis lazuli; at times he extended his hands and feet, emitting the fragrance of sandalwood; at times his excrement and urine were like thick rock honey. He reviled the precepts and held the renunciants in contempt, constantly preaching in his mouth that there is neither cause nor effect, that once dead one is extinguished forever with no further rebirth, and that even though ordinary beings and sages may attain emptiness and stillness, they secretly indulge in lust, and those who receive such desire likewise attain an "empty mind" by denying cause and effect. These are known as the spirits of solar and lunar eclipses, the essences of gold, jade, fungi, and grasses, and the *qilin*, phoenix, tortoise, and crane—beings that do not die for thousands of myriad years and become numinous, being born into the land to grow old and become demons that vex and disturb these people.
When a sense of satiety arises and the spirit departs from the person's body,
both the disciple and the teacher often fall into royal calamity.
You should be aware of this beforehand so that you do not enter the cycle of rebirth.
Deluded and ignorant, they fall into the Avīci Hell.

Furthermore, good son, when the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) is empty and subtle, and one has not encountered perverse thoughts but has instead manifested clarity through perfect concentration, within this samādhi one may develop a love for long life. One undergoes arduous effort in investigating the subtle, greedily seeking eternal years and abandoning the birth of segmented existence, suddenly hoping for the permanence of the subtle characteristics of the transformational body.

At that time, a celestial demon waits for an opportunity to seize him; he sends a refined spirit to possess a person who speaks the sutras and the Dharma. That person does not realize at all that they are possessed by a demon, and claims for themselves that they have attained supreme Nirvana. They come to the place of the seeker of the Way, where the son of good family dwells, to arrange seats and preach the Dharma.

He would skillfully speak of traveling to other lands without obstruction; sometimes after traversing ten thousand *li*, he would return in an instant, having obtained the desired objects from those distant places. Or, while staying in a single house, he would cause a person to travel from the eastern wall to the western wall in just a few paces—a journey that even a man walking at full speed for many years could not complete. Consequently, people’s minds were filled with faith, yet they also harbored doubts as to whether it was the Buddha appearing before them.

He constantly says with his own mouth: "The sentient beings of the ten directions are all my children; I have given birth to all Buddhas, I have produced the worlds, and I am the Primordial Buddha. My arising is spontaneous and not attained through cultivation. This is called the World-Abiding Sovereign Heaven Demon (Lokākṣema-deva-māra), who employs his retinue—such as the Cāmuṇḍas, the Four Heavenly Kings, and the Vaiśravaṇa youths—to exploit those who have not yet resolved their minds for enlightenment, consuming their vital essence, or to lead them astray without the guidance of a teacher.

When the practitioner personally observes this, [the spirit] is called Vajradhara and promises them long life; it manifests in the body of a beautiful woman to incite rampant lust, yet before a year has passed, their liver and brain wither away. They speak to themselves alone, appearing like a *piśāca* or a malevolent ghost; others do not recognize the cause and many fall into royal peril, dying of dehydration even before facing execution—thus it torments and disturbs that person until their death.
"You should awaken first so as not to enter saṃsāra;
if you remain deluded and ignorant, you will fall into the Avīci Hell. Ānanda!"

You should know that these ten kinds of demons, during the final age, will leave the home life to practice the Way within my Dharma; they may either possess a human body or manifest their own forms, all claiming to have already attained Right and Universal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). They praise sexual desire and violate the Buddha’s Vinaya. These former evil demonic teachers and their disciples transmit their lust from one to another. Thus, such perverse spirits bewitch the hearts and viscera of their victims; in the near term this may last for nine lifetimes, and often exceeds a hundred generations, causing those who truly practice cultivation to become entirely part of the demonic retinue. After death, they will surely become subjects of the demons, lose their Right and Universal Enlightenment, and fall into the Avīci Hell.

You need not first seek nirvana at this time; even if you attain the stage of no-more-learning, remain by your vow within that age of the Dharma’s decline, give rise to great compassion, and rescue those sentient beings who possess a correct mind and deep faith, ensuring they do not fall under the influence of demons and that they attain right knowledge and vision.
"I have now delivered you from birth and death; if you follow the Buddha’s words, this shall be called repaying the Buddha’s kindness. Ānanda!

These ten kinds of manifest states during *dhyāna* all appear because the mind is applied in interaction with the *saṃjñā-skandha* (the aggregate of perception). Sentient beings are stubborn and deluded, failing to reflect upon themselves; encountering these conditions, they are confused and fail to recognize them for what they are, claiming instead that they have attained sainthood. Having committed such a great falsehood, they fall into the Avīci Hell."

"You must certainly carry the words of the Tathāgata and, after my parinirvāṇa, transmit them during the age of the Dharma-ending period, causing all sentient beings everywhere to awaken to this meaning. Do not allow celestial Māras to find any opportunity; protect and preserve them so that they may achieve the Unsurpassed Way."
The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Myriad Practices, Scroll Nine.
The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Tathāgata’s Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization,
the Definitive Meaning of the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas, Śūraṅgama Sūtra, Scroll Ten, titled "In Central India at Nālandā."
The *Mahā-maṇḍala-sūtra*, excerpted from the *Abhiṣeka-varga* and circulated separately.

Translated by the Śramaṇa from Central India, Prajñāmitra, at the Zhizhi Daochang in Guangzhou on the twenty-third day (*xinchou*), the second month of the fifth lunar month in the year of Yisi (the first year of the Shénlóng era of the Great Táng). Scribed by Fáng Róng, a disciple of the Bodhisattva Precepts who formerly served as the Right Rectifying Censor, concurrently Acting Minister of the Department of State Affairs and Vice President of the Secretariat, of the Qīnghé clan. Oral interpretation provided by the Śramaṇa Mīgashikya from the country of Udyāna. “Ānanda!...”

When that good man cultivates *samādhi* and the *saṃjñā-skandha* (aggregate of perception) is exhausted, his ordinary dreams and fantasies vanish, and waking and sleeping are always one. His awakened clarity is empty and still, like a cloudless sky; there are no longer any coarse or heavy shadows of external objects. He observes the worlds, the great earth, mountains, and rivers as if in a clear mirror: things come without sticking and pass away without leaving a trace, receiving reflections only in emptiness. Having understood that habitual tendencies are non-existent and that there is only a single, pure reality, the root-source of birth and death is revealed from this point on. He perceives the twelve classes of sentient beings throughout the ten directions and exhausts their various types; though he has not yet penetrated the individual threads of their destinies, he sees their common basis of life, which is like shimmering, flickering heat-mirages—the ultimate pivot-hole for the floating sense-faculties and their objects. This is called the realm of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (aggregate of formations).

If this turbid agitation returns to its original, radiant nature, and that nature enters the fundamental clarity such that the single clarity subsumes all habitual tendencies—like waves subsiding and transforming into still water—this is called the exhaustion of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations). Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of sentient beings.
If one examines its origin, it is rooted in obscure and hidden delusive thoughts.

"Ānanda, you should know that when these sons of good family, having attained correct awareness within *śamatha*, maintain a concentrated, luminous, and upright mind, the ten classes of celestial Māras find no opportunity to harm them. Only then are they able to investigate and exhaustively study the root of all living beings. When the fundamental source of birth is revealed within those various categories of beings, they observe that profound, pure, and perfectly turbulent source of motion. If, within that perfect source, they give rise to speculative calculations, such persons fall into the two theories of causelessness."
First, this person perceives that there is no fundamental cause. Why is this?

Because this person has already attained the complete dissolution of the vital mechanism and rides upon the eight hundred merits of the visual faculty; they see all sentient beings throughout eighty thousand kalpas, their karmic currents winding and circling as they die here and are born there. Seeing only the cyclic wandering of these beings within those realms, and observing nothing beyond the eighty thousand kalpas—shrouded in darkness—they then form this interpretation:
"These sentient beings of the ten directions in this world have existed spontaneously without cause for eighty thousand kalpas.
By such reckoning, they lose sight of Right Universal Knowledge (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and fall into the ways of the heterodox, deluding themselves regarding the nature of Bodhi.
Second, these people see that the end has no cause. Why is this?

Because these people, having already seen its root in birth—knowing that humans produce humans and perceiving that birds produce birds; seeing that crows have been black from the start and cranes have been white from the start; that humans and devas are fundamentally upright while animals are fundamentally horizontal; and that whiteness is not produced by washing nor blackness created by dyeing—they conclude that from eighty thousand kalpas there has been no further change or shift. They think, "Now, even as this present form comes to its end, it shall be likewise. Since I have never before perceived Bodhi, how could there ever be a matter of attaining Bodhi?"
You should know that all phenomena today are fundamentally without cause.

By such speculative reckoning, one loses right and universal knowledge, falls into the ranks of external paths, and becomes deluded regarding the nature of bodhi. This is called the first external path, which establishes the doctrine of no-cause.

“Ānanda! Among these good sons within this samādhi, their minds are concentrated, luminous, and upright, so that Māra finds no opportunity. They exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source. When they give rise to speculative calculations regarding this perfect and eternal reality, such persons fall into the four theories of universal permanence.”
First, this person investigates the nature of the mind and its objects, finding no cause for these two locations;

through cultivation, they are able to know all births and deaths of sentient beings throughout the ten directions within twenty thousand kalpas, seeing that they all circulate in a cycle without ever being lost, and thus reckon them to be permanent.
The second type of person exhaustively investigates the source of the four great elements, concluding that their four natures are eternally abiding;

through cultivation, they are able to know all births and deaths of sentient beings throughout the ten directions within forty thousand kalpas, perceiving that their essence is constant and never dispersed or lost, and thus reckoning them as permanent.

Third, this person exhausts the six sense faculties; because the fundamental source within the *manas* that grasps and sustains the mind, intellect, and consciousness is eternally constant in its nature, they practice until they can know that throughout eighty thousand kalpas, all sentient beings circulate without losing their essence, abiding primordially and eternally without exhausting their inherent nature, and thus they reckon it to be permanent.

Fourth, this person, having exhausted the source of perception, finds that the principle of their nature no longer flows, ceases, or revolves; the mind of birth and death has now been eternally extinguished, and within this principle, non-arising and non-extinction naturally prevail. Based on what the mind has measured, they reckon this state to be permanent.

Because of this reckoning of permanence, one loses the correct and universal knowledge and falls into the ranks of the external paths, becoming deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi; this is called the second type of external path, the doctrine of the established perfect permanence.

"Furthermore, among those good sons within samādhi, their minds are firm, concentrated, and upright, so that Māras find no opportunity. They exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source. Yet, if they give rise to speculative calculations regarding self and others, these people fall into four inverted views: the doctrine that one part is impermanent and one part is permanent."

First, this person contemplates the wondrously luminous mind as pervading the worlds of the ten directions, taking its profound stillness to be the ultimate *ātman*. From this, they reckon that their self pervades the ten directions, concentrated and luminous, immovable; they hold that all sentient beings are born and die within the center of their own mind, and thus declare their own mind-nature to be "constant," while those who undergo birth and death possess a truly impermanent nature.

Second, this person does not contemplate their own mind, but instead surveys throughout the lands of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; seeing places where kalpas are destroyed, they call them the nature of ultimate impermanence, and seeing places where kalpas are not destroyed, they call them ultimate permanence.

Third, this person separately contemplates their own mind as being subtle, refined, and extremely dense, like a fine mote of dust. It transmigrates through the ten directions without its nature ever changing; it can cause this body to arise and perish in an instant. This indestructible nature is called the "eternal nature of the self," while all birth and death that flow forth from it is called the "nature of impermanence."

Fourth, this person knows that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has ended and perceives the flow of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); they reckon this constant flow as having a permanent nature, while regarding the cessation of form, sensation, perception, and so forth as impermanent.

Because they speculate that one part is impermanent and one part is permanent, they fall into the ways of the external paths and become deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi; this is called the third heterodox doctrine of "one-part permanence."

"Furthermore, among those good sons within samādhi, their minds are firm, concentrated, and upright, so that Māra finds no opportunity. They exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source. If, within these various states, they give rise to conceptual calculations, such persons fall into the 'Theory of the Four Finite Extremes'."

First, these people calculate the origin of birth; as their mental activity flows on without ceasing, they calculate the past and future to be "finite," and they calculate the continuous mind to be "infinite."

Second, this person contemplates eighty thousand kalpas; they see that prior to those eighty thousand kalpas, sentient beings were quiescent, beyond hearing or seeing. That which is beyond hearing or seeing is called "boundless," while that where sentient beings exist is called "bounded."

Third, this person calculates that his self possesses universal knowledge and has attained the nature of boundlessness; yet all those people appear within the scope of his own knowledge, while he himself has never known the nature of their knowledge. Thus, he is said not to have attained a mind of boundlessness, but rather possesses only a limited nature.

Fourth, this person exhaustively investigates the emptiness of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Based on the mental pathways he perceives, he calculates that within the single body of every sentient being, all things are half-born and half-extinguished; he clarifies that everything existing in the world is half-finite and half-infinite.

Based on this conceptualization of having limits or being limitless, they fall into the ranks of the non-Buddhists and become deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi; this is called the fourth type of non-Buddhist doctrine, which posits the existence of limits.

"Furthermore, among those good sons within samādhi, their minds are firm, concentrated, and upright, such that Māras cannot find an opportunity. They exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source.
