Yet, if they give rise to conceptual calculations within their knowledge and views, these people will fall into four kinds of inverted, 'neither-dying-nor-chaotic' sophistry and pervasive false theorizing."
First, this person contemplates the source of transformation: where they perceive shifting flow, they designate it as "change"; where they perceive continuity, they designate it as "permanence.
Where they perceive an object of seeing, they designate it as "arising"; where they do not perceive the locus of seeing, they designate it as "cessation.

Where the nature of the cause of continuity is uninterrupted, they designate it as "increase"; within the midst of that very continuity, where there is a point of separation, they designate it as "decrease."
The place where each arises is called existence; the place where each mutually perishes is called non-existence.
When observing through principle as a whole, yet seeing with a particularized mind, there may come a seeker of the Dharma who asks about its meaning, to which one replies:
"I am now both arising and ceasing, both existent and non-existent, both increasing and decreasing.
At all times he confuses his speech in this way, causing the person before him to lose the sequence of the verses.

Second, this person contemplates the mind with discernment and finds that it has no locus; because there is nothing to be found, they attain realization. When someone comes to question them, they respond with only a single word, saying merely "non-existence," and beyond this non-existence, they have nothing further to say.

Third, this person carefully observes the mind and realizes that each has its own locus; through this realization, they attain a form of certification. When someone comes to question them, they respond with only a single word, saying merely "It is so," and apart from this, they have nothing further to say.

Fourth, there are those who hold the view that both existence and non-existence are true; because their object is bifurcated, their minds are likewise distracted. When someone comes to question them, they answer: "To say 'it exists' is the same as saying 'it does not exist,' and within 'it does not exist' it is not the case that 'it exists. All of this is evasive and confused, leaving no room for further inquiry."

Due to this speculative reckoning, deceitful equivocation, and nihilism, they fall into the ranks of the external paths and become deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi. This is called the fifth class of externalists: the fourfold nature of perversion, characterized by the pervasive reckoning of false theories and the equivocation of immortality.

"Furthermore, among those good sons within samādhi, their minds are firm, concentrated, and upright, so that Māras find no opportunity. They exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings, observing that source which is profoundly serene yet eternally subject to agitation. If they then give rise to conceptual calculations regarding this inexhaustible flow, such a person falls into the inverted resolve of perceiving signs after death."
Some fixate on their own bodies, saying that form is the self;
some perceive the self as encompassing and pervading all lands, saying that the self possesses form;
or they see external objects revolving in accordance with the self, saying that form belongs to the self.
Alternatively, based on the continuity within my own practice, I may think, "I am in form.

All such deliberations assert that there is a mark after death; thus, these sixteen marks circulate in rotation. From these deluded calculations, the two natures of ultimate affliction and ultimate bodhi drive side by side, each remaining entirely untouched by the other.

Because they speculate that there is existence after death, they fall into the ranks of the non-Buddhists and become deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi. This is called the sixth type of non-Buddhist, who establishes the inverted doctrine of a mind characterized by the mark of existence after death within the five aggregates.

"Furthermore, among those good sons within samādhi, their minds are firm, concentrated, and upright, so that Māras find no opportunity. They exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings, observing that source of constant agitation within profound stillness. If they first eliminate form, sensation, and perception, yet continue to give rise to conceptual calculations, such persons fall into the inverted resolve of the 'signless' state after death."
Seeing that form ceases, one realizes there is no basis for its manifestation;
observing that perception ceases, one realizes the mind has nothing to which it is bound;
knowing that sensation ceases, one realizes there is no further continuity.
The female organ has dissolved; though its physical form may still exist, it lacks sensation and perception and is thus identical to grass and trees.
Since this substance cannot even be apprehended while present before you, how could it possess any further characteristics after death?

Based on this, one examines that the marks of existence after death do not exist; thus, in such a cycle, there are eight non-marks. From this, one may calculate that the causes and effects of nirvana are entirely empty, existing merely as names, and ultimately subject to total annihilation.

Because of this speculative reckoning that there is nothing after death, one falls away from the Way and becomes deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi; this is called the seventh heterodox school, which establishes the inverted view of mind that there is no sign of existence after death within the five aggregates.

"Furthermore, among those good sons within samādhi, their minds are firm, concentrated, and upright, so that Māra finds no opportunity. They exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings, observing that source which is profound, pure, yet constantly agitated. While abiding in the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra*), they simultaneously suppress sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*). By dualistically calculating existence and non-existence, their own essential natures cancel each other out. These people fall into the 'neither-exist-nor-not-exist' doctrine after death, giving rise to inverted views. Within form, sensation, and perception, they see both existence and non-existence; within the flux of formations, they observe neither existence nor non-existence. Thus they cycle through and exhaust the aggregates (*skandha*) and elements (*dhātu*). Encountering any one of the eight conditions of 'neither-exist-nor-not-exist,' they all claim that after death there is neither a sign of existence nor a sign of non-existence. Furthermore, because they calculate that the nature of all formations is subject to change and distortion, their minds give rise to a penetrating realization that both existence and non-existence are neither, leaving them uncertain as to whether things are real or unreal."

Based on this speculative reckoning that after death there is neither existence nor non-existence, because the future limit is shrouded in darkness and beyond description, they fall into the ranks of externalists and delude themselves regarding the nature of Bodhi. This is called the eighth externalist school, which establishes the inverted theory of mind within the five aggregates concerning the state of being neither existent nor non-existent after death.

"Furthermore, among those good sons within samādhi, their minds are firm, concentrated, and upright, so that Māras find no opportunity. They exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings, contemplating that profound, pure, and eternally agitated source. Yet, regarding the subsequent states of non-arising, they engage in speculative calculations. Such persons fall into the seven theories of annihilationism: either calculating the annihilation of the body, or the annihilation of desire, or the annihilation of suffering, or the annihilation of ultimate bliss, or the annihilation of ultimate equanimity; thus cycling through these until the seven limits are exhausted, they perceive that things are currently being extinguished, and once extinguished, there is nothing more."

Based on this speculative reckoning that there is annihilation after death, they fall into the ranks of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika), deluding themselves regarding the nature of Bodhi. This is called the ninth type of non-Buddhist: those who establish the inverted doctrine of the mind that asserts annihilation after death within the five aggregates (skandhas).

"Furthermore, among those good sons within samādhi, their minds are firm, concentrated, and upright, so that Māra finds no opportunity. They exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source. Yet, if they subsequently engage in speculative calculations regarding future births, such persons fall into the 'Discourse on the Five Nirvāṇas'."
Some take the desire realm as the true basis for transformation because they perceive its perfect clarity and give rise to attachment toward it;
some take the first dhyāna because its nature is free from sorrow;
or some take the second dhyāna because the mind is free from suffering.
Alternatively, it is because they follow the extreme joy of the third dhyāna;
or because in the fourth dhyāna, both suffering and pleasure have vanished, and they do not undergo the nature of birth and death within saṃsāra.

Mistaking the tainted heavens for the realization of the unconditioned, they regard the security of these five abodes as a supreme and pure reliance, thus circling through these five abodes until the end.

Based on this speculative reckoning, they conceive of five kinds of present nirvāṇa; thus they fall into the ranks of the heterodox, deluding themselves regarding the nature of bodhi. This is called the tenth heterodox school: the inverted doctrine of establishing five kinds of present nirvāṇa within the five aggregates.

“Ānanda! These ten kinds of delusory realizations in dhyāna all arise because the mind is applied in a conflicting manner within the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations), thereby manifesting these so-called awakenings. Beings are stubborn and deluded; they do not reflect upon themselves, and when these states appear before them, they mistake delusion for realization and claim to have attained the state of a sage. Having committed this great falsehood, they fall into the Avīci Hell.”

"You must certainly carry the words of the Tathāgata and transmit them after my parinirvāṇa during the age of the final dharma, causing all sentient beings everywhere to awaken to and understand this meaning. Do not allow the demons of the mind to give rise to deep arrogance; maintain and protect them from the spread of false views. Teach their bodies and minds to awaken to the true meaning, so that they do not encounter detours on the unsurpassed path. Do not let them seek only minor attainments and consider them sufficient; rather, act as the pure guiding finger for the Great Awakened King."

“Ānanda! When that son of good family practices samādhi and the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is exhausted, the subtle, clear, and agitated nature of all worldly phenomena—the generative power of the common lot—suddenly collapses and fractures; the fine meshes of the net are submerged, and the deep channels through which the *pudgala* repays its karma and the resonance between cause and effect are suspended. He is about to attain great awakening in the heaven of Nirvāṇa, like a rooster crowing at dawn when it gazes toward the east and already sees the first glimmer of light. The six sense faculties become empty and still, no longer wandering or escaping; internally and externally they are profoundly luminous, entering a state where there is nowhere to enter. He deeply penetrates the fundamental source of life for the twelve types of beings throughout the ten directions. Observing the root of grasping, he finds that none of these classes can summon him back; having attained identity with the ten directions, the refined radiance does not sink away but reveals what was hidden and secret. This is called the domain of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).”

If, within the collective summons, one has already attained uniformity therein, such that the six gates are refined and worn away, achieving the state where they are both integrated and opened; if seeing and hearing interpenetrate their neighbors and the mutual functions are purified, so that the ten directions, the world, as well as body and mind, are as clear and transparent inside and out as vaidūrya lapis lazuli—this is called the exhaustion of the consciousness aggregate (vijñānaskandha). Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of life-span (āyur-kaṣāya).
If one examines its origin, it is formless and void; inverted false thoughts constitute its root.

"Ānanda, you should know that this good man has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned formations and returned the consciousness to its source, thereby extinguishing birth and death. Yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction, he has not yet perfected it. He is able to cause his own body’s sense organs to merge or separate at will, and he can also communicate his awareness with all classes of beings throughout the ten directions. His perception is so pervasive and harmonious that he can enter the perfect source."

If one establishes a cause of true permanence regarding that to which they have taken refuge and develops a resolute conviction therein, such a person falls into the attachment to causes and their underlying reasons. They become a companion to the *sāṃkhya* followers who take refuge in the *pradhāna* (the primal source); they are deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and lose their right knowledge and vision. This is called the first instance of establishing a mind that seeks attainment, forming a fruit of what is taken as refuge; it is far removed from perfect penetration, turning one's back on the city of Nirvana, and giving rise to the seeds of external paths.

“Ānanda! Furthermore, there is a good man who, having exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and extinguished birth and death, has not yet perfected the subtle and wondrous state of cessation. If he takes that which he has returned to as his own self-essence, and develops the conviction that all sentient beings within the twelve categories throughout the entirety of space arise from a single stream within his own body, this person falls into the grasping of ‘the capable’ and ‘the incapable. Maheśvara will appear in an infinite body to become his companion; he becomes deluded regarding the Bodhi of the Buddha and loses his true knowledge and vision. This is called the second [delusion]: establishing the ‘capable’ as the mind, thereby producing the fruit of capable activity. It is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvāṇa, giving rise to the seed of the great-proud devas whose ‘I’ is pervasive and complete.”
"Furthermore, good son, having exhausted all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and realized their emptiness, you have extinguished arising and ceasing;

yet, within this state of quiescent extinction, your subtle and wondrous realization is not yet perfected. If, regarding that to which one returns, you take something as a basis for reliance and suspect that your own body and mind flow forth from it, and that the empty space of the ten directions all arises from it—then, at the very ground where all these things arise and are proclaimed to flow forth,"
They form the understanding that the true, eternal body is without birth or extinction; while amidst birth and extinction, they prematurely calculate it to be eternally abiding.

Thus, they are deluded regarding non-arising and confused about birth and extinction. Those who dwell securely in this deep confusion yet claim to have attained superior resolve will fall into the attachment of grasping at the eternal as non-eternal;
the Lord of Heaven (Īśvara) becomes their companion, and they lose sight of the Buddha’s Bodhi.
This cognitive vision is called the third establishment of causes based on the mind, which accomplishes the fruit of false discrimination;
it is far removed from perfect penetration, turns its back on the city of Nirvana, and gives rise to the seed of inverted perfection.

"Furthermore, good son, having exhausted all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and realized their emptiness, one has extinguished birth and death; yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of cessation (*nirvāṇa*), one has not yet perfected it. If, because one’s knowledge of objects of cognition is all-pervasive and complete, one establishes a view based on that knowledge—such that all grasses and trees in the ten directions are called sentient beings and are no different from humans, and that when these grasses and trees become humans, upon their death they return to becoming the grasses and trees of the ten directions—if one gives rise to such a superior resolve (*adhimukti*) through indiscriminate, universal knowledge, this person falls into the attachment of 'knowing non-knowing. They will become companions to the Pāṭha and Śākya heretics who cling to the awakening of all things. They are deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and have lost their true insight. This is called the fourth: calculating the mind as being perfect and knowing, which results in a false and erroneous fruit. It is far removed from perfect penetration, turns its back on the city of Nirvana, and gives rise to the seed of inverted knowledge."
"Furthermore, son of good family, having exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and brought an end to birth and death,
yet while the subtle and wondrous state of cessation has not yet reached perfection, if one attains conformity within the mutual functioning of the perfectly integrated faculties,
one will then seek the production of all things through perfect transformation— seeking the radiance of fire, delighting in the purity of water, and loving the circulation of wind."

Furthermore, regarding the accomplishment of the elements (*dhātu*), they each revere and serve these various elements, taking them as the primary cause for their arousal and establishing a view of permanence.
Such persons fall into the attachment to "birth" and "non-birth.
They join with the Kāśyapas and the Brahmins who, with diligent minds and laboring bodies, serve fire and revere water, seeking to transcend birth and death and forming companionship with them.
To lose sight of the Buddha’s Bodhi and forfeit one's true knowledge and vision is called the fifth attachment: to revere and serve external objects with a deluded mind that follows after things.

Thus one establishes false causes for seeking and vainly hopes for false fruits; straying far from perfect penetration and turning one's back on the city of Nirvana, one gives rise to the seeds of perverse transformation.

“Furthermore, good son, having exhausted all conditioned phenomena and realized their emptiness, one has extinguished birth and death; yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of cessation, it is not yet perfected. If, within this perfect luminosity, one reckons the midst of clarity to be void, and—failing to extinguish the manifold transformations—takes the eternal extinction as one’s refuge and gives rise to a superior resolve, such a person falls into the attachment of ‘returning to that which has no return. They become companions among the Śūnyatas in the Heaven of No-Thought, becoming deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and losing their true knowledge and vision. This is called the sixth [delusion]: the mind of circular voidness, which results in the fruit of empty extinction; it violates and distances itself from Perfect Penetration, turns its back on the City of Nirvana, and gives rise to the seed of annihilationism.”

"Furthermore, good son, having exhausted all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and realized their emptiness, one has extinguished birth and death; yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*), one has not yet perfected it. If, within this perfect permanence, one seeks to solidify the body so that it remains eternally, and develops a resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) that it will remain forever without decaying or passing away—this person falls into the attachment of 'clinging to life' while falsely claiming it is not clinging. They become companions to those *asita* who seek long life; they lose sight of the Buddha’s Bodhi and forfeit true knowledge and vision. This is called the seventh [delusion]: clinging to the source of life, establishing a cause of solid delusion to pursue the fruit of prolonged toil. It is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seeds of false prolongation."

"Furthermore, good son, having exhausted all conditioned activities (*saṃskāra*) and realized their emptiness, one has brought to an end both arising and ceasing; yet, while within this state of quiescent extinction, one’s subtle and wondrous realization is not yet perfected. Observing that life-force is interpenetrating, one nevertheless retains worldly defilements (*kleśa*), fearing they might be utterly extinguished. At this juncture, one sits within a lotus palace, extensively transforming the seven treasures and increasing the number of precious consorts, indulging the mind at will. Those who develop such superior resolve fall into the attachment to 'the real' within the unreal. They become companions to the *Takkirāja* [gods], becoming deluded regarding the Buddha's Bodhi and losing their true knowledge and vision. This is called the eighth: giving rise to the cause of perverse thought and establishing the fruit of blazing defilement; it is to be far removed from perfect penetration and to turn one's back on the city of Nirvana, giving birth to the seed of celestial Māras."

"Furthermore, good son, having exhausted all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and realized their emptiness, one has extinguished arising and ceasing; yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of cessation, one has not yet perfected it. Within the clarity of life, one discriminates between the refined and the coarse, and analyzes the true and the false, such that cause and effect correspond to one another. Seeking only for spiritual response, one turns away from the path of purity—namely, seeing suffering, abandoning its origin, realizing cessation, and cultivating the path—and having come to rest within cessation, one no longer advances to give rise to superior understanding. Such a person falls into the category of a Śrāvaka of fixed nature; they become companions to those monks who have heard nothing and to those of overweening pride (*adhimāna*). They are deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and lose their knowledge and vision. This is called the ninth stage: when the perfect essence responds to the mind, resulting in the fruit of quiescent pursuit. It violates and distances itself from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvāṇa, giving rise to a seed of entanglement within emptiness."

"Furthermore, good son, having exhausted all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and realized their emptiness, one has extinguished arising and ceasing; yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction, one has not yet perfected it. If, within this perfectly interfused, pure, awakened clarity, one develops an investigation into its profound subtlety and establishes it as *nirvāṇa*, but fails to advance further by generating superior resolve (*adhimukti*), such a person falls into the fixed-nature *pratyekabuddha*. They become companions to those solitary practitioners who do not turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna]. They are deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and lose their true knowledge and vision. This is called the tenth stage: the mind that merges with perfect enlightenment, which achieves a fruit of tranquil clarity, but which violates and distances itself from perfect penetration, turns its back on the city of *nirvāṇa*, and gives rise to a seed of unchanging perfect clarity."

“Ānanda! These ten kinds of causes for becoming insane midway through *dhyāna*—whether it be due to mistaking what is insufficient for a state of fulfillment or realization—are all produced by the interaction of the *vijñāna-skandha* with the mind. Sentient beings, stubborn and deluded, fail to reflect upon themselves; when these states appear before them, they each rely on their own cherished objects and the deluded minds of their past habits to find rest, taking this to be the ultimate ground of refuge and peace. They claim for themselves that they have attained unsurpassed *bodhi*. Having committed such great falsehoods, they become externalists and demonic spirits; when their karma is exhausted, they fall into the Avīci Hell, and those who were *śrāvakas* or *pratyekabuddhas* fail to progress further.”

"You all should maintain your resolve and uphold the Way of the Tathāgata, transmitting this Dharma-door after my parinirvāṇa to the final age, so that all sentient beings may universally awaken to and understand its meaning. Do not allow them to encounter demons and create their own downfall; protect, console, and rescue them from evil conditions, causing their bodies and minds to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Thus, from the very beginning of their accomplishment, they shall not encounter divergent paths. In the past, throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, countless Tathāgatas have relied upon this mind to open and attain the Unsurpassed Way."

If the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is exhausted, then your present sense faculties will function interchangeably; from this mutual functioning, you will be able to enter the Bodhisattva’s adamantine stage of dry wisdom (*vajra-śuṣka-prajñā*). Within this state, the perfectly luminous and refined essence of mind will manifest and transform, like a pure lapis lazuli gem containing a precious moon. In this way, you will transcend the ten stages of faith, the ten abidings, the ten practices, the ten transferences, the four stages of preparatory application, and the Bodhisattva’s practice of the ten adamantine grounds, as well as the perfect luminosity of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), entering the Tathāgata’s ocean of wondrous adornment. Thus, having perfected Bodhi, you shall return to the state of non-attainment.

"This is the *vipaśyanā* within *śamatha* of the past Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, who analyzed subtle demonic affairs through awakened clarity. When such demonic realms appear before you, you shall be able to recognize them; the defilements of the mind will be washed away so that you do not fall into false views. The *skandha-māras* will be extinguished and the *deva-māras* shattered; powerful spirits and ghosts will lose heart and flee, while *chi-mei* and *wang-liang* demons shall no longer arise. Until you reach Bodhi, you will lack nothing and will not regress to inferior states, nor will your mind become confused or distressed regarding Great Nirvana."

If there are sentient beings in the final age who are dull-witted and ignorant, who do not yet recognize *dhyāna* nor know how to preach the Dharma, yet delight in practicing *samādhi*, you should fear they may fall into heterodoxy; therefore, with a single mind, encourage them to uphold my Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Dhāraṇī mantra. If they are unable to recite it, have it written in their meditation hall or worn upon their bodies, and no demons whatsoever will be able to disturb them.
"You should reverently honor the Tathāgatas of the ten directions; this is the ultimate cultivation and progress, the final instruction left behind. Ānanda immediately rose from his seat;
having heard the Buddha’s instructions, he prostrated himself in reverence and received them, memorizing them without loss. Within the great assembly, he addressed the Buddha once more:

"As the Buddha has said, among the characteristics of the five aggregates, five kinds of delusion constitute the fundamental root of the mind. We have not previously received such subtle and detailed instruction from the Tathāgata regarding this. Furthermore, are these five aggregates to be eliminated all at once?"
Is it through successive exhaustion?
Regarding these five layers, what constitutes their boundary?
We pray that the Tathāgata will manifest great compassion, clarify the minds and eyes of this great assembly, and serve as the guiding eye for all sentient beings of the future age.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"The subtle, true, wondrous clarity of original enlightenment is perfectly pure; it does not harbor birth and death, nor any defilements, even up to empty space. All these arise solely from the production of deluded thoughts. This is originally the wondrously clear, true essence of original enlightenment, which through delusion gives rise to the various vessel-worlds, just as Yajñadatta lost his head in confusion and recognized only its reflection."

Delusion originally has no cause; yet within the realm of false conceptualization, one establishes the nature of causes and conditions. Those who are deluded regarding causes and conditions call it "spontaneity.
That very nature of space is itself produced like a real illusion; thus, both causes and conditions and spontaneity are merely the conceptual constructions of the deluded minds of sentient beings.
Ānanda! When one knows that delusion arises, one speaks of the causes and conditions of delusion;

if delusion were fundamentally non-existent, then even speaking of the causes and conditions of delusion would be fundamentally non-existent—how much more so for those who, lacking such knowledge, speculate that it is produced spontaneously?
Therefore, the Tathāgata has revealed to you that the fundamental cause of the five aggregates is likewise nothing but delusive thought.

Your body was originally produced from the thoughts of your parents; had your mind not been characterized by such thought, it could not have entered into this realm of thought to transmit life. As I previously said, when the mind thinks of the taste of vinegar, saliva arises in the mouth; when the mind thinks of climbing a high place, a tingling pain arises in the soles of the feet. Since the precipice does not exist here and the vinegar has not arrived, if your body were not of the same nature as these illusory phenomena, how could saliva flow forth simply because of speaking of vinegar?
Therefore, you should know that this present physical body of yours is called the first delusive thought, "solidity.

Furthermore, the mind of contemplation regarding heights that I have described is able to cause your form to truly experience a stinging sensation; because it arises from sensory reception, it can move the physical substance. Your current state, where you are driven by the two manifest conditions of benefit and harm, is called the second delusive thought, "empty clarity.

It is due to your thoughts and deliberations that your physical body is moved; yet the body is not of the same category as thought—by what cause does your body follow the dictates of thought to grasp various images? The mind gives rise to forms to correspond with thought; when awake, it is the mind of contemplation, and when asleep, it becomes various dreams. Thus, your thoughts and perceptions that cause the physical body to shake and move are called the third delusive thought, "interfusion."

The principle of transformation does not abide; it shifts and migrates in secret. Nails grow and hair sprouts, while vital energy wanes and the face wrinkles. Day and night they alternate, yet one never awakens to this. Ānanda!
If this is not you, how could its substance undergo transformation?
If it must be truly you, why do you have no awareness of it?
Thus, your various formations (saṃskāra) ceaselessly shifting from moment to moment is called the fourth subtle and hidden deluded thought.

Furthermore, regarding that which you call "constant"—the place where your essence is brilliant and profoundly still, unmoving—it does not depart from the body’s functions of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing. If this were truly an essential reality that could not tolerate the conditioning of delusion, for what reason did you once, in years past, behold a strange object? Though many years passed and there was neither recollection nor forgetting, when you later suddenly beheld that same former anomaly again, the memory was as vivid as ever, with nothing lost. Thus, within this brilliance, clarity, and profound stillness, how can one calculate the number of moments it has been permeated by conditioning?

Ānanda, you should know that this stillness is not the true reality. It is like a rapid current that appears tranquil from a distance; because the flow is so swift, it is not perceived, yet it is not that there is no flow at all. If this were not the source of perception, how could it receive the habit-energies of thought?
If your six sense organs do not function interchangeably, and you neither integrate nor open them, will this delusion ever be extinguished?

Therefore, within your current seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, that which has been habitually practiced for so long is a profound clarity that is internally insubstantial and void—a subtle, inverted, and refined conceptualization of the fifth [element].

“Ānanda! These five aggregates of clinging are formed through five kinds of false imagination. If you now wish to know the depth of their causal realms: only form and emptiness constitute the limit of form;
only contact and its cessation constitute the limit of feeling.”
Only recording and forgetting are the limits of perception;
only cessation and arising are the limits of volitional formations;
and the profound entry into the merging with the profound is the limit of consciousness.

These five aggregates originally arise in overlapping succession; their arising is due to the existence of consciousness, and their cessation begins with the elimination of form. In principle, they are suddenly awakened to and eliminated simultaneously with that awakening; in practice, however, they are not suddenly removed but are exhausted through gradual stages.
I have already shown you the knots of the *kārpāsa* cloth; what is it that you do not understand that you must inquire about again?

You should take this root of deluded thought and cause your mind to attain penetration, so that you may transmit it to all practitioners in the future age of the Dharma’s decay, enabling them to recognize the nature of falsehood, to develop a profound weariness with their own arising [of delusion], and to know that there is *nirvāṇa* such that they do not cling to the triple world.

“Ānanda! Suppose there were a person who filled the entirety of the ten directions with the seven treasures, making them so abundant as to fill all of space, and offered these to as many Buddhas as there are motes of dust, serving and making offerings to them with a mind that never for a moment grew weary.”
"What do you think? Based on the causes and conditions of this person’s gift to the Buddha, would they obtain much merit?
Ānanda replied: "Space is inexhaustible and precious jewels are boundless.

In the past, there were sentient beings who gave the Buddha seven coins; by relinquishing their bodies, they still attained the rank of a Wheel-Turning King. How much more so for one who, before the eyes of the Buddha, fills the entirety of space and all Buddha-lands with precious jewels—such that even contemplating it for an entire kalpa could not reach its limit. How could there be any boundary to such merit?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The words of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas are without falsehood.

Suppose there were a person who had committed the four grave offenses and the ten pārājika transgressions, such that in a mere instant they passed through the Avīci hells of this world and other worlds, eventually exhausting them and experiencing every one of the uninterrupted hells throughout the ten directions; yet, if with a single thought they could take up this Dharma-gate and reveal it to those who have not yet studied it during the final kalpa, that person’s karmic obstructions would be extinguished at that very moment. The causes for the suffering of the hells they were to undergo would be transformed into a Land of Peace and Bliss. The merit they would attain would surpass that of the previous donor by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten thousandfold, a hundred millionfold, and even beyond what can be reached by calculation or analogy."

Ānanda! If there are sentient beings who can recite this sutra and uphold this mantra—as I have explained at length, beyond the exhaustion of kalpas—and who follow my instructions and practice the Way according to the teaching, they will directly attain Bodhi without further demonic interference.

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās; all the devas, humans, asuras, and others from other worlds, including bodhisattvas, followers of the two vehicles, and holy seers; as well as the powerful spirits and ghosts who had first resolved their minds—all were filled with great joy, paid homage, and departed.
The Great Buddha-Usnīṣa Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ten Thousand Practices, Scroll Ten.
